items.text: משנת הפתיחה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a sukkah higher than twenty cubits is invalid, though Rabbi Yehuda validates it. It also lists other invalidating conditions: less than ten handbreadths high, lacking three walls, or having more sun than shade.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין סוכה גבוהה מעשרים אמה שהיא פסולה, ורבי יהודה מכשיר. בהמשך מובאים תנאים נוספים לפסול סוכה: גובהה פחות מעשרה טפחים, חוסר בשלוש דפנות, וחמתה מרובה מצילתה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a sukkah higher than twenty cubits is invalid, with Rabbi Yehuda validating it.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין סוכה גבוהה מעשרים אמה, שפסולה, ורבי יהודה חולק ומכשיר.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists additional invalidating conditions: less than ten handbreadths high, lacking three walls, or having more sun than shade.
sub.desc: המשנה מפרטת פסולים נוספים: סוכה נמוכה מעשרה טפחים, חסרת דפנות, או שחמתה מרובה מצילתה.

items.text: השוואת דין סוכה לדין מבוי
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the difference between sukkah and mavoi
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for a mavoi (alleyway) over twenty cubits, the remedy is to reduce its height, while for a sukkah it is outright invalid. It offers two answers: sukkah is Torah law, so it is invalid; mavoi is rabbinic, so a remedy suffices. Alternatively, even in Torah law a remedy is stated, but sukkah's many details lead to a definitive ruling.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע במשנת מבוי גבוה מעשרים אמה נאמר 'ימעט' (תקנתא), ואילו בסוכה נאמר 'פסולה'? התשובה הראשונה: סוכה דאורייתא, מבוי דרבנן. התשובה השנייה: גם בדאורייתא יש תקנתא, אך בסוכה שמרובה פרטיה פוסק וקובע 'פסולה', ובמבוי שאין בו פרטים רבים אומר 'תקנתא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a mavoi (alleyway) over twenty cubits, which requires reduction, with Rabbi Yehuda exempting it.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah rules a sukkah over twenty cubits invalid (פְּסוּלָה) but a mavoi over twenty cubits merely requires a remedy (תַּקַּנְתָּא).
The first answer distinguishes sukkah as Torah law (דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא) so it is invalid, while mavoi is rabbinic (דְּרַבָּנַן) so a remedy suffices.
The second answer offers an alternative: even in Torah law a remedy is stated, but sukkah's many details lead to a definitive ruling of invalidity, while mavoi's few details allow a remedy.

items.text: מקור הפסול מהפסוקים
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for the twenty-cubit limit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the twenty-cubit limit. Rabbah cites the verse about dwelling in sukkot, arguing that above twenty cubits one does not notice the sukkah. Rabbi Zeira cites a verse about shade, arguing that above twenty cubits the shade comes from the walls, not the roof.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מנין למדים דין זה? רבא מביא פסוק 'למען ידעו דורותיכם כי בסוכות הושבתי את בני ישראל', ומסביר: עד עשרים אמה אדם יודע שהוא דר בסוכה, למעלה מכן אינו יודע. רבי זירא מביא פסוק 'וסוכה תהיה לצל יומם מחורב', ומסביר: עד עשרים אמה אדם יושב בצל סוכה, למעלה מכן יושב בצל דפנות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the twenty-cubit limit.
Rabbah cites the verse 'לְמַעַן יֵדְעוּ דוֹרוֹתֵיכֶם כִּי בַסּוּכּוֹת הוֹשַׁבְתִּי' to argue that above twenty cubits one does not notice the sukkah.
Rabbi Zeira cites the verse 'וְסוּכָּה תִּהְיֶה לְצֵל יוֹמָם' to argue that above twenty cubits the shade comes from the walls, not the roof.

items.text: קושיית אביי על רבי זירא ותירוצו
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to Rabbi Zeira and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbi Zeira: if one builds a sukkah in the Ashtorot Karnayim valley (where walls are tall), would it be invalid? Rabbi Zeira responds that there, removing the walls still leaves sukkah shade; here, removing the walls leaves no sukkah shade.
items.desc: אביי מקשה על רבי זירא: אם הטעם הוא צל סוכה, הרי סוכה העשויה בעשתרות קרניים (מקום גבוה) אינה מוצלת מדפנות, ובכל זאת כשרה? רבי זירא משיב: בעשתרות קרניים, אם נסיר את הדפנות, עדיין יש צל סוכה (מהסכך), אבל כאן (בגובה מעל עשרים) אם נסיר את הדפנות, אין צל סוכה כלל.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rabbi Zeira's proof: if one builds a sukkah in the Ashtorot Karnayim valley (where walls are tall), would it also be invalid because the shade comes from the walls?
Rabbi Zeira resolves: there, removing the walls still leaves sukkah shade; here, removing the walls leaves no sukkah shade.

items.text: מקורו של רבא וקושיית אביי
items.text_en: Rava's alternative derivation and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rava derives the limit from the concept of temporary dwelling: up to twenty cubits one makes a temporary dwelling; above that, one makes a permanent dwelling. Abaye objects that even with iron walls, the sukkah should be valid. Rava clarifies that the issue is human nature: above twenty cubits, even if one tries to make a temporary dwelling, it is not considered a temporary dwelling.
items.desc: רבא מביא מקור אחר: 'בסוכות תשבו שבעת ימים' – צא מדירת קבע ושב בדירת עראי. עד עשרים אמה אדם עושה דירתו עראי, למעלה מכן עושה קבע. אביי מקשה: אם כך, סוכה עם מחיצות ברזל (דירת קבע) תיפסל? רבא מבהיר: הכוונה היא שכאשר אדם עושה דירת קבע בגובה נמוך, עדיין יוצא ידי חובה, אך בגובה רב, אפילו עושה עראי – לא יוצא.

sub.desc_en: Rava derives the height limit from the Torah's command to leave a permanent dwelling and sit in a temporary one, arguing that above twenty cubits one naturally makes a permanent dwelling.
sub.desc: רבא מביא מקור מהפסוק 'בסוכות תשבו' ומבסס את ההבחנה בין דירת עראי לדירת קבע לפי גובה הסוכה.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that if the issue is permanent construction, then even a sukkah with iron walls above twenty cubits should be invalid, which seems absurd.
sub.desc: אביי מקשה על רבא: אם הטעם הוא דירת עראי, הרי שאם עשה מחיצות ברזל וסכך על גביהן, האם גם זה לא ייחשב סוכה?

sub.desc_en: Rava clarifies that the criterion is human nature: below twenty cubits, even a permanent structure counts as a temporary dwelling; above twenty cubits, even if one tries to make a temporary dwelling, it is not considered one.
sub.desc: רבא מתרץ: עד עשרים אמה אדם עושה דירתו דירת עראי, ולכן אפילו עשה דירת קבע יוצא; למעלה מעשרים אמה אדם עושה דירתו דירת קבע, ולכן אפילו עשה דירת עראי לא יוצא.

items.text: דחיית שיטות רבא ורבי זירא
items.text_en: Rejection of Rava and Rabbi Zeira's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the other amora'im (Rava and Rabbi Zeira) do not accept each other's reasoning. Rava's proof from the verse about the cloud is rejected because it is a one-time event for the generations. Rabbi Zeira's proof from the verse about the sukkah is rejected because it teaches two things. Rava's position is also rejected due to Abaye's difficulty.
items.desc: הגמרא מסבירה מדוע רבא ורבי זירא אינם מקבלים את טעמי הצד שכנגד: רבא דוחה את טעם רבי זירא בטענה ש'ידיעה לדורות' אינה שייכת, ורבי זירא דוחה את טעם רבא בטענה שהפסוק מלמד שתי משמעויות. כמו כן, רבא דוחה את קושיית אביי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rava's position, explaining that his proof from the cloud is a one-time event for the generations.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בהסבר מדוע שאר החכמים אינם מקבלים את שיטת רבא, משום שהם רואים ב'ידיעה' האמורה בפסוק ידיעה לדורות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rabbi Zeira's position, explaining that his proof from the sukkah verse refers to the messianic era.
sub.desc: הגמרא מוסיפה שגם שיטת רבי זירא נדחית, משום שהפסוק מדבר על ימות המשיח.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara further rejects Rabbi Zeira's position, arguing that the verse teaches two things, not just one.
sub.desc: רבי זירא דוחה את טעם רבא בטענה שהפסוק מלמד שתי משמעויות, שהרי היה יכול לכתוב 'חופה' וכתב 'סוכה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rava's position due to Abaye's difficulty.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסיימת שגם שיטת רבא נדחית בגלל קושיית אביי.

items.text: שיוך דברי רבי יאשיה לשיטת רבא
items.text_en: Rabbi Yoshiya's statement attributed to Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rabbi Yoshiya's statement follows: that the dispute is only when the walls do not reach the roof, but if they do, even above twenty cubits it is valid. It answers that it follows Rava, who said the reason is that the eye does not dominate, and when walls reach the roof, the eye does dominate.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת לאיזה שיטה שייכת אמרתו של רבי יאשיה בשם רב, המחלקת בין סוכה שדפנותיה מגיעות לסכך לבין סוכה שאין דפנותיה מגיעות לסכך. היא משייכת אותה לשיטת רבא, שטעמו הוא 'משום דלא שלטא בה עינא', וכשהדפנות מגיעות לסכך – העין שולטת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rabbi Yoshiya's statement follows, which limits the dispute to when walls do not reach the roof.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת לאיזה חכם יש לשייך את דברי רבי יאשיה בשם רב המחלקים בין סוכה שדפנותיה מגיעות לסכך לבין סוכה שאין דפנותיה מגיעות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yoshiya's statement follows Rava, who holds the reason is that the eye does not dominate, and when walls reach the roof, the eye does dominate.
sub.desc: הגמרא משיבה שדברי רבי יאשיה תואמים את שיטת רבא, שטעמו לפסול סוכה גבוהה הוא משום שהעין אינה שולטת, וכשהדפנות מגיעות לסכך העין שולטת והסוכה כשרה.

items.text: שיוך דברי רב הונא לשיטת רבי זירא
items.text_en: Rav Huna's statement attributed to Rabbi Zeira
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rav Huna's statement follows: that the dispute is only when the sukkah is exactly four cubits by four cubits, but if larger, even above twenty cubits it is valid. It answers that it follows Rabbi Zeira, who said the reason is shade, and since it is spacious, there is sukkah shade.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת לאיזה שיטה שייכת אמרתו של רב הונא בשם רב, המחלקת בין סוכה של ארבע אמות על ארבע אמות לבין סוכה גדולה יותר. היא משייכת אותה לשיטת רבי זירא, שטעמו הוא 'משום צל', ובסוכה גדולה יש צל סוכה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rav Huna's statement follows: that the dispute is only when the sukkah is exactly four cubits by four cubits, but if larger, even above twenty cubits it is valid.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת לאיזה שיטה שייכת אמרתו של רב הונא בשם רב המחלקת בין סוכה קטנה לגדולה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rav Huna's statement follows Rabbi Zeira, who said the reason is shade, and since it is spacious, there is sukkah shade.
sub.desc: הגמרא משייכת את דברי רב הונא לשיטת רבי זירא, שטעמו הוא משום צל, ובסוכה גדולה יש צל סוכה.

items.text: שיוך דברי רב חנן בר רבה – דלא כחד
items.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rabbah's statement unattributed
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rav Chanan bar Rabbah's statement follows: that the dispute is only when the sukkah holds only his head, most of his body, and his table, but if larger, even above twenty cubits it is valid. It concludes that it follows no one (i.e., it is a unique position).
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת לאיזה שיטה שייכת אמרתו של רב חנן בר רבה בשם רב, המחלקת בין סוכה המחזקת ראשו ורובו ושולחנו לבין סוכה גדולה יותר. היא קובעת שדבריו אינם תואמים לאף אחת מהשיטות הקודמות ('דלא כחד').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rav Chanan bar Rabbah's statement follows.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת לאיזה שיטה שייכת אמרתו של רב חנן בר רבה בשם רב, וקובעת שאינה תואמת לאף אחת מהשיטות הקודמות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rav Chanan bar Rabbah's statement follows no one, i.e., it is a unique position.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת לאיזה שיטה שייכת אמרתו של רב חנן בר רבה בשם רב, וקובעת שאינה תואמת לאף אחת מהשיטות הקודמות.

items.text: בירור המחלוקת בין רב הונא לרב חנן בר רבה
items.text_en: Analysis of the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chanan bar Rabbah
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yoshiya disagrees with Rav Huna and Rav Chanan bar Rabbah because he does not give a size limit in length, while they do. It then asks whether Rav Huna and Rav Chanan bar Rabbah disagree about the minimum valid size of a sukkah. It answers that all agree the minimum is head, most of body, and table; they disagree about the scope of the original dispute: one says the dispute is only up to that size, the other says it extends up to four cubits.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת את היחס בין שיטות רב הונא ורב חנן בר רבה. היא דוחה את האפשרות שהם חלוקים בשיעור הכשר סוכה, וקובעת שכולם מודים שהכשר סוכה הוא ראשו ורובו ושולחנו. המחלוקת היא על גודל הסוכה שבה נחלקו התנאים: רב הונא סובר שהמחלוקת היא בסוכה המחזקת ראשו ורובו ושולחנו, אבל יותר מכך – דברי הכל כשרה; רב חנן בר רבה סובר שהמחלוקת היא מראשו ורובו ועד ארבע אמות, אבל יותר מארבע אמות – דברי הכל כשרה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yoshiya disagrees with Rav Huna and Rav Chanan bar Rabbah because he does not give a size limit in length, while they do.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בבירור המחלוקת: רבי יאשיה חלוק על רב הונא ורב חנן בר רבה בכך שהם נותנים שיעור במשך הסוכה והוא אינו נותן שיעור במשך.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav Huna and Rav Chanan bar Rabbah disagree about the minimum valid size of a sukkah.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם רב הונא ורב חנן בר רבה חלוקים בשיעור הכשר סוכה עצמו – האחד סובר הכשר סוכה בארבע אמות והשני בראשו ורובו ושולחנו?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that all agree the minimum is head, most of body, and table; they disagree about the scope of the original dispute: one says the dispute is only up to that size, the other says it extends up to four cubits.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את האפשרות הזו וקובעת שכולם מודים שהכשר סוכה הוא ראשו ורובו ושולחנו, והמחלוקת היא על גודל הסוכה שבה נחלקו התנאים: רב הונא סובר שהמחלוקת היא בסוכה המחזקת ראשו ורובו ושולחנו, אבל יותר מכך – דברי הכל כשרה.

items.text: הבאת ברייתא ודחיית הראיה ממעשה הילני המלכה
items.text_en: Baraita about Queen Helene's sukkah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: a sukkah over twenty cubits is invalid, but Rabbi Yehudah validates up to forty or fifty cubits. Rabbi Yehudah brings a precedent of Queen Helene's sukkah in Lod, which was over twenty cubits, and the elders did not object. The Sages reject this proof because she was a woman exempt from sukkah. Rabbi Yehudah responds that she had seven sons, and all her actions were by rabbinic instruction. The Gemara explains the need for the extra statement: to counter the claim that her sons were minors exempt from sukkah, and that she might not heed rabbinic law.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה סוכה גבוהה מעשרים אמה נפסלת, ורבי יהודה מכשיר עד ארבעים וחמשים אמה, ומביא מעשה בהילני המלכה בלוד שסוכתה היתה גבוהה מעשרים אמה והזקנים לא מיחו בידה. חכמים דוחים את הראיה בטענה שהיתה אשה ופטורה מן הסוכה. רבי יהודה משיב שהיו לה שבעה בנים, ועוד שכל מעשיה נעשו על פי חכמים. הגמרא מבארת את הצורך בתוספת 'ועוד': למנוע את הטענה שהבנים היו קטנים ופטורים, או שהיא לא חששה לחיוב דרבנן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that a sukkah over twenty cubits is invalid, but Rabbi Yehudah validates up to forty or fifty cubits.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא הסותרת לכאורה את הדעה הקודמת, ובה סוכה גבוהה מעשרים אמה פסולה ורבי יהודה מכשיר עד ארבעים וחמישים אמה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehudah brings a precedent of Queen Helene's sukkah in Lod, which was over twenty cubits, and the elders did not object.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מביא מעשה בהילני המלכה בלוד שסוכתה היתה גבוהה מעשרים אמה והזקנים לא מיחו בידה, כראיה לדבריו.

sub.desc_en: The Sages reject the proof because Queen Helene was a woman exempt from the mitzvah of sukkah.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מביא מעשה בהילני המלכה בלוד שסוכתה היתה גבוהה מעשרים אמה והזקנים לא מיחו בידה, כראיה לדבריו.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehudah responds that Queen Helene had seven sons, and all her actions were by rabbinic instruction.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מביא מעשה בהילני המלכה בלוד שסוכתה היתה גבוהה מעשרים אמה והזקנים לא מיחו בידה, כראיה לדבריו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita needed to add the extra statement 'and all her actions were by rabbinic instruction'.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מביא מעשה בהילני המלכה בלוד שסוכתה היתה גבוהה מעשרים אמה והזקנים לא מיחו בידה, כראיה לדבריו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehudah anticipated the objection that her sons were minors exempt from sukkah, and countered that among seven sons, at least one was likely old enough not to need his mother.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מביא מעשה בהילני המלכה בלוד שסוכתה היתה גבוהה מעשרים אמה והזקנים לא מיחו בידה, כראיה לדבריו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara further explains that Rabbi Yehudah also anticipated the objection that even a minor who does not need his mother is only rabbinically obligated, and Queen Helene might not heed rabbinic law; therefore the baraita adds that she acted only by rabbinic instruction.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מביא מעשה בהילני המלכה בלוד שסוכתה היתה גבוהה מעשרים אמה והזקנים לא מיחו בידה, כראיה לדבריו.

items.text: תחילת דיון על דפנות סוכתה של הילני
items.text_en: Reconciliation with Rabbi Yoshiya's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the opinion that the dispute is when walls do not reach the roof, it is fitting for a queen to sit in such a sukkah, implying that Queen Helene's sukkah had walls not reaching the roof, thus not contradicting the Sages' position.
items.desc: הגמרא מתחילה להסביר כיצד מעשה הילני מתיישב עם שיטת רבא, האומרת שהמחלוקת היא דווקא בסוכה שאין דפנותיה מגיעות לסכך, שכן דרכה של מלכה לשבת בסוכה כזו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the baraita adds the phrase 'עוד (furthermore) all her actions were only according to the Sages'.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע יש צורך להוסיף במשנה את הביטוי 'ועוד כל מעשיה לא עשתה אלא על פי חכמים'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda is anticipating an objection: the children might have been small and exempt, but with seven children it is impossible that none was independent of his mother.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהמשנה באה לסתור טענה אפשרית שהבנים היו קטנים ופטורים, שכן בן שבע אינו צריך לאמו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara further explains that Rabbi Yehuda counters a second objection: even if one argues that a child independent of his mother is only rabbinically obligated and the queen might disregard rabbinic law, the phrase 'עוד (furthermore)' shows she acted on the Sages' authority.
sub.desc: הגמרא מעלה השגה אפשרית: שמא חובת קטן שאינו צריך לאמו היא מדרבנן, והמלכה לא חששה לדרבנן, ולכן המשנה מוסיפה 'ועוד' לראיה שהיא נהגה על פי חכמים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that according to Rabbi Yoshiya's view that the dispute is when walls do not reach the roof, Queen Helene's sukkah fits that description, so the baraita does not contradict the Sages.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ראיה לשיטת רבא, האומר שהמחלוקת היא בסוכה שאין דפנותיה מגיעות לסכך, שכן דרכה של מלכה לשבת בסוכה כזו.

items.text: Refining the dispute: small sukkah vs. partitioned sukkah
items.text_en: Refining the dispute: small sukkah vs. partitioned sukkah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a queen would sit in a small sukkah, leading to an explanation that the sukkah was made of small compartments. Rav Ashi further clarifies that the queen sat in the compartments themselves, not the main sukkah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a queen would sit in a small sukkah, given the earlier explanation about airspace.
Rabbah bar Rav Adda answers that the sukkah was made of small compartments (קיטוניות).
The Gemara questions whether a queen would sit in a sukkah made of small compartments.
Rav Ashi clarifies that the queen sat in the compartments themselves, not the main sukkah.

items.text: Explaining the silence of the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Explaining the silence of the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda did not object to the queen's sukkah: the Sages thought her children were in a proper sukkah while she sat in compartments for modesty, and Rabbi Yehuda thought her children were with her, yet still no objection was raised.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the Sages' position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Sages' position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages thought the queen's children were in a proper sukkah (סוכה מעליא) while she sat in compartments for modesty (צניעותא), so they did not object.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda thought the queen's children were with her in the compartments, yet still no objection was raised.

items.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak's ruling and Rabbi Abba's challenge
items.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak's ruling and Rabbi Abba's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak rules that a sukkah must hold one's head, most of his body, and his table. Rabbi Abba questions whether this follows Beit Shammai, and Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak affirms it. An alternative version has Rabbi Abba asserting that the ruling is indeed Beit Shammai's and should not be deviated from.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak rules that a sukkah (סוכה) must hold one's head, most of his body, and his table.
Rabbi Abba asks Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak whether his ruling follows Beit Shammai (בית שמאי).
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak responds rhetorically, implying that the ruling indeed follows Beit Shammai.
An alternative version has Rabbi Abba asserting that the ruling is indeed Beit Shammai's and should not be deviated from.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's objection: perhaps the dispute is about a large sukkah
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's objection: perhaps the dispute is about a large sukkah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges the assumption that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argue about a small sukkah, suggesting they might argue about a large sukkah where one sits at the entrance and his table is inside the house. Beit Shammai fears he will be drawn after his table, while Beit Hillel does not. He supports this from the mishnah's wording, which implies a case where the sukkah is large enough to hold the person but not the table.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel might be about a large sukkah where one sits at the entrance and his table is inside the house, with Beit Shammai fearing he will be drawn after his table and Beit Hillel not fearing this.

The gemara supports Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's objection by noting that the mishnah's wording (describing a person with his head and most of his body in the sukkah and his table in the house) implies a large sukkah, because if it were a small sukkah the mishnah should have said 'a sukkah that holds and does not hold'.

items.text: Contradictory baraitot about the minimum size
items.text_en: Contradictory baraitot about the minimum size
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two baraitot: one states that a sukkah holding head, most of the body, and table is valid, while Rabbi requires four by four cubits. Another baraita states Rabbi requires four cubits, while the Sages say even holding only head and most of the body is valid, omitting the table. These appear contradictory, but the Gemara resolves that the first follows Beit Shammai and the second Beit Hillel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel do not dispute regarding a small sukkah, citing a baraita that validates a sukkah holding head, most of the body, and table.
The first baraita records Rabbi's position that a sukkah must be four by four cubits.
The second baraita repeats Rabbi's requirement of four cubits, while the Sages validate a sukkah holding only head and most of the body, omitting the table.
The Gemara notes that the second baraita omits the table requirement, making the two baraitot contradictory.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by concluding that the first baraita follows Beit Shammai and the second follows Beit Hillel.

items.text: Mar Zutra's proof and resolution of the mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's proof and resolution of the mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra proves from the mishnah's language that it discusses a small sukkah, as it uses 'poslin' and 'machshirin' rather than 'lo yatza' and 'yatza'. The Gemara then resolves the difficulty by explaining that the mishnah is missing a clause: it actually discusses both cases—a large sukkah where the table is in the house (using 'lo yatza'/'yatza') and a small sukkah that doesn't hold the table (using 'poslin'/'machshirin').

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra argues that the mishnah's language (using 'פוסלין' and 'מכשירין' rather than 'לא יצא' and 'יצא') proves it discusses a small sukkah.
The Gemara objects that the mishnah's wording 'מי שהיה' (one whose head and most of his body were) still seems to refer to a person's position, not the sukkah's size.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by explaining that the mishnah is incomplete and actually discusses both cases: a large sukkah (using 'לא יצא'/'יצא') and a small sukkah (using 'פוסלין'/'מכשירין').

items.text: Baraita about a house less than four cubits
items.text_en: Baraita about a house less than four cubits
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing the halakhot of a house that is less than four cubits by four cubits: it is exempt from mezuzah, ma'akeh, and various other laws, and cannot be used for eiruv or shituf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Who is the tanna who taught the baraita about a house less than four cubits?

The baraita lists the halakhot of a house less than four cubits: exempt from מזוזה (mezuzah), מעשה (parapet), טומאת נגעים (leprosy impurity), and various other laws, and it cannot be used for עירוב (eiruv) or שיתוף (shituf).

items.text: Clarifying the Tanna's identity regarding the sukkah's status
items.text_en: Clarifying the Tanna's identity regarding the sukkah's status
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the ruling that a sukkah of less than four cubits is exempt from certain laws follows Rabbi Yehuda or the Rabbis. It explains that even the Rabbis would agree that for a permanent house, four cubits are required, but for a temporary sukkah, they are more lenient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the mishnah's ruling that a sukkah of less than four cubits is exempt from certain laws follows Rabbi Yehuda's position or the Rabbis'.
The Gemara answers that even the Rabbis would agree that for a permanent house (בית), four cubits are required for dwelling, but for a temporary sukkah (סוכה), they are more lenient.

items.text: Listing exemptions for a small sukkah
items.text_en: Listing exemptions for a small sukkah
items.desc_en: The Gemara enumerates the exemptions that apply to a sukkah lacking four cubits: it is exempt from mezuzah, ma'akeh, impurity of leprosy, the laws of a walled city, and returning soldiers from war, all because the Torah uses the term 'house' for these laws.

sub.desc_en: Mar lists the exemptions that apply to a sukkah lacking four cubits, explaining that all these laws require the term 'house' (בית).

items.text: Eiruv and shituf in a small sukkah
items.text_en: Eiruv and shituf in a small sukkah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that one may not place an eiruv chatzeirot in such a sukkah, but one may place a shituf mavo'ot there. The reason is that it is not inferior to a courtyard in an alleyway, where shituf is placed in the courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one may not place an eiruv chatzeirot or a shituf mavo'ot in a small sukkah, nor deposit an eiruv there.
The Gemara explains the reason: the sukkah is not fit for permanent dwelling.
The Gemara distinguishes: one may not place an eiruv chatzeirot in the sukkah, but one may place a shituf mavo'ot there.

The Gemara supports the distinction by citing a baraita: eiruv chatzeirot is placed in the courtyard, while shituf mavo'ot is placed in the alleyway, so the sukkah is not inferior to a courtyard in an alleyway.

items.text: Resolving a contradiction about eiruv chatzeirot
items.text_en: Resolving a contradiction about eiruv chatzeirot
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier statement that eiruv chatzeirot is placed in a courtyard, citing a mishnah that it must be in a house. It resolves by rephrasing: eiruv chatzeirot is placed in a house in the courtyard, and shitufei mavo'ot in a courtyard in the alleyway.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the statement that eiruv chatzeirot is placed in a courtyard, citing a mishnah that requires it to be placed in a house.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by rephrasing: eiruv chatzeirot is placed in a house in the courtyard, and shitufei mavo'ot in a courtyard in the alleyway.

items.text: Not used for extending city boundaries
items.text_en: Not used for extending city boundaries
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that such a sukkah cannot be used to extend the city limits for Shabbat, as it is not even fit for watchmen's huts (burgnin), which are suitable for their purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a sukkah smaller than 4x4 cubits cannot be used to extend city boundaries for Shabbat, because it is not even fit for watchmen's huts (בורגנין), which are suitable for their purpose.

items.text: Division of property among brothers and partners
items.text_en: Division of property among brothers and partners
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses that a sukkah of less than four cubits cannot be divided, but if it had four cubits, it could be divided. It then addresses a contradiction from a mishnah requiring eight cubits for division, resolving that the sukkah lacks the law of division like a courtyard, citing Rav Huna and Rav Chisda's opinions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a sukkah smaller than four cubits cannot be divided among brothers or partners, implying that if it had four cubits, they could divide it.

The Gemara objects by citing a mishnah that a courtyard cannot be divided unless each party receives at least four cubits, implying a minimum of eight cubits total, contradicting the sukkah's four-cubit threshold.

The Gemara resolves that the sukkah lacks the law of division like a courtyard, citing Rav Huna's opinion that a courtyard is divided according to its entrances and Rav Chisda's opinion that each entrance gets four cubits and the rest is divided equally.
The Gemara explains that for a permanent house (בית), which stands to remain, we allocate a courtyard, but for a sukkah, which stands to be dismantled, we do not allocate a courtyard.

items.text: Reducing height with pillows and bedding
items.text_en: Reducing height with pillows and bedding
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if a sukkah is higher than twenty cubits and one comes to reduce its height with pillows and bedding, it is not considered a valid reduction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that reducing a sukkah's height with pillows and bedding is not a valid reduction.

items.text: The status of straw and dirt as nullified filler
items.text_en: The status of straw and dirt as nullified filler
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether straw or dirt that has been nullified (batel) counts as a valid partition. It cites a Tosefta where Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between straw that will not be removed (treated like dirt, nullified) and dirt that will be removed (treated like straw, not nullified).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether straw or dirt that has been nullified (בטל) can serve as a valid partition, since the owner's intent is nullified in everyone's eyes.
The Gemara answers that straw that has been nullified is considered a minimal partition (מיעוט), and all the more so dirt that has been nullified.

The Gemara cites a Tosefta where the Tanna Kamma rules that straw or pebbles filled in a house and nullified are void, and Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: straw not to be removed is like ordinary dirt and nullified, while dirt to be removed is like ordinary straw and not nullified.

items.text: Branches descending into the valid space
items.text_en: Branches descending into the valid space
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's case of a sukkah higher than 20 cubits with branches descending into the valid height is examined. Abaye thought that if the shade from the branches is greater than the sunlight, it is valid, but Rava objects that this is a 'disgusting dwelling' (dirah seruchah) and invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case of a sukkah higher than 20 cubits with branches descending into the valid height, ruling that if the branches' shade exceeds their sunlight it is valid, otherwise invalid.
Abaye thought to apply the same logic to a low sukkah (10 handbreadths) with branches descending into the valid space, ruling that if sunlight exceeds shade it is valid.
Rava objects that such a sukkah is a 'disgusting dwelling' (דירה סרוחה) and therefore invalid, regardless of the shade-sunlight ratio.

items.text: Platform built along the middle wall
items.text_en: Platform built along the middle wall
items.desc_en: If a sukkah is too high and a platform (itzteva) is built along the entire middle wall, it is valid. From the side, if the platform is within 4 cubits of the wall, it is valid due to the principle of 'dofen akumah' (bent wall). The Gemara clarifies that this teaching is necessary even though a similar case was taught, because here the platform is not visible as a wall.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a sukkah is too high and a platform is built along the entire middle wall, it is valid.
The Mishnah adds that from the side, if the platform is within 4 cubits of the wall, it is valid due to the principle of 'דופן עקומה (bent wall)'.
The Gemara questions what novel teaching this provides, since the principle of 'דופן עקומה (bent wall)' was already taught in a mishna about a breached house.
The Gemara explains that the novel element is that here the wall is not visible as a wall due to its height, yet the principle still applies.

items.text: Platform in the center of the sukkah
items.text_en: Platform in the center of the sukkah
items.desc_en: If a platform is built in the center of the sukkah, the same rule applies: if the distance from the platform's edge to the wall is less than 4 cubits on each side, it is valid via 'dofen akumah'. The Gemara notes that this case teaches that the principle applies to all four directions, not just one.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a platform built in the center of a sukkah higher than 20 cubits: if the distance from the platform's edge to the wall is 4 cubits on each side, it is invalid; less than that, it is valid.
The Gemara asks what novel point this case teaches, since the principle of דופן עקומה (curved wall) was already established.
The Gemara answers that this case teaches that the principle of דופן עקומה (curved wall) applies in all four directions, not just one.

items.text: Digging to complete the height
items.text_en: Digging to complete the height
items.desc_en: If a sukkah is less than 10 handbreadths high and one digs to complete the height, the sukkah is invalid if the distance from the edge of the dug area to the wall is 3 handbreadths or more.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a sukkah is less than 10 handbreadths high and one digs to complete the height, the sukkah is invalid if the distance from the edge of the dug area to the wall is 3 handbreadths or more.

items.text: Minimum wall height for sukkah
items.text_en: Minimum wall height for sukkah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the threshold for a valid sukkah wall is less than three handbreadths, while for a courtyard partition it is less than four cubits. It answers that in the courtyard case the wall already exists, so a gap of less than four cubits suffices; here, the wall must be created, so less than three handbreadths is required, otherwise it is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a sukkah with walls less than three handbreadths high is valid.
The Gemara asks why the threshold for a valid sukkah wall is less than three handbreadths, while for a courtyard partition it is less than four cubits.

The Gemara answers that in the courtyard case the wall already exists, so a gap of less than four cubits suffices; here, the wall must be created, so less than three handbreadths is required, otherwise it is invalid.

items.text: Abaye and Rava on גוד אסיק מחיצתא
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava on גוד אסיק מחיצתא
items.desc_en: Abaye thought that if a sukkah is too tall (over twenty cubits) and one builds a ten-handbreadth pillar inside, the principle of גוד אסיק מחיצתא (extend the wall upward) would validate it. Rava rejected this, arguing that the walls must be visible (מחיצות הניכרות), which they are not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes that if a sukkah is over twenty cubits high and one builds a ten-handbreadth pillar inside, we apply the principle of גוד אסיק מחיצתא (extend the partition upward) to validate it.
Rava objects that we require recognizable partitions, and here there are none.
Rava rejected Abaye's position, arguing that the walls must be visible (מחיצות הניכרות), which they are not.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yaakov and Sages on four poles
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yaakov and Sages on four poles
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if one drove four poles and placed s'chach on top, Rabbi Yaakov validates it (using גוד אסיק מחיצתא) while the Sages invalidate. Rav Huna explains that the dispute is only when the poles are at the edge of the roof; in the middle, all agree it is invalid. Rav Nachman argues that even in the middle there is a dispute.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who drove four poles and placed סכך (roofing) on top — Rabbi Yaakov validates it and the Sages invalidate it.
Rav Huna explains that the dispute is only at the edge of the roof, but in the middle all agree it is invalid; Rav Nachman says the dispute is in the middle.
Rav Nachman objects, asserting that even in the middle of the roof there is a dispute.

items.text: Unresolved question about the dispute's scope
items.text_en: Unresolved question about the dispute's scope
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: Is the dispute only in the middle of the roof, with the edge universally valid, or does the dispute apply to both locations? It concludes with תיקו (let it stand unresolved).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question: is the dispute in the middle of the roof, with the edge universally valid, or is there a dispute in both cases?

items.text: Refutation of Rav Huna from a baraita
items.text_en: Refutation of Rav Huna from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita about poles driven into the ground (like the middle of a roof) shows Rabbi Yaakov validates it, contradicting Rav Huna's claim that in the middle all agree it is invalid. This is a refutation of Rav Huna. Additionally, the baraita implies that only in the middle is there a dispute, but at the edge all agree it is valid, which also refutes Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites a baraita about poles driven into the ground with a sukkah on top, where Rabbi Yaakov validates and the Sages invalidate.
The gemara objects that the ground is like the middle of a roof, yet Rabbi Yaakov validates it, which refutes Rav Huna's claim that in the middle all agree it is invalid.
The gemara adds a second objection: the baraita implies that only in the middle is there a dispute, but at the edge all agree it is valid, which also refutes Rav Huna's position.

items.text: Rav Huna's defense
items.text_en: Rav Huna's defense
items.desc_en: Rav Huna responds that the dispute actually applies to both the middle and the edge of the roof; the baraita specifically mentions the middle to show the strength of Rabbi Yaakov's opinion, that he validates even in the middle.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna responds that the dispute applies equally to the middle and the edge, and the baraita specifies the middle only to show the strength of Rabbi Yaakov's position.

items.text: Baraita with Rabbi Yaakov's reasoning
items.text_en: Baraita with Rabbi Yaakov's reasoning
items.desc_en: Another baraita elaborates: Rabbi Yaakov says we consider the poles as if they are carved and divided, and if there is a handbreadth on each side, they are treated as דיומד (a corner post). The Sages require two proper walls and a third even a handbreadth.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited detailing Rabbi Yaakov's opinion that we apply the principle of דיומד (a corner post) if there is a handbreadth on each side, and the Sages require two proper walls and a third even a handbreadth.

items.text: Source for minimum height of ten handbreadths
items.text_en: Source for minimum height of ten handbreadths
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a sukkah must be at least ten handbreadths high. It cites a tradition from Rav, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Chaviva (with a note about a variant name). The proof comes from the Ark (nine handbreadths) plus the cover (one handbreadth) totaling ten, as per the verse 'and I will meet with you there from above the cover'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a sukkah must be at least ten handbreadths high?
The Gemara notes that Rav, Rabbi Chanina, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rav Chaviva transmitted this tradition.
The Gemara notes a pattern: throughout Seder Moed, whenever this pair appears, they substitute Rabbi Yochanan with Rabbi Yonatan.

The Gemara answers by citing a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): the Ark was nine handbreadths and the cover one handbreadth, totaling ten, and the verse says 'I will meet with you there and speak with you from above the cover.'

items.text: Opening Mishnah/Baraitha: Rabbi Yosei's statement on Shekhinah never descending below ten handbreadths
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah/Baraitha: Rabbi Yosei's statement on Shekhinah never descending below ten handbreadths
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei asserts that the Shekhinah never descended below ten handbreadths from the earth, and Moses and Elijah never ascended above ten handbreadths, citing verses. The Gemara questions this with counterexamples.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yosei's statement that the Shekhinah never descended below ten handbreadths and Moses and Elijah never ascended above ten handbreadths, supported by a verse.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Did Shekhinah descend? Counterexample from Sinai
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Did Shekhinah descend? Counterexample from Sinai
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei with the verse 'And the Lord descended on Mount Sinai' — but explains that this was above ten handbreadths, as the mountain is high.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yosei's statement that the Divine Presence never descended below, citing the verse 'וַיֵּרֶד ה׳ עַל הַר סִינַי' (And the Lord descended on Mount Sinai), and answers that it was above ten handbreadths.
The Gemara resolves that these descents were only to a point above ten handbreadths, not to the ground itself, preserving the principle that the Divine Presence remains above ten handbreadths.

items.text: Second counterexample: Elijah's ascent and the verse about the chariot
items.text_en: Second counterexample: Elijah's ascent and the verse about the chariot
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites 'And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven' and 'He holds the face of His throne and spreads His cloud over it' — but explains these are above ten handbreadths, as the throne is high.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Did Moses and Elijah not ascend to heaven? It cites the verse 'וַיַּעַל אֵלִיָּהוּ בַּסְעָרָה הַשָּׁמָיִם' (And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven) and the verse 'מְאַחֵז פְּנֵי כִּסֵּא' (He holds the face of His throne) with Rabbi Tanchum's explanation, and answers that they remained below ten handbreadths.
The Gemara answers that these ascents reached only to a point below ten handbreadths from the divine realm, not into the heavenly heights itself.

items.text: Third counterexample: The verse 'He holds the face of His throne' and the deduction that the throne is above ten handbreadths
items.text_en: Third counterexample: The verse 'He holds the face of His throne' and the deduction that the throne is above ten handbreadths
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse 'He holds the face of His throne' implies the throne is above ten handbreadths, and Rabbi Tanchum explains that God spread His cloud over it, still above ten.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'He holds the face of His throne' implies the throne is above ten handbreadths, and answers that the throne was extended down to ten handbreadths for Moses to grasp.
The Gemara rejects the objection by explaining that the throne was extended down to ten handbreadths, and Moses grasped it there, but he himself remained below ten handbreadths.

items.text: Gemara's deduction: The ark's dimensions and the cherubim's height
items.text_en: Gemara's deduction: The ark's dimensions and the cherubim's height
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates that the ark (aron) was 2.5 cubits long, 1.5 wide, 1.5 high, and the kaporet (cover) was one handbreadth thick. The cherubim stood on the kaporet, so their faces were above ten handbreadths from the ground.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the ark's height is nine handbreadths, citing the verse that gives its dimensions.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that the kaporet (cover) was one handbreadth thick?
The Gemara cites a baraita of Rabbi Chanina that for all vessels the Torah gave dimensions, but for the kaporet it did not give the height.

items.text: Deduction of kaporet thickness from the menorah's base
items.text_en: Deduction of kaporet thickness from the menorah's base
items.desc_en: The Gemara learns the kaporet's thickness (one handbreadth) from the menorah's base (also one handbreadth), using the principle 'learn from the smallest vessel' and the verse about the base.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the derivation of the Ark cover's thickness by learning from the smallest vessel (the table's border of one handbreadth) and applying the principle that grasping the smaller measure is valid.

The Gemara objects that one could derive the thickness from the vessels themselves, which have a minimum dimension of a cubit, and the answer is that if one grasps many one grasps nothing, but if one grasps few one grasps something — so the smaller measure is preferred.

items.text: Alternative deduction from the tzitz (frontlet)
items.text_en: Alternative deduction from the tzitz (frontlet)
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers learning from the tzitz (gold plate on the high priest's forehead), which is two fingerbreadths wide and has two lines of writing, but rejects because the tzitz is an adornment (tachshit), not a vessel (kli).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes deriving the thickness of the Ark cover from the tzitz (frontlet), which is only two fingerbreadths wide, citing a baraita that describes the tzitz as a gold plate two fingerbreadths wide with two lines of writing.
Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Yosei testifies that he saw the tzitz in Rome and it had the inscription 'קדש לה׳' (Sacred to the Lord) on a single line, supporting the description of the tzitz's dimensions.
The Gemara answers that one derives the dimension of a vessel from a vessel, not from an ornament, and the frontplate is an ornament of the High Priest, not a vessel.

items.text: Principle: Vessels are deduced from vessels, not from adornments
items.text_en: Principle: Vessels are deduced from vessels, not from adornments
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the rule: 'We deduce a vessel from a vessel, and we do not deduce a vessel from an adornment.' The tzitz is an adornment, so it cannot teach about the kaporet (a vessel).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that one may derive the dimension of a vessel from another vessel but not from an adornment, thereby rejecting the derivation from the frontplate (ציץ).
The Gemara answers that one derives a vessel from a vessel, not from the finish of a vessel, and the crown is a decorative finish.

items.text: Attempt to learn from the zer (crown) and the misgeret (rim)
items.text_en: Attempt to learn from the zer (crown) and the misgeret (rim)
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to learn from the zer (crown of the ark) which is 'something' (mashshehu), but the rule says 'deduce a vessel from a vessel, not a vessel from a vessel's accessory'. The misgeret (rim) is an accessory, so rejected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests deriving the thickness of the Ark cover from the crown (זֵר), but notes that the rule is to derive a vessel from a vessel, not a vessel from a vessel's accessory.
The Gemara objects that the border (מִסְגֶּרֶת) of the table is also an accessory, yet it was used to derive the thickness; the answer is that the border was below, making it integral.

items.text: Dispute on misgeret position: below vs above — both are vessel accessories
items.text_en: Dispute on misgeret position: below vs above — both are vessel accessories
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a dispute: some say the misgeret was below (making it a vessel accessory), others say above (making it a vessel itself). If above, it qualifies as a vessel, but the deduction from the menorah's base still stands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to the opinion that the border was above the tabletop, the border is merely a vessel accessory, so the derivation from it is invalid.
The Gemara answers that the derivation is from a vessel to a vessel, not from a vessel to an ornament, so the border above is still a vessel part, not an ornament.

items.text: Final ruling: Deduce from a thing that Torah gave a measure, not from tzitz or zer
items.text_en: Final ruling: Deduce from a thing that Torah gave a measure, not from tzitz or zer
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: 'We deduce a thing that Torah gave a measure from a thing that Torah gave a measure, and we do not deduce from tzitz or zer, which Torah did not give a measure.' The kaporet's thickness is thus one handbreadth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the thickness of the Ark cover is derived from a vessel whose dimensions the Torah specified, not from the frontplate or crown, which lack any specified dimension.

The Gemara answers: Rather, one derives the dimension of a vessel from a vessel whose dimensions were specified, and the frontplate and crown, whose dimensions were not specified, will not prove anything.

items.text: Rav Huna's alternative: Learn from the verse 'on the face of the kaporet eastward'
items.text_en: Rav Huna's alternative: Learn from the verse 'on the face of the kaporet eastward'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna cites the verse 'on the face of the kaporet eastward' to argue that 'face' implies at least one handbreadth, so the kaporet's thickness is one handbreadth. The Gemara questions this logic.

sub.desc_en: רב הונא (Rav Huna) offers an alternative derivation from the verse 'על פני הכפרת קדמה' (upon the face of the Ark cover eastward), arguing that 'face' implies at least one handbreadth, so the Ark cover's thickness is one handbreadth.

items.text: Gemara's objection: 'Face' could mean the surface, not a minimum thickness
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: 'Face' could mean the surface, not a minimum thickness
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: 'Face' (panim) might refer to the surface area, not a dimensional minimum. The phrase 'on the face of the kaporet' could mean 'on top of' it, not requiring a handbreadth thickness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Perhaps 'face' (פני) means the surface, not a dimensional minimum; the phrase 'on the face of the kaporet' could mean 'on top of' it, not requiring a handbreadth thickness.

items.text: Objection to the derivation from the cherubim's faces
items.text_en: Objection to the derivation from the cherubim's faces
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the derivation from 'faces' (פנים) might imply a very small measure, like a bird's face. Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that Rav Huna learned a verbal analogy from 'faces' to 'faces' (the face of Isaac), establishing a specific size.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the principle 'if you grasp too much you grasp nothing, if you grasp a little you grasp it' applies, and asks why the measure could not be as small as a bird's face.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that Rav Huna derived a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from 'faces' to 'faces', linking the cherubim's faces to the face of Isaac, establishing a specific size.

items.text: Rejection of alternative derivations from higher faces
items.text_en: Rejection of alternative derivations from higher faces
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers deriving the measure from 'faces of God' but rejects it with the principle that grasping too much is not grasping, while grasping a little is.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes deriving the measure from the 'faces of God' above, citing the verse 'כִּרְאוֹת פְּנֵי אֱלֹהִים וַתִּרְצֵנִי' (like seeing the face of God and you accepted me).

The Gemara rejects the derivation using the principle that grasping too much (תָּפַשְׂתָּ מְרוּבֶּה) is not grasping, while grasping a little (תָּפַשְׂתָּ מוּעָט) is grasping, implying the measure cannot be determined from an indeterminate 'face'.

items.text: Derivation from the cherubim themselves
items.text_en: Derivation from the cherubim themselves
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes deriving the measure from the cherubim's faces. Rav Acha bar Yaakov states a tradition that the cherubim's faces are no less than a handbreadth, and Rav Huna learned this from the same source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses: 'Here it says: 'toward the face of the kaporet', and there it says: 'from the face of his father Isaac'.

items.text: Etymology of 'cherub'
items.text_en: Etymology of 'cherub'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that 'cherub' (כרוב) means 'like a child' (כרביא), as in Babylonia they call a child 'ravya'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks what the word 'cherub' (כרוב) means.
Rabbi Avahu explains that 'cherub' (כרוב) means 'like a child' (כרביא), as in Babylonia they call a child 'ravya'.

items.text: Abaye's objection from Ezekiel's vision
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from Ezekiel's vision
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that in Ezekiel, 'cherub' and 'man' are distinguished, implying cherub faces are not human. The Gemara answers that cherub faces are large and human faces are small.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the verse 'פני האחד פני הכרוב ופני השני פני אדם' (the face of the one was the face of a cherub, and the face of the second was the face of a man) distinguishes between cherub and man, implying cherub faces are not human; the Gemara answers that cherub faces are large (אפי רברבי) and human faces are small (אפי זוטרי).

items.text: Derivation of ten handbreadths from the Tabernacle
items.text_en: Derivation of ten handbreadths from the Tabernacle
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know the sukkah's height is ten handbreadths excluding the roofing. It derives from the Temple: the cherubim stood in one-third of the Tabernacle's height (ten cubits), and their wings spread above the ark cover, teaching that the roofing (sukkah) is above ten handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know the sukkah's height of ten handbreadths excludes the roofing, and proposes it might include the roofing.

The Gemara derives the ten handbreadths from the Tabernacle: the cherubim stood in one-third of its height (ten cubits), and their wings spread above the ark cover, teaching that the roofing (sukkah) is above ten handbreadths.

items.text: Clarification of the cherubim's wing position
items.text_en: Clarification of the cherubim's wing position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the wings were above the heads or alongside, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that 'above' is written. It then asks if they were very high, and answers that 'above' is not repeated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the cherubim's wings were above their heads or alongside them.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the verse writes 'above' (לְמַעְלָה), indicating the wings were above the heads.
The Gemara asks whether the wings were raised very high above the heads.
The Gemara answers that the verse does not write 'above, above' (לְמַעְלָה לְמַעְלָה), so the wings were not excessively high.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Yehuda's measurements
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Yehuda's measurements
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the derivation works for Rabbi Meir who uses medium cubits, but for Rabbi Yehuda who uses six-handbreadth cubits for building and five for vessels, the calculation yields 11.5 handbreadths. It answers that for Rabbi Yehuda, the halakha is a tradition from Sinai, as stated by Rav Chiya bar Ashi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the derivation works for Rabbi Meir who uses medium cubits, but challenges: for Rabbi Yehuda who uses six-handbreadth cubits for building and five for vessels, what can be said?

The Gemara calculates that for Rabbi Yehuda, the ark and cover total 8.5 handbreadths, leaving 11.5 handbreadths, which would imply a sukkah must be up to 11.5 handbreadths high, contradicting the ten-handbreadth minimum.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Rav Chiya bar Ashi
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Rav Chiya bar Ashi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that for Rabbi Yehuda, the ten-handbreadth minimum is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai (הלכה למשה מסיני), as stated by Rav Chiya bar Ashi quoting Rav.

items.text: Scriptural support for halakhic measurements
items.text_en: Scriptural support for halakhic measurements
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that measurements are from the Torah, citing a verse about the Land of Israel. Rav Chanin explains that the verse teaches measurements, and the Gemara begins to elaborate with the example of wheat for a leprous house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that measurements (שיעורין) are from the Torah, citing the verse about the Land of Israel and Rav Chanin's statement that the entire verse was said for measurements.
The Gemara elaborates with the example of wheat (חיטה) as a measurement for a leprous house (בית המנוגע), citing a mishnah about entering such a house with items on one's shoulders.
The Gemara infers: 'The Tabernacle too — cherubim stand in a third of the house.'

items.text: Opening baraita listing shiurim
items.text_en: Opening baraita listing shiurim
items.desc_en: The baraita lists various halakhic measurements: a bone the size of a barley grain, a grape's worth of wine for a nazirite, a dried fig for carrying on Shabbat, a pomegranate for vessels, olives for most measurements, and a large date for Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing the shiurim (halakhic measurements) for various contexts, beginning with the case of a person wearing clothes and sandals who becomes impure immediately, while the vessels remain pure until the time it takes to eat a פרס (half-loaf) of wheat bread, not barley, reclining and eating with a relish.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the baraita's shiurim
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the baraita's shiurim
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains each shiur in the baraita, citing relevant mishnayot and verses. It notes that the verse 'a land of olive oil and honey' implies that most shiurim are olive-sized, but corrects this to 'most of its shiurim are olive-sized' because some are not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that a bone the size of a barley grain (שעורה) imparts טומאה (ritual impurity) by contact and carrying but not in a tent.
The Gemara cites the shiur (measure) of a grape as a quarter-log of wine for a nazirite.
The Gemara cites the shiur of a fig as a dried fig (גרוגרת) for the prohibition of carrying on שבת (Sabbath).
The Gemara cites the Mishnah that vessels of ordinary people have their shiur (measure) as pomegranates.
The Gemara cites the verse 'a land of olive oil and honey' and initially infers that all shiurim are olive-sized, then corrects to 'most of its shiurim are olive-sized' because some are not.
The Gemara cites the shiur of honey as a large date (כותבת הגסה) on Yom Kippur.

items.text: Question: Are shiurim biblical?
items.text_en: Question: Are shiurim biblical?
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that shiurim are biblical, but immediately objects: shiurim are not explicitly written in the Torah. It concludes that shiurim are halakhot le-Moshe mi-Sinai, and the verses are mere support (asmakhta).

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: Are these shiurim (שיעורין) from the Torah (דאורייתא)?
The gemara rejects the idea that shiurim are written in the Torah, asking rhetorically: Are shiurim written (in the Torah)?
The gemara resolves that these shiurim are halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai (הלכתא למשה מסיני) and the verse is merely an אסמכתא (support).

items.text: Question: Are chatzitzin biblical?
items.text_en: Question: Are chatzitzin biblical?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the laws of interpositions (chatzitzin) in immersion are biblical, citing the verse 'and he shall wash his flesh in water' which implies no interposition between the water and the body.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: Are the laws of interpositions (חציצין) from the Torah?
The gemara answers that they are from the Torah, citing the verse 'ורחץ בשרו במים' (and he shall wash his flesh in water), implying nothing should interpose between him and the water.

items.text: Answer: Halakha came for hair
items.text_en: Answer: Halakha came for hair
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai regarding chatzitzin came specifically for hair, citing Rabba bar bar Chana's ruling: one tied hair interposes, three do not, and two are uncertain.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution with Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution with Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that the halacha le-Moshe mi-Sinai (הלכתא) came specifically for the case of hair, as per Rabba bar bar Chana's ruling: one tied hair is an interposition, three are not, and two are uncertain.
The Gemara cites Rabba bar bar Chana's ruling: one tied hair interposes, three do not, and two are uncertain.

items.text: Objection: Hair itself is biblical
items.text_en: Objection: Hair itself is biblical
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that hair itself is included in the biblical requirement to wash 'his flesh' (including what is attached to it). It concludes that the halakha came for Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching, which is cited in the next segment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that hair itself is included in the biblical requirement to wash 'his flesh' (including what is attached to it), citing the verse 'וְרָחַץ אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ בַּמַּיִם' (and he shall wash his flesh in water) and the principle that hair is טפל (subordinate) to the flesh.
The Gemara resolves that the halakha (הלכה) about hair came specifically for Rabbi Yitzchak's teaching, which is cited in the next segment.

items.text: Gemara's question on the decree of ḥaṣiẓah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the decree of ḥaṣiẓah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Sages did not also decree against a minority that is not bothersome, given their decrees regarding a majority that is bothersome and a minority that is bothersome. The Gemara responds that such a decree would be a decree upon a decree, which is not done.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes the Torah law that a majority that bothers the person is a חוצץ (interposition), while a minority that does not bother is not, and notes that the Sages decreed against a non-bothersome majority and a bothersome minority due to the bothersome majority.
The Gemara asks why the Sages did not also decree against a non-bothersome minority, either due to the bothersome minority or the non-bothersome majority.
The Gemara answers that such a decree would be a decree upon a decree (גזירה לגזירה), which is not enacted.

items.text: Transition to the laws of sukkah walls
items.text_en: Transition to the laws of sukkah walls
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous discussion applies according to Rabbi Yehuda, but asks what can be said according to Rabbi Meir. It answers that the halakha came for the principles of gud, lavud, and dofen akumah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the halakha of מחיצין (partitions) was stated earlier, and asks what applies according to Rabbi Meir, who differs from Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara answers that the halakha (הלכה) came to teach the principles of גוד (extend), לבוד (join), and דופן עקומה (curved wall).

items.text: Mishnah: Sukkah without three walls
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sukkah without three walls
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a sukkah lacking three walls is invalid, setting the stage for the dispute about the minimum number of walls.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a sukkah without three walls is invalid.

items.text: Baraita: Dispute between Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Baraita: Dispute between Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute: the Rabbis require two walls of full length and a third even a handbreadth, while Rabbi Shimon requires three walls of full length and a fourth even a handbreadth. The Gemara explains their disagreement as based on whether one follows the tradition (masoret) or the reading (mikra) of the word 'sukkot' in the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the dispute: the Rabbis require two full walls and a third of even one handbreadth, while Rabbi Shimon requires three full walls and a fourth of even one handbreadth.

The Gemara asks: On what principle do they disagree? It explains that the Rabbis hold that the tradition (masoret) is authoritative, while Rabbi Shimon holds that the reading (mikra) is authoritative.
The Gemara elaborates: The Rabbis, following the tradition, count the written forms 'בסכת' (twice) and 'בסכות' (once) as four mentions of 'sukka'.
The Gemara explains: Subtract one mention for the mitzva itself, leaving three; two are full walls, and the halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai reduces the third to a handbreadth.

The Gemara explains: Rabbi Shimon, following the reading, counts the three vocalized 'בסכות' as six mentions; subtract one for the mitzva, leaving four; three are full walls, and the halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai reduces the fourth to a handbreadth.

items.text: Alternative explanations for the dispute
items.text_en: Alternative explanations for the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers three alternative explanations for the dispute: whether the halakha requires a verse for the roofing, whether the halakha subtracts or adds, and whether one expounds initial verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a first alternative explanation: everyone agrees that the vocalization is authoritative, and the dispute is whether the roofing requires a verse.
The Gemara offers a second alternative explanation: everyone agrees that the tradition of the verses is authoritative, and the dispute is whether the halakha subtracts or adds.
The Gemara offers a third alternative explanation: everyone agrees that the halakha subtracts and the tradition of the verses is authoritative, and the dispute is whether one expounds initial verses.

items.text: Rav Mattana's proof and the placement of the handbreadth
items.text_en: Rav Mattana's proof and the placement of the handbreadth
items.desc_en: Rav Mattana brings a verse to support Rabbi Shimon's opinion. The Gemara then asks where that handbreadth is placed, and Rav answers that it is placed opposite the entrance. The daf ends with Rav Kahana and Rav Asi asking Rav a question.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mattana cites a verse (Isaiah 4:6) to support Rabbi Shimon's opinion that a sukkah requires four walls, interpreting the verse's four terms for protection as alluding to four walls.
The Gemara asks where the additional handbreadth (טפח) of the fourth wall is placed according to Rabbi Shimon's opinion.
Rav answers that the handbreadth is placed opposite the entrance (היוצא), i.e., the opening of the sukkah.
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi begin to ask Rav a question (the daf ends before the question is recorded).

items.text: Rav's silence and Levi's ruling on the direction of the board
items.text_en: Rav's silence and Levi's ruling on the direction of the board
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the board should be placed opposite the Torah reader. Rav remains silent, and a tradition from Shmuel in Levi's name states it should be placed opposite the exit, as taught in the study hall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the board should be placed opposite the Torah reader, and Rav remains silent.
Shmuel reports in Levi's name that the board should be placed opposite the exit, and the study hall teaches accordingly.

items.text: Rabbi Simon's first opinion: a playful handbreadth
items.text_en: Rabbi Simon's first opinion: a playful handbreadth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simon (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) says one makes a 'playful handbreadth' (tefach soḥek) and places it within three handbreadths of the wall, invoking the principle of lavud.

sub.text: Rabbi Simon (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Simon (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simon (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) rules that one makes a loose handbreadth and places it within three handbreadths of the wall, invoking the principle of לבוד (connection).

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on a sukkah shaped like an alleyway
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on a sukkah shaped like an alleyway
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that a sukkah shaped like a mavoy is valid, and one may place that handbreadth in any direction they wish.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that a sukkah (סוכה) shaped like an alleyway is valid, and one may place the handbreadth board in any direction.

items.text: Rabbi Simon's second opinion and the distinction between cases
items.text_en: Rabbi Simon's second opinion and the distinction between cases
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simon (or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) requires a four-handbreadth board (pas arba'ah) placed within three handbreadths of the wall. The Gemara explains the difference: where there are two proper walls, a playful handbreadth suffices; where there are not, a four-handbreadth board is needed.

items.text: Rava's three versions on the need for a tzurat hapetah
items.text_en: Rava's three versions on the need for a tzurat hapetah
items.desc_en: Three versions of Rava's statement are cited: one says it is only permitted with a tzurat hapetah (doorway shape), another says it is also permitted with it, and a third says it requires it as well.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that a sukkah made like an alleyway is only permitted with a צורת הפתח (doorway shape).
A second version reports Rava saying that the sukkah is also permitted with a צורת הפתח (doorway shape).
A third version reports Rava saying that the sukkah also requires a צורת הפתח (doorway shape).

items.text: Rav Ashi's encounter with Rav Kahana
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's encounter with Rav Kahana
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi finds Rav Kahana making both a playful handbreadth and a tzurat hapetah. Rav Kahana explains he follows the version of Rava that requires the tzurat hapetah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi finds Rav Kahana making a loose handbreadth and a צורת הפתח (doorway shape), and Rav Kahana explains he follows the version that requires the doorway shape.
Rav Ashi asks Rav Kahana whether he does not hold of Rava's version that the sukkah is also permitted with a tzurat hapetah (doorway shape).
Rav Kahana explains that he follows the other version of Rava's statement, which requires a tzurat hapetah (doorway shape) in addition to the playful handbreadth.

items.text: Rava's extension to Shabbat and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rava's extension to Shabbat and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rava extends the leniency of sukkah walls to Shabbat boundaries (eruvin) using the principle of 'miggo' (since it is a wall for sukkah, it is a wall for Shabbat). Abaye objects with a baraita that distinguishes between sukkah and Shabbat, and the Gemara resolves the objection by clarifying that the baraita compares Shabbat in general to Shabbat of sukkah, not sukkah to Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rava extends the leniency of sukkah walls to Shabbat boundaries (עירובין) using the principle of מיגו (since it is a wall for sukkah, it is a wall for Shabbat).

Abaye objects by citing a baraita that compares sukkah walls to Shabbat walls, but adds that Shabbat has a stricter requirement (עומד מרובה על הפרוץ) that sukkah does not, implying that the leniency does not transfer from sukkah to Shabbat.
The Gemara infers from the baraita that the extra stringency of Shabbat over sukkah (דופן סוכה) means we do not apply the מיגו principle to extend sukkah leniencies to Shabbat.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the baraita compares general Shabbat laws to the Shabbat laws of a sukkah, not sukkah to Shabbat, so the מיגו principle remains valid.

The Gemara objects that if the baraita compares Shabbat to Shabbat, it should also note that general sukkah requires a טפח שוחק (playful handbreadth) while sukkah for Shabbat does not, citing Rava's own ruling that a sukkah atop an alleyway with a side-post is valid.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita did not need to mention the sukkah leniency because it is obvious: if we apply the leniency from the lenient case (sukkah) to the strict case (Shabbat), then certainly we apply it from the strict case (Shabbat) to the lenient case (sukkah).

items.text: Introduction to the body of the sugya
items.text_en: Introduction to the body of the sugya
items.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the main topic with 'Gufa' (the body), introducing Rava's statement that will be discussed further.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara transitions to the main body of Rava's statement.

items.text: Sukkah atop an alleyway or water pits
items.text_en: Sukkah atop an alleyway or water pits
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a sukkah placed on an alleyway with a sidepost or on water pits is valid. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary: the alleyway has two proper walls, while the water pits have the status of four walls, and the combination teaches a principle about lenient and stringent cases.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states that a sukkah placed atop an alleyway with a sidepost is valid.
Rava adds that a sukkah placed atop water pits with sideposts is also valid.
The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary: if only the alleyway case were taught, one might think the water pits case is invalid because it lacks two proper walls.
Conversely, if only the water pits case were taught, one might think the alleyway case is invalid because it lacks the status of four walls.
The Gemara concludes that both cases are necessary to teach a principle about lenient and stringent cases, and to prevent erroneous inference from one to the other.

items.text: Shade must exceed sunlight and the status of partitions
items.text_en: Shade must exceed sunlight and the status of partitions
items.desc_en: A sukkah whose sunlight exceeds its shade is invalid. A baraita debates whether the shade must come from the roofing alone or can include shade from the walls. Rabbi Yoshiya derives from the verse about the Ark that a partition is considered like roofing, while the Sages explain that the verse refers to a slight bend that appears like roofing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a sukkah whose sunlight exceeds its shade is invalid.
A baraita records a dispute: the Tanna Kamma says the shade must come from the roofing alone, while Rabbi Yoshiya includes shade from the walls.

sub.text: Rav Yemar bar Shelemya citing Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Yemar bar Shelemya citing Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Yemar bar Shelemya in the name of Abaye explains Rabbi Yoshiya's reasoning: the verse 'וְסַכּוֹתָ עַל הָאָרוֹן אֶת הַפָּרוֹכֶת' (you shall screen the ark with the curtain) calls a partition (the curtain) a 'סְכָכָה' (sukkah/covering), proving that a partition is considered like roofing.
The Sages reject the proof: the verse refers to a slight bend in the curtain that makes it appear like roofing, not that a partition itself is considered roofing.

items.text: List of Tannaim who require a permanent dwelling
items.text_en: List of Tannaim who require a permanent dwelling
items.desc_en: Abaye lists eight authorities who hold that a sukkah must be a permanent dwelling: Rabbi, Rabbi Yoshiya, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, Rabban Gamliel, Beit Shammai, Rabbi Eliezer, and Acheirim. Each is cited with a specific ruling that reflects this principle.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by listing eight authorities who all hold that a sukkah must be a permanent dwelling (דִּירַת קֶבַע).
A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi requires a sukkah to be at least four amot by four amot, reflecting a permanent dwelling.

sub.text: Reference to earlier statement for Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.text_en: Reference to earlier statement for Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.desc_en: Abaye references the earlier ruling of Rabbi Yoshiya (that a sukkah's shade must come from walls as well) as evidence for his position.
A mishnah is cited where Rabbi Yehuda validates a sukkah higher than twenty cubits, implying a permanent structure requirement.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Shimon requires three walls of proper size and a fourth even a handbreadth, reflecting a permanent dwelling.
A baraita is cited where Rabban Gamliel disqualifies a sukkah on a wagon or ship, indicating it must be a permanent dwelling.
A mishnah is cited where Beit Shammai disqualify a sukkah if one's table is inside the house, reflecting a permanent dwelling requirement.
A mishnah is cited where Rabbi Eliezer disqualifies a sukkah shaped like a hut or leaning against a wall, indicating it must be a permanent dwelling.
A baraita is cited where Acheirim disqualify a dovecote-shaped sukkah for lacking corners, reflecting a permanent dwelling requirement.

items.text: Sukkah shaped like a kiln and its required circumference
items.text_en: Sukkah shaped like a kiln and its required circumference
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a sukkah shaped like a kiln is valid only if its circumference can seat 24 people, aligning with Rabbi's requirement of four by four cubits. The Gemara questions whether a person's width of one cubit (with a circumference of three handbreadths per handbreadth of width) would suffice with twelve, but the text ends abruptly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a sukkah shaped like a kiln is valid only if its circumference can seat 24 people, otherwise it is invalid.
The Gemara identifies that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling aligns with Rabbi's position that a sukkah must be four by four cubits.
The Gemara questions why 24 people are needed, given that a person sits in one cubit and a circumference of three handbreadths per handbreadth of width would require only twelve people.

items.text: Initial statement: circular vs. square sukkah
items.text_en: Initial statement: circular vs. square sukkah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the previous calculation applies to a circular sukkah, but a square one requires more.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the previous calculation applies to a circular sukkah, but a square one requires more.
The Gemara asks: since a square exceeds a circle by a quarter, why is sixteen cubits not sufficient for a square sukkah?
The Gemara answers: that quarter-ratio applies to a circle inscribed in a square, but a square circumscribed around a circle requires more due to the corners' projection.
The Gemara asks: since each cubit in a square yields a diagonal of one and two-fifths cubits, why is seventeen minus a fifth not sufficient, and answers that the calculation is imprecise.
The Gemara objects: we may say the calculation is imprecise by a small amount, but can we say it is imprecise by a large amount?

Mar Kashisha son of Rav Chisda answers Rav Ashi: a person does not sit in a full cubit, but three people sit in two cubits, so the required perimeter is sixteen cubits, not seventeen minus a fifth, and the calculation is imprecise.
