The Gemara objects: we may say the calculation is imprecise to be stringent, but can we say it is imprecise to be lenient?

Rav Asi answers Rav Ashi: a person always sits in a full cubit, and Rabbi Yochanan does not count the space of the people, so the required perimeter is eighteen cubits, and the calculation is imprecise by a small amount and to be stringent.
The Rabbis of Caesarea, or the judges of Caesarea, state that a circle circumscribed around a square exceeds it by a quarter.

items.text: First objection and resolution: square within a circle
items.text_en: First objection and resolution: square within a circle
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if a square exceeds a circle by a quarter, 16 cubits should suffice, but answers that this applies only when the circle is inscribed in the square, not when the square is inscribed in the circle, due to the corners' protrusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that since a square exceeds its inscribed circle by a quarter, a 16-cubit perimeter should suffice for the sukkah.
The Gemara resolves that the quarter-ratio applies only when the circle is inscribed in the square, not when the square is inscribed in the circle, due to the protrusion of the corners.

items.text: Second objection: diagonal calculation
items.text_en: Second objection: diagonal calculation
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that since each cubit in a square adds 1.4 cubits to the diagonal, 17 minus a fifth should suffice, but the Gemara says the sages were not precise in this small amount.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that since each cubit in a square adds 1.4 cubits to the diagonal, 17 minus a fifth should suffice for the diagonal of a 12-cubit square.
The Gemara answers that the sages were not precise in this small amount, but the objection persists that the discrepancy is too large to dismiss as imprecision.

items.text: Mar Kashisha's challenge: person's width
items.text_en: Mar Kashisha's challenge: person's width
items.desc_en: Mar Kashisha challenges that a person sits in one cubit, so three people need two cubits, totaling 16 cubits, but we need 17 minus a fifth; the Gemara says they were not precise, but the objection is that leniency cannot rely on imprecision.

sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha challenges that a person sits in one cubit, so three people need two cubits, totaling 16 cubits, but we need 17 minus a fifth.
The Gemara objects that the leniency of relying on imprecision (לא דק) cannot be applied to a lenient ruling.

items.text: Rabbi Asi's resolution: Rabbi Yochanan's method
items.text_en: Rabbi Asi's resolution: Rabbi Yochanan's method
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi answers that a person indeed sits in one cubit, but Rabbi Yochanan did not count the space of the people, leading to 18 cubits, so 17 minus a fifth suffices, and the imprecision is for stringency.

sub.text: Rabbi Asi's answer to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Asi's answer to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi answers that a person sits in one cubit, but Rabbi Yochanan did not count the space of the people, so the calculation is based on 18 cubits.
The Gemara concludes that 17 minus a fifth suffices for 18 cubits, and the imprecision is for stringency.

items.text: Rabbis of Caesarea's principle
items.text_en: Rabbis of Caesarea's principle
items.desc_en: The Rabbis of Caesarea state that a circle inscribed in a square has a quarter less area.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis of Caesarea state that a circle inscribed in a square has a quarter less area than the square.

items.text: Gemara's mathematical observation
items.text_en: Gemara's mathematical observation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the square that emerges from a circle is only half (the area), but then observes that this is not the case, as we see it is not that much.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the square that emerges from a circle is only half (the area), but then rejects this, observing that it is not that much.

items.text: Rabbi Levi's ruling on two potters' sukkot
items.text_en: Rabbi Levi's ruling on two potters' sukkot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi cites Rabbi Meir: If there are two potters' sukkot, one inside the other, the inner one is not a valid sukkah but is obligated in mezuzah, while the outer one is a valid sukkah and exempt from mezuzah. The Gemara questions why the outer one is not considered a gateway to the inner and thus obligated in mezuzah, and answers that it is not permanent.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi cites Rabbi Meir's ruling: two potters' sukkot, one inside the other — the inner one is not a valid sukkah but is obligated in mezuzah, the outer one is a valid sukkah and exempt from mezuzah.
The Gemara questions why the outer sukkah is not considered a gateway to the inner one, which would obligate it in mezuzah.
The Gemara answers that the outer sukkah is not permanent (קביע), so it is not considered a gateway.

items.text: Baraita of Ganba"kh and Rav Chisda's explanation
items.text_en: Baraita of Ganba"kh and Rav Chisda's explanation
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: A sukkah of gentiles, women, animals, or Cutheans (Ganba"kh) is valid in any case, provided it is covered according to its halakhah. Rav Chisda explains that 'according to its halakhah' means it was made for the sake of the sukkah (le-tzel sukkah).

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught a baraita listing four types of sukkot (gentiles, women, animals, Cutheans) that are valid provided they are covered according to their halakhah.
Rav Chisda explains that the baraita's condition 'according to its halakhah' means the sukkah was made for the sake of shade (le-tzel sukkah).

items.text: Baraita of Rakba"sh and Rav Chisda's explanation
items.text_en: Baraita of Rakba"sh and Rav Chisda's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'in any case' (mikol makom) in the Ganba"kh baraita includes, and answers that it includes the sukkah of Rakba"sh (shepherds, guards, etc.). The Sages taught a baraita about Rakba"sh, and Rav Chisda again explains that 'according to its halakhah' means it was made for the sake of the sukkah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'in any case' (מכל מקום) in the Rakba"sh baraita comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it comes to include the sukkah of Rakba"sh (shepherds, guards, etc.).
The Sages taught a baraita listing the sukkot of Rakba"sh, stating that they are valid provided they are covered according to their halakhah.
The Gemara asks what 'according to its halakhah' (כהלכתה) in the Rakba"sh baraita means.
Rav Chisda explains that 'according to its halakhah' means the sukkah was made for the sake of the sukkah (i.e., for shade of the sukkah).

items.text: Gemara's question on the Rakba"sh baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Rakba"sh baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'in any case' (mikol makom) in the Rakba"sh baraita includes, and answers that it includes the sukkah of Ganba"kh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'in any case' comes to include in this second baraita.
The Gemara answers that it comes to include the sukkot of gentiles, women, animals, and Cutheans (גנב״ך).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the two baraitot
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the two baraitot
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning behind the two baraitot: The tanna of Ganba"kh emphasizes Ganba"kh because they are permanent, and includes Rakba"sh (which are not permanent) via 'mikol makom'. The tanna of Rakba"sh emphasizes Rakba"sh because they are obligated in mitzvot, and includes Ganba"kh (who are not obligated) via 'mikol makom'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the tanna of Ganba"kh prioritizes these sukkot because they are permanent (קביעי), and includes Rakba"sh via 'mikol makom'.
The Gemara explains that the tanna of Rakba"sh prioritizes these sukkot because their occupants are obligated in mitzvot (בני חיובא), and includes Ganba"kh via 'mikol makom'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding an old sukkah: Beit Shammai invalidates it, Beit Hillel validates it. An old sukkah is defined as one built thirty days before the festival, but if built for the sake of the festival even at the beginning of the year, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute: Beit Shammai invalidates an old sukkah, Beit Hillel validates it, defining an old sukkah as one built thirty days before the festival, but if built for the sake of the festival even at the beginning of the year it is valid.

items.text: Gemara's first question and Beit Hillel's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and Beit Hillel's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for Beit Shammai's reasoning, citing the verse 'חג הסוכות שבעת ימים לה׳' to require a sukkah made for the festival. Beit Hillel counters that this verse is needed for Rabbi Shimon's derivation that sukkah wood is forbidden for seven days, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira adds that just as the festival is dedicated to God, so is the sukkah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning of Beit Shammai.
Beit Shammai cites the verse 'חג הסוכות שבעת ימים לה׳' to require a sukkah made for the festival.
Beit Hillel objects that the verse is needed for Rav Sheishet's derivation.
Rav Sheishet in the name of Rabbi Akiva derives that sukkah wood is forbidden for seven days from the same verse.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira adds that just as the festival is dedicated to God, so is the sukkah.

items.text: Beit Shammai's alternative verse
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's alternative verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Beit Shammai also need the verse for the same derivation, so they must have another reason. They cite a second verse, 'חג הסוכות תעשה לך שבעת ימים', to require a sukkah made for the festival.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Beit Shammai also need the verse for the derivation of Rav Sheishet, so what is their source for requiring a sukkah made for the festival? It answers: Indeed, they do.

The Gemara explains that Beit Shammai derive the requirement from a second verse, 'חג הסוכות תעשה לך שבעת ימים' (You shall make the festival of Sukkot for yourself for seven days), teaching that a sukkah must be made for the festival.

items.text: Beit Hillel's alternative use and Beit Shammai's position
items.text_en: Beit Hillel's alternative use and Beit Shammai's position
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel uses the second verse to permit building a sukkah during Chol HaMoed. Beit Shammai, however, follows Rabbi Eliezer who forbids building a sukkah during Chol HaMoed, so they can use the verse for their requirement.

sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel responds that that verse is needed to permit building a sukkah during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days), while Beit Shammai holds like Rabbi Eliezer who forbids building a sukkah during that time.
The Gemara notes that Beit Shammai follows Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that one does not build a sukkah during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days).

items.text: Objection from Rav Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Objection from Rav Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Beit Hillel should accept Rav Yehuda's ruling that a sukkah made from certain materials is invalid unless made for the sake of the festival, implying a general requirement of intent. Shmuel adds that even from reeds it is invalid, requiring preparation for its sake.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Do Beit Hillel not accept the teaching of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav, that a sukkah made from thorns, twigs, or palm fibers is invalid, but from reeds is valid?
Shmuel objects that even from reeds it is invalid, requiring that the material be prepared for its purpose (טויה לשמה), and analogously here we require a sukkah made for its sake.
The Gemara concludes that here too a sukkah made for its sake is required, challenging Beit Hillel's position.

items.text: Resolution distinguishing the cases
items.text_en: Resolution distinguishing the cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes the cases: there the verse 'גדילים תעשה לך' teaches that tzitzit must be for one's obligation, and here 'חג הסוכות תעשה לך' could similarly require intent. However, that verse is needed to exclude a stolen sukkah, and there another verse 'ועשו להם' excludes a stolen one, so the requirement of intent is not derived here.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a sukka under a tree is invalid, and a sukka atop another sukka: the upper is valid, the lower invalid; Rabbi Yehuda qualifies the latter.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a sukka under a tree is invalid, as if built inside a house.
The Mishnah states that a sukka atop another sukka: the upper is valid, the lower invalid.
Rabbi Yehuda qualifies: if no one dwells in the upper sukka, the lower one is valid.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the tree case
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the tree case
items.desc_en: Rava limits the Mishnah's tree ruling to when the tree's shade exceeds its sunlight; otherwise the sukka is valid. The Gemara proves this from the Mishnah's wording, and Rav Papa explains that the case involves beaten-down branches, with no decree against doing so initially.

sub.desc_en: Rava limits the Mishnah's tree ruling to a tree whose shade exceeds its sunlight, but if sunlight exceeds shade the sukka is valid.
The Gemara asks how Rava derives this, noting the Mishnah's unusual wording 'as if he made it in the house' instead of simply 'invalid'.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's comparison to a house teaches that the tree must have shade exceeding sunlight, just like a house.
The Gemara objects that even if sunlight exceeds shade, the tree branches still constitute invalid סכך (sukka covering) mixed with valid סכך, which should invalidate the sukka.
Rav Papa answers that the case involves beaten-down branches, which are no longer considered invalid סכך.
The Gemara objects that if the branches are beaten down, the ruling is obvious, and questions why a decree was not enacted against doing so initially.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah teaches that no decree is enacted against beaten-down branches to prevent confusion with unbeaten ones.

items.text: Support from a baraita
items.text_en: Support from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a sukka covered with vines, gourds, or ivy, which is invalid unless the invalid sechakh is minimal or cut. This supports that beaten-down branches are valid even initially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a sukka covered with vines, gourds, or ivy, which is invalid unless the invalid sechakh is minimal or cut.
The Gemara asks: how is this case? If the vines were not beaten down, invalid sechakh joins with valid sechakh.
The Gemara concludes: it must be when they were beaten down, and we learn that we do not decree a prohibition.
The Gemara resolves: one might have thought this applies only בדיעבד (after the fact), but לכתחילה (the ideal standard) it is invalid; the baraita teaches that it is valid even initially.

items.text: Derivation from the verse for the upper sukka
items.text_en: Derivation from the verse for the upper sukka
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita deriving from 'ba-sukkot' that one may not sit in a sukka under another sukka, under a tree, or in a house. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak notes the defective spelling to exclude the second sukka.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'בַּסֻּכֹּת תֵּשְׁבוּ' (you shall dwell in sukkot) and derives that one may not sit in a sukka under another sukka, under a tree, or in a house.
The Gemara objects that the plural form 'בַּסֻּכּוֹת' (in sukkot) could imply two sukkot, not exclude a second one.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the verse is written defectively as 'בַּסֻּכֹּת' (without the letter vav), indicating a single sukka and excluding a second one.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's four cases for two sukkot
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's four cases for two sukkot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya enumerates scenarios where both sukkot are valid, both invalid, or one valid and the other invalid, based on shade ratios and height relative to twenty cubits.

sub.desc_en: רבי ירמיה (Rabbi Yirmeya) opens by stating that there are four possible scenarios for two sukkot one atop the other: both fit, both unfit, lower fit and upper unfit, or lower unfit and upper fit.

The Gemara explains the first case: both sukkot are fit when the lower one has more sunlight than shade (making it invalid on its own) and the upper one has more shade than sunlight and is within twenty cubits, so the upper's roofing serves both.

The Gemara explains the second case: both sukkot are unfit when both have more shade than sunlight but the upper one is above twenty cubits, making its roofing invalid and casting shade on the lower one.
The Gemara begins to explain the third case — where the lower sukka is fit and the upper one is unfit — but the text breaks off, leaving the details implicit.

items.text: Two sukkot one atop the other: cases of validity and invalidity
items.text_en: Two sukkot one atop the other: cases of validity and invalidity
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's cases: when the lower sukkah has more shade than sun and the upper has more sun than shade, and both are within twenty cubits, the lower is valid and the upper invalid. When both have more shade than sun and the upper is within twenty cubits, the upper is valid and the lower invalid. The Gemara notes that the case of lower valid and upper invalid was necessary to teach, lest one think that invalid sechach might combine with valid sechach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Mishnah's case of lower valid and upper invalid is possible, and answers with a scenario where the lower has more shade than sun, the upper has more sun than shade, and both are within twenty cubits.
The Gemara asks how the case of upper valid and lower invalid is possible, and answers with a scenario where both have more shade than sun and the upper is within twenty cubits.

The Gemara notes that the case of lower valid and upper invalid was necessary to teach, lest one think that invalid sechach (סכך) might combine with valid sechach, so the Mishnah teaches that it does not.

items.text: Dispute over the minimum space between the sukkot
items.text_en: Dispute over the minimum space between the sukkot
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how much space must be between the two sukkot for the lower one to be invalid. Rav Huna says a handbreadth, based on the laws of tents regarding impurity. Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna say four handbreadths, as no significant space is less than four. Shmuel says ten handbreadths, reasoning that just as a valid sukkah requires ten handbreadths, so too the space that invalidates it is ten.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how much space must be between the two sukkot for the lower to be invalid.
Rav Huna answers that a handbreadth (טפח) suffices, citing the rule of אהלי טומאה (tent impurity) where a handbreadth transmits and blocks impurity.

sub.text: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna answer that four handbreadths are required, since no significant space (מקום חשוב) is less than four handbreadths.

Shmuel answers that ten handbreadths are required, applying the principle that just as a valid sukkah requires ten handbreadths in height, so too the space that invalidates the lower sukkah requires ten handbreadths.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's statement and its interpretation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's statement and its interpretation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Yehuda says if there are no dwellers in the upper sukkah, the lower one is valid. The Gemara questions what 'no dwellers' means, concluding it means the upper sukkah is not fit for dwelling, i.e., less than ten handbreadths high. This implies the first Tanna holds that even if unfit for dwelling, the lower is invalid. Rav Dimi reports that in the West they say the lower is valid if it cannot bear the bedding of the upper, implying the first Tanna holds it is invalid even if it can bear it. The difference between these interpretations is whether the lower can bear the load with difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yehuda's statement that if there are no dwellers in the upper sukkah, the lower one is valid.
The Gemara asks what 'no dwellers' means, first suggesting it means literal dwellers.
The Gemara rejects the literal interpretation, arguing that dwellers themselves do not cause the lower sukkah's invalidity.
The Gemara answers that 'no dwellers' means the upper sukkah is not fit for dwelling, i.e., less than ten handbreadths high.
The Gemara infers that the first Tanna holds that even if the upper sukkah is unfit for dwelling, the lower one is invalid.
Rav Dimi reports that in the West they say the lower sukkah is valid if it cannot bear the bedding of the upper one.
The Gemara infers that the first Tanna holds that even if the lower sukkah can bear the bedding, it is invalid.
The Gemara notes that the difference between the two interpretations is whether the lower sukkah can bear the load with difficulty.

items.text: Mishnah: Spreading a sheet over the sukkah and Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Mishnah: Spreading a sheet over the sukkah and Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one spreads a sheet over the sukkah because of the sun, or under it because of nesting birds, or over a bed-frame, the sukkah is invalid. However, one may spread a sheet over the posts of a bed. Rav Chisda clarifies that this invalidity applies only when done for the nesting, but if done for beautification, it is valid. The Gemara notes that this is obvious from the Mishnah, but Rav Chisda teaches that the Mishnah's phrasing is just the common case, not exclusive.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that spreading a sheet over the sukkah for sun protection, under it for nesting birds, or over a bed-frame invalidates the sukkah, but one may spread over bed-posts.

Rav Chisda clarifies that the Mishnah's invalidity applies only when the sheet is spread for nesting birds (מִפְּנֵי הַנֶּשֶׁר), but if done for beautification (לְנָאוֹתָהּ), the sukkah remains valid.
The Gemara objects that Rav Chisda's ruling is obvious, since the Mishnah explicitly mentions nesting birds (מִפְּנֵי הַנֶּשֶׁר).

The Gemara explains that Rav Chisda's teaching is necessary to counter a possible assumption that the Mishnah's phrasing is merely the common case (אוֹרְחָא דְמִילְּתָא), but the invalidity would apply even for beautification; Rav Chisda teaches that it does not.

items.text: Supporting baraita for Rav Chisda's distinction
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rav Chisda's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that seems to support Rav Chisda: if one roofed the sukkah properly and decorated it with embroidered cloths and painted sheets, and hung nuts, almonds, peaches, pomegranates, grape clusters, wreaths of ears of grain, wines, oils, and flours, it is forbidden to benefit from them. This implies that beautification is permitted, supporting Rav Chisda's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests a supporting baraita about a sukkah decorated with cloths and fruits, from which it is forbidden to benefit, implying that decoration does not invalidate the sukkah.

items.text: Opening Mishnah continuation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah continuation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one stipulated conditions regarding the Sukkah decorations, everything follows the stipulation. The Gemara raises a concern about decorations on the side.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that Sukkah decorations may be removed until the end of the festival, and if one stipulated conditions, everything follows the stipulation.
The Gemara raises a concern about decorations placed on the side of the Sukkah, questioning whether they reduce the valid space.

items.text: Decorations on the side and the incident with Minyamin
items.text_en: Decorations on the side and the incident with Minyamin
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that Sukkah decorations on the side reduce the Sukkah's validity. The Gemara recounts an incident where Minyamin, Rav Ashi's servant, spread a wet garment on the Sukkah roofing, and Rav Ashi told him to remove it once it dries, lest people think he is roofing with something susceptible to impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: decorations of a Sukkah do not reduce the Sukkah's validity.
Rav Ashi adds that decorations on the side of the Sukkah do reduce its validity.
The Gemara recounts that Minyamin, Rav Ashi's servant, spread a wet garment on the Sukkah roofing.
Rav Ashi tells Minyamin to remove the garment once it dries, to avoid the appearance of roofing with something susceptible to impurity.

items.text: Dispute about decorations four handbreadths away
items.text_en: Dispute about decorations four handbreadths away
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that a Sukkah whose decorations are four handbreadths away from it is valid, while Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna rule it invalid. The Gemara relates that when these latter rabbis visited the Exilarch's house, Rav Nachman had them sleep in such a Sukkah, and they remained silent, later explaining they were exempt as messengers of a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the dispute: Rav Nachman rules that a Sukkah whose decorations are four handbreadths away from it is valid, while Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna rule it invalid.

The Gemara relates that when Rav Chisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna visited the Exilarch's house, Rav Nachman had them sleep in such a Sukkah; they remained silent, and when asked, they explained they were exempt as messengers of a mitzvah (שלוחי מצוה).

items.text: Permissibility of sleeping under a canopy in the Sukkah
items.text_en: Permissibility of sleeping under a canopy in the Sukkah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that it is permitted to sleep under a canopy (כילה) in the Sukkah, even if it has a roof, provided it is less than ten handbreadths high.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that sleeping under a canopy (כילה) in the Sukkah is permitted, provided the canopy is less than ten handbreadths high.

items.text: Challenges and resolutions regarding the canopy
items.text_en: Challenges and resolutions regarding the canopy
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that one who sleeps under a canopy in the Sukkah has not fulfilled his obligation, and resolves it by saying the canopy is ten handbreadths high. It then challenges with a case of sleeping under a bed, which Shmuel himself explains as a bed ten handbreadths high. Another challenge about a canopy over a bed is also resolved by saying it is ten handbreadths high.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel's ruling by citing a baraita that one who sleeps under a canopy in the Sukkah has not fulfilled his obligation.
The Gemara resolves the challenge by explaining that the baraita refers to a canopy ten handbreadths high, which creates a separate tent and invalidates the Sukkah.
The Gemara raises another challenge from a baraita that one who sleeps under a bed in the Sukkah has not fulfilled his obligation.
Shmuel himself explains that the baraita refers to a bed ten handbreadths high, consistent with his own ruling.
The Gemara challenges further with a baraita that one who spreads a canopy over a bed-frame invalidates the Sukkah.
The Gemara resolves this challenge as well by stating that the case involves a canopy ten handbreadths high.

items.text: Distinction between poles and canopies
items.text_en: Distinction between poles and canopies
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous resolution with a baraita that distinguishes between poles (נקלטין) and canopies (קינופות), implying that canopies invalidate even if less than ten handbreadths high. The Gemara answers that canopies are fixed, and a fixed structure creates a tent even below ten handbreadths, unlike the Sukkah's own invalidating height of ten.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that distinguishes between poles (נקלטין) and canopies (קינופות), implying that canopies invalidate even when less than ten handbreadths high.
The Gemara answers that canopies are fixed structures, and a fixed structure creates a tent (אוהל) even below ten handbreadths, unlike the Sukkah's own invalidating height of ten.

items.text: Sleeping naked under a canopy and reciting Shema
items.text_en: Sleeping naked under a canopy and reciting Shema
items.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi in the name of Shmuel rules that one who sleeps naked under a canopy may stick his head out and recite Shema. The Gemara challenges with a baraita that forbids this, and resolves it by saying the canopy is ten handbreadths high. The Gemara supports this from the baraita's continuation comparing it to a house.

sub.text: Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi in the name of Shmuel rules that one who sleeps naked under a canopy may stick his head out and recite Shema.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that forbids one who sleeps naked under a canopy from sticking his head out to recite Shema.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to a canopy ten handbreadths high, which creates a separate domain.
The Gemara supports this resolution by noting that the baraita's continuation compares the canopy to a house, implying it is ten handbreadths high.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection to Rav Yehuda's leniency
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection to Rav Yehuda's leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even a house less than ten handbreadths high is considered a tent because it is fixed, so a canopy should be no different. This sets up the debate about the status of a canopy in the sukkah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even a house less than ten handbreadths high is considered a tent because it is fixed, so a canopy should be no different.

items.text: Alternative version of Rav Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: A second version of Rav Yehuda's ruling permits sleeping under a wedding canopy in the sukkah because it has no roof, even if it is ten handbreadths high. This version emphasizes the absence of a roof as the key factor.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Yehuda's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Yehuda's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: one may sleep in a wedding canopy in the sukkah because it has no roof, even if it is ten handbreadths high.

items.text: Challenges and resolution regarding the canopy
items.text_en: Challenges and resolution regarding the canopy
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from a mishnah that says sleeping under a canopy in the sukkah is invalid, and distinguishes that case as having a roof. A further challenge from the laws of naklitin (poles) and kinofot (canopies) is answered by noting that naklitin are fixed, unlike a canopy which is temporary relative to them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from a mishnah stating that one who sleeps under a canopy in the sukkah has not fulfilled his obligation, and the Gemara answers that the case involves a canopy with a roof.

The Gemara brings a further challenge from a baraita about naklitin (poles) and kinofot (canopies), where a canopy without a roof is invalid if it is ten handbreadths high, implying that a canopy is always invalid regardless of a roof.

The Gemara answers that naklitin are different because they are fixed (קביעי), and while they are not fixed relative to kinofot, they are fixed relative to a canopy, so the canopy is temporary and permitted.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's leniency and Rabbi Yehuda's principle
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's leniency and Rabbi Yehuda's principle
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna permits sleeping under a canopy even with a roof and height, aligning with Rabbi Yehuda's view that a temporary tent does not nullify a permanent one. The Gemara explains that this ruling teaches that the principle applies equally to a bed and a canopy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna teaches that it is permitted to sleep under a canopy in the sukkah even if it has a roof and is ten handbreadths high.
The Gemara asks why Rabbah bar Rav Huna did not simply state that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda.

The Gemara explains that if the ruling had merely stated the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda, one might think it applies only to a bed, but not to a canopy; therefore Rabbah bar Rav Huna explicitly teaches the principle that a temporary tent (אוהל עראי) does not nullify a permanent one (אוהל קבע), applying equally to both.

items.text: Mishnah: Disqualifying vines, gourds, and ivy for s'chach
items.text_en: Mishnah: Disqualifying vines, gourds, and ivy for s'chach
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if one places vines, gourds, or ivy over the sukkah and then covers them with s'chach, it is invalid. However, if the s'chach is more abundant than these plants, or if they are cut, it is valid. The general rule is that anything susceptible to impurity and not grown from the ground cannot be used for s'chach.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that if one places vines, gourds, or ivy over the sukkah and then covers them with s'chach, it is invalid, but if the s'chach is more abundant or the plants are cut, it is valid.

The mishnah concludes with the general rule: anything susceptible to impurity and not grown from the ground cannot be used for s'chach, while anything not susceptible to impurity and grown from the ground may be used.

items.text: Gemara: Rav's requirement to shake cut plants
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav's requirement to shake cut plants
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that Rav requires shaking the cut plants. Rav Huna corrects him, attributing the statement to Shmuel, not Rav, and supports this with a story about Rav Amram the Pious who hung tekhelet strings without cutting their ends. Rav Chiya bar Ashi then rules that cutting the ends is the act of making them valid.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's statement before Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's statement before Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef sits before Rav Huna and states that the mishnah's ruling 'or if he cut them, it is valid' requires shaking the cut plants, citing Rav as the source.
Rav Huna objects that Shmuel, not Rav, said this, and supports his claim with a story about Rav Amram the Pious who hung tekhelet (תכלת) strings without cutting their ends.
Rav Chiya bar Ashi rules that cutting the ends of the strings is the act that makes them valid, applying the same principle to the cut plants in the mishnah.

items.text: Challenge to Shmuel's position from tzitzit
items.text_en: Challenge to Shmuel's position from tzitzit
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether Shmuel holds that cutting is the act of making, citing a baraita where Shmuel rules that if one ties tzitzit and then cuts the strings, they are valid. The Gemara initially assumes this means tying before cutting, but then reinterprets it as cutting before tying, leaving the matter unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel's position by asking whether he does not hold that cutting the strings constitutes their making, citing a baraita where Shmuel rules that tzitzit tied and then cut are valid.
The Gemara initially assumes the baraita means tying before cutting, but then reinterprets it as cutting before tying, leaving the matter unresolved.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of Rav's position
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of Rav's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav's statement that a detached wing is valid only if the threads are cut at the time of attachment means that without cutting at that moment, the wing is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav's statement implies that a detached wing is valid only if the threads are cut at the time of attachment, otherwise it is invalid.

items.text: Challenge to Rav from a baraita and the responses
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav from a baraita and the responses
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if one hung threads and did not cut their ends, they are invalid. The Gemara challenges Rav, who requires cutting at the time of attachment. Rav explains that 'invalid' means only until cut, while Shmuel and Levi hold they are permanently invalid. A second version quotes Rav Mattana confirming Shmuel's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav by citing a baraita that states threads hung without cutting their ends are invalid, implying permanent invalidity.
Rav explains that the baraita's 'invalid' means only until the ends are cut, not permanently.
Shmuel and Levi hold that the threads are permanently invalid, contrasting with Rav's view.
Rav Mattana confirms that Shmuel rules the threads are permanently invalid.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Mattana's story
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Mattana's story
sub.desc_en: An alternative version quotes Rav Mattana recounting a personal case where Shmuel ruled the threads are permanently invalid.

items.text: Second challenge: sukkah with attached vegetation
items.text_en: Second challenge: sukkah with attached vegetation
items.desc_en: Another baraita teaches that if one placed a vine, gourd, or ivy over a sukkah and then covered it, it is invalid due to 'תעשה ולא מן העשוי'. The Gemara analyzes: if the vegetation was not cut, the problem is that it is attached; if it was cut, the ruling implies that cutting is not considered its making, challenging Rav's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that if one placed a vine, gourd, or ivy over a sukkah and covered it, it is invalid due to the principle of 'תעשה ולא מן העשוי' (you shall make, not from what is already made).

The Gemara analyzes the baraita: if the vegetation was not cut, the problem is that it is attached, not the 'תעשה' principle; if it was cut, the ruling implies that cutting is not considered its making, which challenges Rav's principle.

items.text: Rav's defense and remaining difficulty
items.text_en: Rav's defense and remaining difficulty
items.desc_en: Rav answers that the case involves pulling the vegetation out entirely, so the act of making is not recognizable. Nevertheless, the baraita about hanging and then cutting remains a difficulty for Rav.

sub.desc_en: Rav responds that the case involves vines that were pulled out without being recognizable as having been cut, so the cutting is not evident.
Nevertheless, the Gemara concludes that the baraita about hanging and then cutting still poses a difficulty for Rav, and it remains unresolved.

items.text: Dispute among Tanna'im about lulav and sukkah
items.text_en: Dispute among Tanna'im about lulav and sukkah
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the Sages regarding a lulav whose leaves were gathered after being detached. The Gemara initially assumes both agree that a lulav requires binding and derive from sukkah, and they argue whether cutting is considered making for sukkah and gathering for lulav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to resolve the issue by citing a Tannaic dispute: if one gathered the leaves of a lulav after they were detached, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai disqualifies it, while the Sages validate it.

The Gemara explains the shared assumption: everyone agrees that a lulav requires binding (אגוד), and they derive this requirement from sukkah via the verse 'תעשה — ולא מן העשוי' (you shall make — not from that which is already made).
The Gemara asks: is the dispute about whether we apply the principle that cutting (for sukkah) or gathering (for lulav) is considered their making (עשייתן)?

items.text: Alternative explanation: dispute about deriving lulav from sukkah
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: dispute about deriving lulav from sukkah
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous assumption and suggests that all agree cutting is not considered making for sukkah; rather, they argue whether lulav is derived from sukkah at all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects this, stating that everyone agrees cutting does not constitute making for sukkah, and the dispute is about whether lulav is derived from sukkah.

items.text: Third explanation: dispute about lulav binding requirement
items.text_en: Third explanation: dispute about lulav binding requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another possibility: all agree lulav is derived from sukkah, but they argue whether lulav requires binding. This is linked to a Tannaic dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis about binding, with Rabbi Yehuda deriving the requirement from a gezerah shavah between 'taking' in lulav and the hyssop bundle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers a third explanation: all agree that lulav is derived from sukkah, but they dispute whether lulav requires binding (אגד).
The Gemara cites a Tannaic dispute: the Rabbis deem a lulav valid whether bound or not, while Rabbi Yehuda requires binding.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Yehuda's position.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda derives the binding requirement from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the word 'taking' in lulav and the hyssop bundle.
The Rabbis reject the verbal analogy, asserting that 'taking' from 'taking' is not derived.

items.text: Reconciling a baraita with the dispute
items.text_en: Reconciling a baraita with the dispute
items.desc_en: A baraita states that binding a lulav is a mitzvah but not essential. The Gemara determines it follows the Rabbis, and the mitzvah aspect is derived from 'זה אלי ואנוהו' — beautifying the commandment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which authority holds that binding a lulab is a מצוה (commandment) but not essential, questioning whether it aligns with Rabbi Yehuda or the Sages.

The Gemara answers that it is the Sages' view, and the מצוה (commandment) to bind is based on the verse 'זה אלי ואנוהו' (this is my God and I will glorify Him), meaning one should beautify the mitzvah.

items.text: Source for the rule that s'chach must be from something that does not accept impurity
items.text_en: Source for the rule that s'chach must be from something that does not accept impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the scriptural source for the rule that s'chach must be from something that does not accept impurity and grows from the ground. Resh Lakish cites 'ואד יעלה מן הארץ'. The Gemara addresses the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer (clouds of glory) and Rabbi Akiva (actual sukkot), and Rabbi Yochanan offers an alternative derivation from the juxtaposition of sukkah to the festival offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the rule that s'chach must be from something that does not accept impurity and grows from the ground.
Resh Lakish cites the verse 'וְאֵד יַעֲלֶה מִן הָאָרֶץ' (a mist rises from the earth) to derive that s'chach must be like the mist — something that does not accept impurity and grows from the ground.
The Gemara objects that Resh Lakish's derivation works only for Rabbi Eliezer, who says the sukkot were clouds of glory, but not for Rabbi Akiva, who says they were actual sukkot.
A baraita cites the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says the sukkot were clouds of glory, Rabbi Akiva says they were actual sukkot.
The Gemara reiterates that Resh Lakish's derivation is fine for Rabbi Eliezer, but asks what source Rabbi Akiva would use.

Rabbi Yochanan, reported by Rav Dimi, offers an alternative derivation: the verse 'חַג הַסּוּכּוֹת תַּעֲשֶׂה לְךָ' juxtaposes sukkah to the festival offering (חגיגה), teaching that just as the offering must be from something that does not accept impurity and grows from the ground, so too s'chach.

items.text: Initial a fortiori argument from Chagigah
items.text_en: Initial a fortiori argument from Chagigah
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that just as the Chagigah offering requires living animals, so too sukkah roofing might require living materials (i.e., still attached to the ground). This is the opening challenge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an a fortiori argument: just as the Chagigah offering requires living animals, so too sukkah roofing might require living materials (still attached to the ground).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's derivation from the verse and subsequent refinements
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's derivation from the verse and subsequent refinements
items.desc_en: Ravin quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the verse 'in your gathering from your threshing floor and from your winepress' speaks of waste products, not the floor or press itself. Rabbi Zeira notes that 'winepress' is written and cannot be used for roofing. Rabbi Yirmeya objects with the case of congealed wine from Senir, which Rabbi Zeira dismisses. Rav Ashi then clarifies the verse's exclusion of the threshing floor and winepress themselves.

sub.desc_en: Ravin quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the verse 'בְּאָסְפְּךָ מִגָּרְנְךָ וּמִיִּקְבֶךָ' (when you gather from your threshing floor and winepress) speaks of waste products of the threshing floor and winepress, not the floor or press themselves.
The gemara objects: perhaps the verse permits roofing with the threshing floor and winepress themselves (i.e., their materials).
Rabbi Zeira answers that the word 'יֶקֶב' (winepress) is written here, and it is impossible to roof with a winepress itself (since it is a hollowed-out pit).
Rabbi Yirmeya objects: perhaps the verse refers to congealed wine from Senir, which is like cakes of pressed figs and could be used for roofing.
Rabbi Zeira dismisses the objection, saying that the matter was clear to him until Rabbi Yirmeya threw an axe into it (i.e., raised a difficult challenge).

Rav Ashi resolves the issue by explaining that the verse explicitly says 'מִגָּרְנְךָ' (from your threshing floor) and 'מִיִּקְבֶךָ' (from your winepress), excluding the threshing floor and winepress themselves.

items.text: Rav Chisda's alternative derivation from Nechemya
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's alternative derivation from Nechemya
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites a verse from Nechemya listing materials for the sukkah. The Gemara questions the redundancy of 'hadass' and 'etz avot'. Rav Chisda explains that 'hadass' refers to wild myrtle for the sukkah, while 'etz avot' refers to the myrtle for the lulav.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites the verse from Nechemya listing materials for the sukkah.
The Gemara questions the redundancy of 'hadass' and 'etz avot' in the verse.
Rav Chisda explains that 'hadass' refers to wild myrtle for the sukkah, while 'etz avot' refers to the myrtle for the lulav.

items.text: Mishnah: Bundles of stalks are invalid for roofing
items.text_en: Mishnah: Bundles of stalks are invalid for roofing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that bundles of straw, wood, or brushwood may not be used for sukkah roofing. However, if they are untied, they become valid. All such materials are valid for walls.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that bundles of straw, wood, or brushwood are invalid for sukkah roofing unless untied, but all are valid for walls.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yaakov's uncertainty about the reason for the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yaakov's uncertainty about the reason for the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov heard two rulings from Rabbi Yochanan: one about bundles (the Mishnah) and another about one who hollows out a stack for a sukkah. He knows one reason is a decree against storage and the other is 'ta'aseh ve-lo min he-asuy', but he does not know which applies to which. Rabbi Yirmeya resolves this by citing Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan that the bundles' invalidity is due to 'ta'aseh ve-lo min he-asuy', implying the other case is due to the decree against storage. Rabbi Yaakov simply had not heard that statement.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov reports that he heard two rulings from Rabbi Yochanan: one about bundles (the Mishnah) and one about one who hollows out a stack for a sukkah.

Rabbi Yaakov states that one reason is a decree against storage and the other is 'תעשה ולא מן העשוי' (you shall make, not from that which is already made), but he does not know which reason applies to which case.

Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the uncertainty by citing Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan that the bundles' invalidity is due to 'תעשה ולא מן העשוי', implying the other case is due to the decree against storage.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yaakov simply had not heard the statement of Rabbi Chiya bar Abba, which is why he remained uncertain.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects: surely both cases involve both reasons? Rabbi Yochanan would respond that the Mishnah's statement 'ein mesakchin bahen' refers only to the initial action (lechatchilah), not to a post-facto invalidity, thus the distinction stands.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects that both cases (bundles and the granary) involve both reasons (גזירת אוצר (concern for storage) and תעשה ולא מן העשוי (the requirement of making, not from what is already made)), so Rabbi Yochanan's distinction is unclear.

Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the Mishnah's statement 'אין מסככין בהן' (one may not roof with them) refers only to the initial action (לכתחילה), not to a post-facto invalidity, thus the distinction between the two cases stands.

items.text: Distinguishing Torah-level from rabbinic disqualification
items.text_en: Distinguishing Torah-level from rabbinic disqualification
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier Mishnah's ruling about a sukkah roofed with certain materials being invalid applies even post-facto, because the disqualification is Torah-level, not merely a rabbinic decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's disqualification of certain roofing materials applies even post-facto because the invalidity is Torah-level (דאורייתא), not merely a rabbinic decree.

items.text: Arrow shafts: male vs. female
items.text_en: Arrow shafts: male vs. female
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that a sukkah roofed with male arrow shafts is valid, but with female shafts it is invalid. The Gemara questions why these rulings are not obvious, and explains that the statements are needed to counter potential decrees or alternative interpretations of kabolah.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that a sukkah roofed with male arrow shafts is valid, but with female shafts it is invalid.
The Gemara questions why the ruling about male shafts is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is needed to counter a potential decree that would forbid male shafts due to female shafts.
The Gemara questions why the ruling about female shafts is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is needed to counter the alternative interpretation that a receptacle made for filling is not considered a receptacle.

items.text: Flax stalks: anitzai vs. hutznei vs. hushnei
items.text_en: Flax stalks: anitzai vs. hutznei vs. hushnei
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that a sukkah roofed with anitzai (coarse flax stalks) is invalid, but with hutznei (fine flax stalks) it is valid. He is uncertain about hushnei. The Gemara then analyzes the definitions of hushnei and hutznei, questioning whether hushnei refers to stalks that are beaten but not combed, or also to those that are split but not beaten.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that a sukkah roofed with anitzai (coarse flax stalks) is invalid, with hutznei (fine flax stalks) it is valid, and he is uncertain about hushnei.
The Gemara analyzes the definition of hushnei, questioning whether it refers to stalks that are beaten but not combed, or also to those that are split but not beaten.

items.text: Palm branches: shushei and shvotzrei
items.text_en: Palm branches: shushei and shvotzrei
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that one may roof with both shushei (palm branches) and shvotzrei (palm branches with thorns). Abaye disagrees, permitting only shushei but not shvotzrei, because the thorns may fall and invalidate the sukkah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that one may roof a sukkah with both shushei (palm branches) and shvotzrei (palm branches with thorns).
Abaye objects, permitting only shushei but not shvotzrei, because the thorns may fall and invalidate the sukkah.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind Abaye's distinction.

items.text: Opening statement on thorny plants
items.text_en: Opening statement on thorny plants
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that thorny plants whose smell is foul are left and one exits the sukkah, implying they are invalid for s'chach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that thorny plants with foul smell are left and one exits the sukkah, implying they are invalid for s'chach.

items.text: Rav Chanan bar Rava and Abaye on thorn bushes and palm branches
items.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava and Abaye on thorn bushes and palm branches
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava permits s'chach with thorn bushes (hizmei) and palm branches (higei). Abaye disagrees, permitting only hizmei because higei shed their leaves, causing one to leave the sukkah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rava rules that thorny plants (היזמי and היגי) are valid for s'chach.
Abaye distinguishes: היזמי (thorny plants) are valid for s'chach, but היגי (reeds) are not, because their leaves fall off and one would leave the sukkah.
Abaye explains that higei shed their leaves, causing one to leave the sukkah.

items.text: Rav Giddel and Rav Chisda on palm branches and reeds
items.text_en: Rav Giddel and Rav Chisda on palm branches and reeds
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel says palm branches (apakuta d'dikla) are valid for s'chach even if tied, as a tie made by heaven is not considered a valid tie. Rav Chisda says the same for reed stalks (dukrei d'kanei).

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel says in the name of Rav that palm offshoots (אפקותא דדיקלא) are valid for סכך (roofing) even if naturally bound, since a heavenly binding is not considered a binding.
Rav Giddel adds that even if one later ties the branches together, a single tie is not considered a valid binding.

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Sheila
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Sheila
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda says in the name of Ravina bar Sheila that reed offshoots (דוקרי דקני) are valid for סכך (roofing) even if naturally bound, since a heavenly binding is not a binding.
Rav Chisda adds that even if one later ties the reeds together, a single tie is not considered a valid binding.

items.text: Supporting baraita for reeds
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for reeds
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited supporting that reeds and stalks are valid for s'chach, and the Gemara clarifies it means reeds of stalks.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that reeds and stalks may be used for s'chach.
The Gemara questions why the baraita mentions reeds, as their validity is obvious.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to offshoots of reeds, not ordinary reeds.

items.text: Rav Chisda on maroryata for Passover
items.text_en: Rav Chisda on maroryata for Passover
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that marsh maror (maroryata d'agma) can be used to fulfill the obligation of bitter herbs on Passover.

sub.text: Rav Chisda quoting Ravina bar Sheila
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda quoting Ravina bar Sheila
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Ravina bar Sheila rules that marsh bitter herbs (מררייתא דאגמא) fulfill one's obligation for maror on Passover.

items.text: Objection and resolution about maroryata
items.text_en: Objection and resolution about maroryata
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita listing invalid types of ezov. Abaye explains that only plants whose name changed before the Torah was given are invalid, and these maroryata never changed. Rava says their name is simply "maror" and the specification "of the marsh" is just a location.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists types of ezov (hyssop) that are invalid, including those with a secondary name (לווי), challenging the permissibility of maroryata.
Abaye answers that only plants whose name changed before the Torah was given and which the Torah specifically disqualified are invalid, but these maroryata never changed their name.
Rava answers that the name of these plants is simply 'maror' (bitter herbs), and the specification 'of the marsh' is merely a description of their location, not a secondary name.

items.text: Debate on the number of stems in an ezov bundle
items.text_en: Debate on the number of stems in an ezov bundle
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that a bundle of one is not called a bundle, three is a bundle, and two is disputed between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis. The Gemara analyzes a mishnah and baraitot to determine whether three stems are required for validity or just for the mitzvah, concluding that for Rabbi Yosei three are essential, while for the Rabbis three are only optimal.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states the general rule: a bundle of one is not called a bundle, three is a bundle, and two is disputed between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis.
The Gemara cites a mishnah about the mitzvah of ezov: three stems with three buds, and Rabbi Yosei says the mitzvah requires three buds, its remnants two, and its stumps any amount.
The Gemara initially assumes that since remnants are two, the initial bundle is also two, so the three mentioned are only for the mitzvah, and for the Rabbis three are essential.
The Gemara objects with a baraita where Rabbi Yosei says an ezov with initial two and remnant one is invalid, requiring initial three and remnant two.
The Gemara reverses the initial assumption: for Rabbi Yosei three are essential, for the Rabbis three are only for the mitzvah.
The Gemara cites another baraita stating that an ezov with initial two and remnant one is valid, and it is invalid only when both initial and remnant are one.
The Gemara objects: the baraita says remnant one is invalid, but earlier it said remnant one is valid, creating a contradiction.

items.text: Refinement of the principle regarding s'chach
items.text_en: Refinement of the principle regarding s'chach
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the rule requiring the beginning of a bundle to be like its remnants applies uniformly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara refines the principle, stating that the beginning of the bundle must be uniform with its remnants.

items.text: Bundled reeds and their validity for s'chach
items.text_en: Bundled reeds and their validity for s'chach
items.desc_en: Marimar permits using bundled reeds from Sura, as the binding is only for counting. Rabbi Abba discusses willow twigs whose heads are loosened, and Rav Papa explains they are untied. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua adds that any bundle not made for handling is not considered a binding.

sub.desc_en: Marimar permits using bundled reeds from Sura for s'chach, explaining the binding is only for counting.
Rabbi Abba rules that willow twigs whose heads are loosened are valid for s'chach.
The gemara objects that the twigs are still bound from below.
Rav Papa answers that the twigs are untied.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua adds that any bundle not made for handling is not considered a binding.

items.text: Vegetables that are invalid for sukkah due to air
items.text_en: Vegetables that are invalid for sukkah due to air
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba citing Shmuel states that certain vegetables used for the Passover obligation convey impurity, do not interpose, and invalidate the sukkah due to air, because when dry they crumble and fall.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba cites Shmuel that vegetables used for the Passover obligation convey impurity, do not interpose, and disqualify a sukkah due to airspace, because when dry they crumble and fall.
Shmuel explains the reason: because when these vegetables dry, they crumble and fall, so they are considered as if they are not present.

items.text: Handles for produce: grapes vs. grain for roofing
items.text_en: Handles for produce: grapes vs. grain for roofing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba citing Rav Huna says one who harvests grapes for the winepress has no handles. Rav Menashya bar Gadda citing Rav Huna says one who reaps for roofing has no handles. The Gemara explains the difference: for grapes, handles are undesirable to avoid souring wine; for grain, handles are desirable to prevent scattering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba citing Rav Huna states that one who harvests grapes for the winepress has no handles (ידות).

sub.text: Rav Menashya bar Gadda citing Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Menashya bar Gadda citing Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Menashya bar Gadda citing Rav Huna adds that one who reaps grain for roofing also has no handles.
The Gemara explains the difference: for grapes, handles are undesirable to avoid souring wine; for grain, handles are desirable to prevent scattering.

items.text: Is Rav Menashya's view a Tannaic dispute?
items.text_en: Is Rav Menashya's view a Tannaic dispute?
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav Menashya bar Gadda's ruling may be subject to a Tannaic dispute, where one opinion holds there are handles and another holds there are none.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav Menashya bar Gadda's ruling is subject to a Tannaic dispute.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Tanna Kamma and Acherim dispute whether handles (ידות) are counted as part of the material for s'chach.
The Gemara concludes that the dispute is precisely about whether handles (ידות) exist, aligning with Rav Menashya's view.

items.text: Resolution: change of intention and nullification
items.text_en: Resolution: change of intention and nullification
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that for Rabbi Abba it is a Tannaic dispute, but for Rav Menashya all agree that one who reaps for roofing has no handles. The case involves produce initially cut for food and later reconsidered for roofing. The Gemara questions whether a change of intention nullifies the original designation, citing a Mishnah about vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that for Rabbi Abba the dispute is certainly Tannaic, but for Rav Menashya bar Gadda all agree that one who reaps for roofing has no handles.
Rav Menashya explains that the baraita deals with produce initially cut for food and later reconsidered for roofing.
The Gemara questions why the Rabbis would disagree if the produce was cut for food, and whether a change of intention nullifies the original designation.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah about vessels to challenge whether a change of intention nullifies the original designation.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Susceptibility to impurity through intention and action
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Susceptibility to impurity through intention and action
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that items become susceptible to impurity through intention but can only be purified through a change in action. Action overrides both action and intention, while intention does not override either.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: items become susceptible to impurity through intention but are purified only through a change in action; action overrides both action and intention, while intention overrides neither.

items.text: Gemara's question: Handles of produce
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Handles of produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether handles of produce, which are needed for eating, can become susceptible to impurity through intention and be purified by intention. It cites a Mishnah about handles attached to produce in the granary being pure, with Rabbi Yose declaring them impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a potential objection: perhaps the Mishnah's rule applies only to significant vessels, but handles (ידות) of produce, which are merely for eating convenience, might become susceptible and purified through intention alone.
The Gemara cites a baraita: all produce-handles whose 'בססן' (base/attachment) is in the granary are pure, and Rabbi Yosei declares them impure.

items.text: Interpretation of 'בססן'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'בססן'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the opinion that 'בססן' means 'untied their bundles', the Mishnah is clear. But according to the opinion that 'בססן' means 'their bases' literally, what is the explanation?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to the view that 'בססן' means 'untied their bundles', the baraita is fine; but according to the view that 'בססן' means literally 'their base', what can be said?

items.text: Answer: Handles attached to the produce
items.text_en: Answer: Handles attached to the produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that here too the handles are attached to the produce. It questions why others (the Sages) disagree with Rabbi Yose, and suggests they follow Rabbi Yose's reasoning. The Gemara then asks what the rationale is here, and answers that the handles are useful for turning the produce with a pitchfork.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that here too the handles are attached to the produce (בססן ממש).
The Gemara asks why the Sages (אחרים) disagree with Rabbi Yose if the handles are attached.
The Gemara answers that the Sages follow Rabbi Yose's reasoning, citing the Mishnah that Rabbi Yose declares impure.
The Gemara objects that the comparison is invalid, asking what practical use the handles have here.
The Gemara answers that the handles are useful for turning the produce with a pitchfork (בגילייהו).

items.text: Dispute about 'בססן' and Rabbi Yose's reasoning
items.text_en: Dispute about 'בססן' and Rabbi Yose's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah again and explains the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Eliezer about the meaning of 'בססן'. Rabbi Yochanan says it means literally 'their bases', while Rabbi Eliezer says it means 'untied their bundles'. The Gemara then asks why Rabbi Yose would declare impure according to Rabbi Yochanan, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish answers that the handles are useful for turning the produce with a pitchfork.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah about handles of produce that are 'בססן' (their bases) in the granary being pure, with Rabbi Yose declaring them impure.
The Gemara asks what the word 'בססן' means.
Rabbi Yochanan says 'בססן' means their actual bases.
Rabbi Eliezer says 'בססן' means they untied their bundles.
The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yose's ruling is understandable, but asks why Rabbi Yose would declare impure according to Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish answers that the handles are useful for turning the produce with a pitchfork (עתר), so they are considered significant and can become impure.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's homily on prayer
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's homily on prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer explains why the prayer of the righteous is compared to a pitchfork (עתר): just as a pitchfork turns produce from place to place, so too prayer turns God's attribute from cruelty to mercy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer offers a homiletical interpretation: the prayer of the righteous is compared to an עתר (winnowing shovel), just as it turns produce from place to place, so prayer turns God's attribute from cruelty to mercy.

items.text: Mishnah: Roofing with boards
items.text_en: Mishnah: Roofing with boards
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may roof a sukkah with boards according to Rabbi Yehuda, but Rabbi Meir forbids it. If one placed a board four handbreadths wide, the sukkah is valid provided one does not sleep under it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: one may roof a sukkah with boards — Rabbi Yehuda permits, Rabbi Meir forbids. If one placed a board four handbreadths wide, the sukkah is valid provided one does not sleep under it.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rav says the dispute is about boards four handbreadths wide, while Shmuel says it is about boards less than four handbreadths. Rav Pappa clarifies that boards four handbreadths wide are universally invalid, boards less than three are universally valid, and the dispute is between three and four handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir is about boards four handbreadths wide, but boards less than four are universally valid.
Shmuel argues that the dispute is about boards less than four handbreadths, while boards four handbreadths wide are universally invalid.
The Gemara questions whether boards less than three handbreadths are merely reeds and thus universally valid.

Rav Pappa resolves the question by clarifying that boards four handbreadths wide are universally invalid, boards less than three are universally valid, and the dispute is only between three and four handbreadths, based on whether we decree due to the rule of לבוד (the principle of joining gaps).

items.text: Support from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Support from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's statement about a board four handbreadths wide. According to Shmuel, it is consistent. According to Rav, the Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda would prohibit sleeping under it. The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's ruling is according to Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that a board four handbreadths wide renders the sukkah valid but prohibits sleeping under it.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah is consistent with Shmuel's view that the dispute is about narrow boards, but questions how it fits Rav's view that the dispute is about wide boards.
The Gemara asks: according to Rav, why would Rabbi Yehuda prohibit sleeping under a four-handbreadth board, since he permits wide boards for s'chach?
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's ruling is not a consensus but follows Rabbi Meir, who prohibits sleeping under any wide board.

items.text: New teaching: Two sheets combine
items.text_en: New teaching: Two sheets combine
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a new teaching: two sheets (of material) combine (to form a valid covering).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a supporting baraita: two sheets (of s'chach material) combine (to form a valid covering).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that two boards do not combine (to form a width of four tefachim), but Rabbi Meir says that boards are like a sheet (and do combine).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute: two boards do not combine to form a valid width, but Rabbi Meir says they combine like a sheet.

items.text: Gemara's analysis according to Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis according to Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah according to Shmuel's view that the dispute is about boards lacking four tefachim, but all agree boards of four tefachim are invalid. It then questions Rav's view that the dispute is about boards of four tefachim, and resolves that the Mishnah refers to combining for four amot from the side.

sub.text: Gemara's opening analysis according to Shmuel
sub.text_en: Gemara's opening analysis according to Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Shmuel's view that the dispute is about boards lacking four tefachim, the Mishnah's 'join' means they join to form four tefachim.
The Gemara questions Rav's view that the dispute is about boards of four tefachim: if they have four tefachim, why join? If they lack four tefachim, they are mere reeds.
The Gemara resolves that the boards indeed have four tefachim, and 'join' means they join to form four amot from the side.

items.text: Alternative version of the analysis
items.text_en: Alternative version of the analysis
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative version: according to Shmuel, the Mishnah's 'combine' refers to combining for four amot from the side. According to Rav, for Rabbi Meir it means combining for four amot from the side, but for Rabbi Yehuda who validates even boards of four tefachim, the Mishnah's statement is merely a response to Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative version of the analysis, explaining that according to Shmuel, the Mishnah's 'combine' refers to combining for four amot from the side.

The Gemara explains that according to Rav, for Rabbi Meir the Mishnah's 'combine' means combining for four amot from the side, but for Rabbi Yehuda, who validates even boards of four tefachim, the Mishnah's statement 'they do not combine' is merely a response to Rabbi Meir's position.

items.text: Baraitot supporting Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Baraitot supporting Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one supports Rav by stating that boards of four tefachim are disputed between Rabbi Meir (invalid) and Rabbi Yehuda (valid), with a story from a time of danger. Another supports Shmuel by stating that boards of four tefachim are universally invalid, and boards lacking four tefachim are disputed, with concessions from both rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara announces that there are baraitot supporting both Rav and Shmuel.
A baraita supports Rav: boards lacking four tefachim are universally valid; boards of four tefachim are disputed between Rabbi Meir (invalid) and Rabbi Yehuda (valid).
Rabbi Yehuda cites a precedent from a time of danger where they used boards of four tefachim for the סכך (roofing) and sat under them.
The Sages reject Rabbi Yehuda's proof, arguing that a time of danger provides no halachic precedent.

A baraita supports Shmuel: boards of four tefachim are universally invalid; boards lacking four tefachim are disputed between Rabbi Meir (invalid) and Rabbi Yehuda (valid), with concessions from both rabbis.

items.text: Dispute about boards turned on their sides
items.text_en: Dispute about boards turned on their sides
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that boards placed on their sides are invalid, while Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna rule they are valid. Rav Nachman, when asked, rules invalid because they become like metal spits. Rav Huna then chides the others for not accepting his ruling, and they explain they had not heard his reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute about boards turned on their sides: Rav Huna rules invalid, while Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna rule valid.
Rav Nachman visits Sura, is asked the same question by Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna, and rules invalid because the boards become like metal spits.

sub.text: Rav Huna's rebuke and the sages' response
sub.text_en: Rav Huna's rebuke and the sages' response
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna chides Rav Chisda and Rabbah bar Rav Huna for not accepting his ruling, and they explain they had not heard his reasoning.

items.text: Attempted support and resolution
items.text_en: Attempted support and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Rav Huna from a baraita about a board four tefachim wide placed on the sukkah, but rejects the proof, explaining the case is about a board placed on the sukkah's opening with part extending outside, which is considered valid as part of the sukkah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that a baraita about a board placed on a sukkah supports Rav Huna's position.
The Gemara rejects the support, explaining the baraita refers to a board placed on the sukkah's opening with part protruding, not turned on its side.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute about a roof without plaster: Beit Shammai requires both loosening and removing a board, Beit Hillel allows either, and Rabbi Meir requires only removing a board without loosening.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute about a roof without plaster: Beit Shammai requires both loosening and removing a board, Beit Hillel allows either, and Rabbi Meir requires only removing a board without loosening.

items.text: Gemara's question on Beit Shammai's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Beit Shammai's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Beit Shammai's requirement for both actions: if the concern is 'תעשה ולא מן העשוי', one action suffices; if it is a decree against using a roof (גזרת תקרה), removing a board alone should suffice. The Gemara answers that Beit Shammai holds that even with loosening, removal is still required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Beit Shammai's reasoning: if the concern is 'תעשה ולא מן העשוי' (you shall make and not from that already made), one action suffices; if it is a decree against using a roof (גזרת תקרה), removing a board alone should suffice.
The Gemara answers that Beit Shammai indeed holds the decree against using a roof (גזרת תקרה), but they require both loosening and removal: even after loosening, removal is still necessary.

items.text: Question on Rabbi Meir's position
items.text_en: Question on Rabbi Meir's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Meir's view (remove a board but do not loosen) seems identical to Beit Shammai's, and resolves that Rabbi Meir meant that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree on this point.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If so, consider the latter clause of the Mishnah — Rabbi Meir's position (remove a board but do not loosen) seems identical to Beit Shammai's, so why is it stated separately?
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Meir meant that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree on this point, so his statement is not redundant but clarifying the consensus.

items.text: Challenge: redundant dispute
items.text_en: Challenge: redundant dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats the dispute about the decree of the roof (גזרת תקרה) when it was already debated elsewhere regarding planks, where Rabbi Yehuda permits and Rabbi Meir forbids.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Meir's statement is necessary, since the dispute about the decree against using a roof (גזירת תקרה) already appears in a Mishnah about using boards for סכך (covering).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution: planks are smoothed
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's resolution: planks are smoothed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the earlier dispute (about planks) deals with smoothed planks, where the concern is a decree against using vessels (גזרת כלים), not the roof decree. The Gemara objects based on Rav Yehuda's principle that one does not decree for similar cases.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the dispute in the Mishnah deals with smoothed planks (נסרים משופין), and the concern is a decree against using vessels (גזרת כלים), not the roof decree.
The Gemara objects based on Rav Yehuda's principle that one does not decree for similar cases (לא גזרינן), arguing that smoothed planks should not be forbidden due to a decree against vessels.

items.text: Alternative resolution: both disputes are about the roof decree
