sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the willow overrides Shabbat for them, why did they not override it? It answers that since we do not override, they also did not, but notes that the first festival day overrides for them but not for us.
The Gemara answers that since we in Babylonia do not override, they also did not override, just as the first day of Sukkot does not override for us but does for them.

items.text: Reconciling two baraitot about where the lulav is taken
items.text_en: Reconciling two baraitot about where the lulav is taken
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two baraitot: one says people bring their lulavim to the Temple Mount, another says to the synagogue. It resolves that one refers to when the Temple stands, the other to when it does not. Alternatively, both refer to when the Temple stands, but one is in the Temple and the other in the provinces.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two baraitot: one says people bring their lulavim to the Temple Mount, another says to the synagogue.
The Gemara resolves that one baraita refers to when the Temple stands, the other to when it does not.
Alternatively, both baraitot refer to when the Temple stands, but one is in the Temple and the other in the provinces.

items.text: Abaye's question to Rava about the willow
items.text_en: Abaye's question to Rava about the willow
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rava why the lulav is taken for seven days as a memorial to the Temple but the willow is not. Rava answers that one fulfills the obligation with the willow in the lulav. Abaye objects that this is due to the lulav, and if one lifts it separately, that is not done daily.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rava why the lulav is taken for seven days as a memorial to the Temple but the willow is not.
Rava answers that one fulfills the obligation with the willow that is part of the lulav.
Abaye objects that the willow's inclusion is due to the lulav, and if one lifts it separately, that is not done daily.

items.text: Rav Zevid's first answer in the name of Rava
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's first answer in the name of Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid says in the name of Rava that the lulav, which is Torah law, is taken for seven days as a memorial to the Temple, but the willow, which is rabbinic, is not.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid answers in the name of Rava that the lulav, which is Torah law, is taken for seven days as a memorial to the Temple, but the willow, which is rabbinic, is not.

items.text: Questioning the premise: whose opinion is this?
items.text_en: Questioning the premise: whose opinion is this?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion this answer follows. If it is Abba Shaul, he derives two willows from the verse, one for the lulav and one for the Temple. If it is the Rabbis, they have a tradition from Rabbi Nechunya that the willow is a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion this follows, suggesting it might be Abba Shaul, who derives two willows from the verse.
The Gemara suggests alternatively that it follows the Rabbis, who have a tradition from Rabbi Nechunya that the willow is a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai.

items.text: Rav Zevid's second answer in the name of Rava
items.text_en: Rav Zevid's second answer in the name of Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid says in the name of Rava that the lulav, which has a Torah source, is taken for seven days in the provinces as a memorial to the Temple, but the willow, which has no Torah source, is not taken for seven days in the provinces.

sub.text: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid resolves the contradiction by distinguishing lulav, which has a Torah source, from willow, which lacks a Torah source, so only lulav is taken for seven days in the provinces as a memorial to the Temple.

items.text: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan debate the willow in the Temple
items.text_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan debate the willow in the Temple
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish says that blemished priests may enter between the Entrance Hall and the Altar to fulfill the willow ceremony. Rabbi Yochanan questions this, citing the tradition that the willow is a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai. The Gemara suggests that perhaps the tradition refers to planting, not taking, or to unblemished priests, not blemished ones.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that blemished priests may enter between the Entrance Hall and the Altar to perform the willow ceremony.
Rabbi Yochanan objects, citing the tradition that the willow ceremony is a הלכה למשה מסיני (halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai), implying it has strict rules.
The Gemara resolves the objection by suggesting that the tradition may refer to planting (זקיפה) rather than taking (נטילה), or to unblemished priests rather than blemished ones.

items.text: Dispute over the status of the willow: foundation or custom of prophets
items.text_en: Dispute over the status of the willow: foundation or custom of prophets
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi disagree: one says the willow is a foundation of the prophets, the other says it is a custom of the prophets. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan holds it is a foundation, based on a statement by Rabbi Avahu. Rabbi Zeira challenges this, citing Rabbi Yochanan's own tradition that it is a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai. Rabbi Avahu is stunned and explains that it was forgotten and then re-established.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: one says the willow is a foundation of the prophets (יסוד נביאים), the other says it is a custom of the prophets (מנהג נביאים).
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yochanan is the one who said 'foundation of the prophets', based on Rabbi Avahu's explicit statement in his name.

Rabbi Zeira challenges Rabbi Avahu: Did Rabbi Yochanan really say that? He himself transmitted a tradition from Rabbi Nechunya that the willow is a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai (הלכה למשה מסיני), which is a higher authority than a prophetic foundation.
Rabbi Avahu is stunned for a moment and then explains: they (the people) had forgotten the halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai tradition, and the prophets re-established it as a foundation.

items.text: Final question and unresolved conclusion
items.text_en: Final question and unresolved conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks again whether Rabbi Yochanan really said this, citing another statement of his that seems to contradict. It concludes that there is no difficulty, but the text breaks off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yochanan really said this, citing another statement of his that seems to contradict.
The Gemara concludes that there is no difficulty, but the text breaks off without further explanation.

items.text: Opening distinction between Temple and provinces
items.text_en: Opening distinction between Temple and provinces
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by distinguishing between the practice of the willow branch in the Temple and in the provinces, setting up the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by distinguishing between the practice of the willow branch in the Temple and in the provinces.

items.text: Rabbi Ami's ruling on the willow and Rav Chisda's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's ruling on the willow and Rav Chisda's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami states that the willow requires a minimum size, is taken alone, and one cannot fulfill the obligation with the willow in the lulav. The Gemara questions the redundancy of the last point, and Rav Chisda cites Rabbi Yitzchak who permits using the willow in the lulav on the first festival day.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami rules that the willow requires a minimum size, is taken alone, and one cannot fulfill the obligation with the willow in the lulav.
The Gemara questions the redundancy of the last point, since if the willow is taken alone, it is obvious that one cannot fulfill the obligation with the willow in the lulav.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is needed to counter a possible distinction between lifting the willow alone and lifting it with the lulav.
Rav Chisda cites Rabbi Yitzchak who permits fulfilling the obligation with the willow in the lulav on the first festival day, contradicting Rabbi Ami's ruling.

items.text: Dispute over the minimum size of the willow
items.text_en: Dispute over the minimum size of the willow
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman requires three moist branches, while Rav Sheshet says even one leaf on one branch suffices. The Gemara clarifies Rav Sheshet's statement to avoid absurdity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the minimum size of the willow branch is.
Rav Nachman answers that three moist branches are required.
Rav Sheshet answers that even one leaf on one branch suffices.
The Gemara objects that the literal reading of Rav Sheshet's statement is absurd.
The Gemara resolves the objection by clarifying that Rav Sheshet meant even one leaf on a single branch.

items.text: The custom of beating the willow without a blessing
items.text_en: The custom of beating the willow without a blessing
items.desc_en: Aivu testifies that Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok beat the willow without reciting a blessing, considering it a custom of the prophets. Similarly, Aivu and Chizkiyah brought a willow to Rav, who also beat it without a blessing.

sub.desc_en: Aivu testifies that Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok beat the willow without reciting a blessing, considering it a custom of the prophets.
Aivu and Chizkiyah brought a willow to Rav, who also beat it without a blessing, confirming the same custom.

items.text: Story about gleaning in the Sabbatical year
items.text_en: Story about gleaning in the Sabbatical year
items.desc_en: Aivu recounts a story where a man asked Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok whether he should protest people gleaning his vineyards and olives. The rabbi initially said no, but later advised him to declare the olives ownerless for the poor and pay the gleaners to prevent damage.

sub.desc_en: Aivu recounts a story where a man asked Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok whether he should protest people gleaning his vineyards and olives. The rabbi initially said no, but later advised him to declare the olives ownerless for the poor and pay the gleaners to prevent damage.

items.text: Clarification of permitted and forbidden gleaning
items.text_en: Clarification of permitted and forbidden gleaning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the permissibility of gleaning (קישוקש) during the Sabbatical year, citing a baraita that prohibits it. Rav Ukva bar Chama distinguishes between two types: closing cracks (permitted) and strengthening trees (forbidden).

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: is gleaning (קישושי) permitted during the Sabbatical year?
A baraita is cited: the verse 'the seventh year you shall let it rest and abandon it' teaches that one must refrain from gleaning (קישוש) and from clearing stones (סקילה).
Rav Ukva bar Chama resolves: there are two types of gleaning — one that strengthens trees (אברויי אילני) is forbidden, and one that closes cracks (סתומי פילי) is permitted.

items.text: Limit on walking on Shabbat eve and Rav Kahana's qualification
items.text_en: Limit on walking on Shabbat eve and Rav Kahana's qualification
items.desc_en: Aivu quotes Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok that one should not walk more than three parsangs on Shabbat eve. Rav Kahana limits this to returning home, but another version says even for home it applies, and Rav Kahana testifies that he once could not even find a cup of water.

sub.text: Aivu citing Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
sub.text_en: Aivu citing Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
sub.desc_en: Aivu quotes Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok's ruling that one should not walk more than three parsangs on Shabbat eve.
Rav Kahana limits the restriction to returning home, but not to going to a host's home where one carries provisions.
An alternate version states that Rav Kahana applied the restriction even to returning home, and he testifies from personal experience that he once could not even find a cup of water.

items.text: Beginning of the Mishnah on the lulav ritual
items.text_en: Beginning of the Mishnah on the lulav ritual
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Mishnah's description of the lulav ritual, with a Tanna reciting before Rav Nachman about placing scarves on the platform.

sub.desc_en: A tanna recites before Rav Nachman: the mitzvah of the lulav is performed with cloths on the roof of the platform.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the willow placement
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the willow placement
items.desc_en: Rachava quoting Rav Yehuda explains that the Temple Mount had a double portico, resolving the earlier question about where the willows were placed.

sub.desc_en: Rachava citing Rav Yehuda resolves the earlier question by stating that the Temple Mount had a double portico (סטיו כפול), one portico inside the other.

items.text: Mishnah: The willow ceremony
items.text_en: Mishnah: The willow ceremony
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for the willow ceremony: gathering branches from Motza, placing them by the altar, circling the altar daily and seven times on Hoshana Rabbah, and the declarations made. It also notes the Sabbath procedure and Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's alternative practice.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing the procedure for the willow ceremony: gathering branches from Motza, placing them by the altar with their tops bent over it.
The Mishnah describes the daily circling of the altar with blasts of the shofar and the recitation of 'Ana Hashem hoshia na'.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the declaration was 'Ani Vahu hoshia na'.
The Mishnah notes that on Hoshana Rabbah they circled the altar seven times and upon departing said 'Yofi lekha mizbe'ach'.
Rabbi Elazar says the declaration was 'LeYah ulekha mizbe'ach'.
The Mishnah describes the Sabbath procedure: branches were gathered on the eve and placed in golden basins to prevent wilting.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka describes an alternative practice of bringing palm branches and beating them on the ground, and notes that children would then take their lulavim and eat their etrogim.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of 'Motza'
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of 'Motza'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the place called 'Motza' was a place of willows (קָלָנְיָא), and the Tanna of our Mishnah calls it 'Motza' because it was exempt from the king's tax (כְּרָגָא דְמַלְכָּא).

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the place called 'Motza' was a place of willows (קָלָנְיָא).
The Gemara asks why the Tanna of our Mishnah calls it 'Motza' rather than using the baraita's name.
The Gemara answers that it is called 'Motza' because it was exempt from the king's tax (כְּרָגָא דְמַלְכָּא), i.e., a place of 'exemption' (מוֹצָא).

items.text: Gemara: Height of the willow branches
items.text_en: Gemara: Height of the willow branches
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the willow branches were eleven cubits long so that they would lean over the altar by one cubit.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the willow branches were tall, long, and eleven cubits high so that they would lean over the altar by one cubit.

items.text: Gemara: Placement on the foundation
items.text_en: Gemara: Placement on the foundation
items.desc_en: Marimar in the name of Mar Zutra proves from the height of the branches that they were placed on the foundation (yesod) of the altar, not on the ground, because otherwise they could not lean over the altar by a cubit given the altar's dimensions.

sub.text: Marimar in the name of Mar Zutra
sub.text_en: Marimar in the name of Mar Zutra
sub.desc_en: Marimar in the name of Mar Zutra proves that the willow branches were placed on the foundation (יסוד) of the altar, not on the ground, by calculating that otherwise they could not lean over the altar by a cubit given the altar's stepped dimensions.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural basis for binding lulav and hadas
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural basis for binding lulav and hadas
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu cites a verse linking the altar to the binding of the lulav and hadas, and Rabbi Avahu quoting Rabbi Elazar states that one who takes a lulav bound with its hadas is considered as if they built an altar and offered a sacrifice.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu asks what is the scriptural basis for binding the lulav and hadas, citing the verse 'אִסְרוּ חַג בַּעֲבוֹתִים עַד קַרְנוֹת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ' (bind the festival with ropes to the horns of the altar).

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu quoting Rabbi Elazar's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu quoting Rabbi Elazar's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu, in the name of Rabbi Elazar, states that one who takes a lulav bound with its hadas is considered by Scripture as if they built an altar and offered a sacrifice.

items.text: Teaching on binding the festival offering
items.text_en: Teaching on binding the festival offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon HaMachozi, teach that one who binds the festival with eating and drinking is considered by Scripture as if they built an altar and offered a sacrifice, based on the verse 'Bind the festival with cords to the horns of the altar.'

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and Rabbi Shimon HaMachozi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and Rabbi Shimon HaMachozi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Yochanan teach that one who binds the festival with eating and drinking is credited as if they built an altar and offered a sacrifice, based on the verse 'Bind the festival with cords to the horns of the altar.'

items.text: Principle of performing mitzvot in their natural state
items.text_en: Principle of performing mitzvot in their natural state
items.desc_en: Chizkiya quotes Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that all mitzvot must be performed in their natural state of growth, as derived from the verse 'Acacia wood, standing.' A baraita supports this with three interpretations: they stand as they grow, they support their plating, and they stand forever.

sub.text: Chizkiyah citing Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Chizkiyah citing Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Chizkiyah states that all commandments must be performed in their natural growth direction, citing the verse 'Acacia wood standing upright.'
A baraita supports the principle with three interpretations of 'standing': they stand in their growth direction, they support their plating, and they endure forever.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's claim to exempt the world from judgment
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's claim to exempt the world from judgment
items.desc_en: Chizkiya quotes Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that he could exempt the entire world from judgment from his birth until now, and with his son Eliezer from the creation until now, and with Yotam ben Uziyahu from creation until the end.

sub.text: Chizkiyah citing Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Chizkiyah citing Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Chizkiyah reports that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai claimed he could exempt the entire world from judgment from creation until now, and with his son Eliezer and Yotam ben Uziyahu, from creation until the end.

items.text: The few who see the Divine Presence and the resolution of contradictions
items.text_en: The few who see the Divine Presence and the resolution of contradictions
items.desc_en: Chizkiya quotes Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai that he saw few 'sons of the upper chamber' (righteous). The Gemara questions this based on Rava's statement of 18,000 and Abaye's statement of 36 righteous who receive the Divine Presence daily. It resolves that those who see through a clear speculum are few, while those who enter without permission are many.

sub.text: Chizkiya quoting Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Chizkiya quoting Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Chizkiya reports Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's statement that he saw few 'sons of the upper chamber' (righteous), and if there are only two, he and his son are those two.
The Gemara questions how the righteous can be so few, given Rava's statement about 18,000 righteous before God.
The Gemara cites Rava's statement that there are 18,000 righteous in the row before the Holy One, based on the verse 'around eighteen thousand'.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai refers to those who see through a clear speculum (the Divine Presence directly), while Rava refers to those who see through a non-luminous speculum.
The Gemara questions how even those who see through a clear speculum can be so few, given Abaye's statement about 36 righteous who receive the Divine Presence daily.
The Gemara cites Abaye's statement that the world never lacks 36 righteous who receive the Divine Presence daily, based on the gematria of 'לו' (36) in the verse 'אשרי כל חוכי לו'.

The Gemara resolves the second contradiction: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai refers to those who enter the Divine Presence without permission (בלא בר), while Abaye refers to those who enter with permission (בבר).

items.text: The willow ceremony and the issue of associating God's name with another
items.text_en: The willow ceremony and the issue of associating God's name with another
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the willow ceremony can include a phrase that associates God's name with another entity, citing a baraita that such association leads to being uprooted from the world. It explains that the phrase means 'To Yah we give thanks, and to You we praise'—separating the addresses.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions how the departing formula can associate God's name with another entity, citing the rule that one who associates God's name with another is uprooted from the world.
The gemara resolves that the formula means 'To God we give thanks, and to You we praise; to God we give thanks, and to You we extol.'

items.text: Debate on the number of willow branches
items.text_en: Debate on the number of willow branches
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka holds that 'kappot' (plural) indicates two willows—one for the lulav and one for the altar—while the Rabbis read it as 'kappat' (singular), implying one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna explains Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's reasoning: the verse 'כַּפּוֹת' (plural) indicates two willows, one for the lulav and one for the altar.
The rabbis counter that the verse is written 'כַּפַּת' (singular), implying only one willow.

items.text: Allegorical interpretation of the lulav
items.text_en: Allegorical interpretation of the lulav
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi says that just as a palm tree has only one heart (growing point), so Israel has only one heart for their Father in heaven.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi compares Israel to a palm tree, which has only one heart, meaning Israel has only one heart for their Father in heaven.

items.text: Dispute on the duration of lulav and sukkah
items.text_en: Dispute on the duration of lulav and sukkah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says lulav is observed for seven days because nights interrupt the days, making each day a separate mitzvah, while sukkah is one day because nights do not interrupt. Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says sukkah is seven days (Torah law) and lulav is one day (rabbinic). Ravin reports Rabbi Yochanan says both are seven. Rav Yosef rules like Rabba bar bar Chana since all Amoraim agree with him regarding sukkah.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's ruling that lulav is observed for seven days because nights interrupt, making each day a separate mitzvah, while sukkah is one day because nights do not interrupt.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports Rabbi Yochanan's opposing ruling that sukkah is seven days (Torah law) and lulav is one day (rabbinic).

sub.text: Ravin's report and Rav Yosef's ruling
sub.text_en: Ravin's report and Rav Yosef's ruling
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan says both lulav and sukkah are seven days, and Rav Yosef rules to adopt Rabba bar bar Chana's position because all Amoraim agree with him regarding sukkah.

items.text: Challenge to the ruling
items.text_en: Challenge to the ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection (from a baraita) against the previous ruling.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces an objection by citing a baraita.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Blessing schedules for lulav and sukkah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Blessing schedules for lulav and sukkah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who makes a lulav for himself recites Shehecheyanu, and when taking it to fulfill the mitzvah recites the blessing on lulav, repeating it each of the seven days. For sukkah, one recites Shehecheyanu when making it and the blessing on dwelling when entering, but does not repeat after the first day.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the blessing schedules for lulav and sukkah: for lulav, one recites Shehecheyanu when making it and the blessing on lulav when taking it, repeating each day; for sukkah, one recites Shehecheyanu when making it and the blessing on dwelling when entering, but does not repeat after the first day.

items.text: Gemara's question and first resolution: lulav vs. lulav and sukkah vs. sukkah
items.text_en: Gemara's question and first resolution: lulav vs. lulav and sukkah vs. sukkah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: lulav requires a blessing each day, but sukkah only on the first day. It resolves the lulav contradiction by distinguishing between when the Temple stands (biblical obligation each day) and when it does not (rabbinic). The sukkah contradiction remains unresolved here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah requires a blessing on lulav each day but on sukkah only the first day, yet both are seven-day mitzvot.
The Gemara resolves the lulav contradiction by distinguishing between the Temple era (biblical obligation each day) and the post-Temple era (rabbinic), but leaves the sukkah contradiction unresolved.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about tefillin blessings
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about tefillin blessings
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute to resolve the sukkah contradiction: Rabbi says one blesses on tefillin each time he puts them on, while the Sages say only once in the morning. This parallels the lulav/sukkah difference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about tefillin where Rabbi holds that one blesses each time he puts them on, while the Sages say one blesses only in the morning, showing that the sukkah dispute reflects a Tannaitic disagreement.
The baraita states Rabbi's position: one blesses on tefillin each time he puts them on.
The baraita states the Sages' position: one blesses only once in the morning.

items.text: Amoraic rulings and practice on tefillin blessings
items.text_en: Amoraic rulings and practice on tefillin blessings
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava dispute the halakha: Abaye follows Rabbi (bless each time), Rava follows the Sages. However, Rava's own practice contradicts his ruling, as he blesses each time he puts on tefillin. Mar Zutra and the rabbis of Rav Ashi's house also report blessing each time they handle tefillin.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports the dispute: Abaye rules like Rabbi (bless each time), Rava rules like the Sages (bless only in the morning).

sub.text: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel's testimony
sub.text_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel's testimony
sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Bat Shmuel testifies that Rava's own practice contradicts his ruling: Rava blesses each time he puts on tefillin, even after going to the bathroom.
Mar Zutra testifies that Rav Pappi also blesses each time he puts on tefillin.
The rabbis of Rav Ashi's house report that they bless each time they handle tefillin.

items.text: Dispute on the nature of the lulav mitzvah: biblical vs. rabbinic
items.text_en: Dispute on the nature of the lulav mitzvah: biblical vs. rabbinic
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says the mitzvah of lulav applies all seven days. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says only the first day is a mitzvah; thereafter it is a 'mitzvah of the elders.' Rabbi Yitzchak says every day is a mitzvah of the elders, but the Gemara clarifies he excludes the first day, making his view identical to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents three opinions: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says lulav is a mitzvah all seven days; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says only the first day is a mitzvah, thereafter a rabbinic enactment; Rabbi Yitzchak says every day is a rabbinic enactment.
The Gemara objects to Rabbi Yitzchak's statement: even the first day is a rabbinic enactment? But we know the first day is biblical! The Gemara corrects: exclude the first day.
The Gemara objects further: if so, Rabbi Yitzchak's corrected view is identical to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's; the Gemara resolves by saying Rabbi Yitzchak actually said 'and so said Rabbi Yitzchak'.
The Gemara objects: can Rabbi Yitzchak really include the first day, which is clearly a biblical commandment?
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yitzchak meant 'except for the first day,' aligning his view with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
The Gemara notes that this makes Rabbi Yitzchak's view identical to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's, and rephrases: 'And thus said Rabbi Yitzchak.'

items.text: Rav's view on lulav and Chanukah candle blessings
items.text_en: Rav's view on lulav and Chanukah candle blessings
items.desc_en: Rav holds that the lulav mitzvah applies all seven days, as inferred from his ruling on Chanukah candles: the one lighting recites three blessings on the first day and two thereafter, while the one seeing recites two and then one. The Gemara discusses the source for the Chanukah blessing, citing 'lo tasur' and 'she'al avicha.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rav also holds the lulav mitzvah applies all seven days, introducing the proof from his Chanukah candle ruling.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Ashi reports in Rav's name that one who lights the Chanukah candle must recite a blessing.
Rabbi Yirmeya adds that one who sees the Chanukah candle must also recite a blessing.
The Gemara asks what blessing is recited.
Rav Yehuda answers that on the first day the lighter recites three blessings and the seer two, and thereafter the lighter recites two and the seer one.
The Gemara asks what specific blessing is recited for the Chanukah candle.
The Gemara states the blessing: 'Who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to light the Chanukah candle.'
The Gemara asks where the commandment to light the Chanukah candle is found in the Torah.
The Gemara answers that the source is the verse 'לֹא תָּסוּר' (Do not deviate from all that they teach you).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative source: the verse 'שְׁאַל אָבִיךָ וְיַגֵּדְךָ' (Ask your father and he will tell you).

items.text: Clarification of Rav's statement on lulav
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav's statement on lulav
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explicitly teaches that Rav said the lulav mitzvah applies all seven days, confirming the earlier inference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara briefly digresses: what does the Chanukah blessing exclude? Time? No, the miracle is present every day.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explicit teaching
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explicit teaching
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explicitly teaches that Rav said: all seven days are a mitzvah of lulav, resolving the earlier dispute.

items.text: Baraita on sukkah blessings and Rav Kahana's practice
items.text_en: Baraita on sukkah blessings and Rav Kahana's practice
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: one who makes a sukkah recites Shehecheyanu; when entering to dwell, the blessing on dwelling. If the sukkah was pre-existing, one blesses only if he can renew it; otherwise, he recites both blessings upon entering. Rav Ashi reports that Rav Kahana would recite all blessings over the cup of kiddush.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches: one who makes a sukkah recites Shehecheyanu; when entering to dwell, recites the blessing on dwelling; if the sukkah was already standing, if he can renew it he blesses, otherwise when entering he recites both blessings.
Rav Ashi reports that he saw Rav Kahana recite all the blessings over a cup of sanctification (kiddush), demonstrating the practice of combining blessings.

items.text: Dispute on blessings for multiple mitzvot
items.text_en: Dispute on blessings for multiple mitzvot
items.desc_en: A baraita states: if one has many mitzvot before him, he recites a single blessing 'al hamitzvot.' Rabbi Yehuda says he blesses on each individually. Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa) rules like Rabbi Yehuda, citing the verse 'Baruch Hashem yom yom' to mean one should give each matter its appropriate blessing.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches: if one has many mitzvot before him, he recites one blessing over all of them; Rabbi Yehuda says he blesses over each one individually.

Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa) rules that the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda, and explains his reasoning from the verse 'Blessed be God day by day' — each day give Him its due blessing, so here each mitzvah gets its own blessing.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa) rules the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa) provides the scriptural basis for Rabbi Yehuda's position, citing the verse 'Baruch Hashem yom yom' to mean one should give each matter its appropriate blessing.

items.text: Analogy between divine and human attributes
items.text_en: Analogy between divine and human attributes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa) teaches that God's attribute differs from humans: a human vessel, when empty, holds more; but God fills the full, as it is written 'I will fill the soul of the priests with fatness.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira (or Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa) adds a homily: come and see how the measure of the Holy One differs from that of flesh and blood — a full vessel cannot hold more, but an empty vessel can.

items.text: Opening homily on hearing and holding
items.text_en: Opening homily on hearing and holding
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a homiletic interpretation of the verse 'If you shall surely hear,' contrasting human vessels that cannot hold when full with God's attribute of filling those who are full, and linking hearing to both old and new teachings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a homiletic interpretation of the verse 'If you shall surely hear,' contrasting human vessels that cannot hold when full with God's attribute of filling those who are full, and linking hearing to both old and new teachings.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on etrog and sukkah
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on etrog and sukkah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the etrog is forbidden on the seventh day but permitted on the eighth, while the sukkah is forbidden even on the eighth. Reish Lakish permits the etrog even on the seventh. The Gemara explains their dispute: one holds the etrog is designated only for the mitzvah time, the other for the entire day.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the etrog is forbidden on the seventh day of Sukkot but permitted on the eighth, while the sukkah is forbidden even on the eighth.
Reish Lakish permits the etrog even on the seventh day.
The Gemara explains the dispute: one holds the etrog is designated only for the mitzvah time, the other for the entire day.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah about children's etrogs
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah about children's etrogs
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan from the Mishnah that children immediately take their lulavim and eat their etrogs, implying adults may also do so. Rabbi Yochanan deflects, saying it applies only to children. An alternative version has Rabbi Yochanan challenging Reish Lakish, who responds that the Mishnah merely teaches the common practice.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan from the Mishnah that children immediately take their lulavim and eat their etrogs, implying the same rule applies to adults.
Rabbi Yochanan deflects, saying the Mishnah applies only to children, not adults.
An alternative version has Rabbi Yochanan challenging Reish Lakish from the same Mishnah, arguing that it distinguishes children from adults.
Reish Lakish responds that the Mishnah merely teaches the common practice (אורחה דמילתא), but the same rule applies to adults as well.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question and Abaye's answer on sukkah vs. etrog
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question and Abaye's answer on sukkah vs. etrog
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye why the sukkah is forbidden on the eighth day while the etrog is permitted according to Rabbi Yochanan. Abaye explains that the sukkah is fit for twilight (bein hashemashot) of the seventh day, so it becomes designated for the entire eighth day, whereas the etrog is not fit at twilight and thus not designated.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye why, according to Rabbi Yochanan, the sukkah is forbidden on the eighth day while the etrog is permitted.

Abaye explains that the sukkah is fit for twilight (בין השמשות) of the seventh day, so it becomes designated for the entire eighth day, whereas the etrog is not fit at twilight and thus not designated.

items.text: Levi and Avuh d'Shmuel's positions, and Rabbi Zeira's ruling
items.text_en: Levi and Avuh d'Shmuel's positions, and Rabbi Zeira's ruling
items.desc_en: Levi forbids the etrog even on the eighth day, while Avuh d'Shmuel permits it on the eighth. The Gemara notes that Avuh d'Shmuel aligns with Levi, and Rabbi Zeira aligns with Avuh d'Shmuel, ruling that a disqualified etrog is forbidden to eat all seven days.

sub.desc_en: Levi rules that an etrog is forbidden even on the eighth day, while Avuh d'Shmuel permits it on the eighth; Rabbi Zeira aligns with Avuh d'Shmuel and adds that a disqualified etrog is forbidden to eat all seven days.
Avuh d'Shmuel rules that the etrog is forbidden on the seventh day but permitted on the eighth.
The Gemara notes that Avuh d'Shmuel aligns with Levi's view, and Rabbi Zeira aligns with Avuh d'Shmuel's view.
Rabbi Zeira rules that a disqualified etrog is forbidden to eat all seven days, supporting Avuh d'Shmuel's position.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's rulings on giving a lulav to a minor and promising a child
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's rulings on giving a lulav to a minor and promising a child
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira advises not to acquire a lulav for a minor on the first festival day because a minor can acquire but not transfer ownership, leading to the adult using a lulav not his own. He also warns against promising a child something and not giving it, as it teaches falsehood.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira rules that one should not acquire a lulav for a minor on the first festival day, because the minor can acquire but not transfer ownership, resulting in the adult using a lulav not his own.

Rabbi Zeira further warns against promising a child something and not giving it, as it teaches falsehood, citing the verse 'לִמְּדוּ לְשׁוֹנָם דַּבֶּר שֶׁקֶר' (they taught their tongue to speak falsehood).

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rav Asi on designating multiple etrogs
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rav Asi on designating multiple etrogs
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a dispute: if one designates seven etrogs for seven days, Rav says one may eat each immediately after use, while Rav Asi says one must wait until the next day. The dispute mirrors the earlier one about designation for the mitzvah vs. the entire day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rav and Rav Asi: if one set aside seven etrogim for seven days, Rav says one fulfills the mitzvah with each and eats it immediately, while Rav Asi says one eats it the next day; the dispute hinges on whether the etrog is designated only for the mitzvah time or for the entire day.

The Gemara explains that the dispute mirrors the earlier one between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish: one holds the etrog is designated only for the mitzvah (למצותה), the other holds it is designated for the entire day (לכולי יומא).

items.text: Practice for Diaspora with two days, and final ruling
items.text_en: Practice for Diaspora with two days, and final ruling
items.desc_en: For those observing two days, Abaye rules that the eighth day (doubtful seventh) is forbidden, while the ninth (doubtful eighth) is permitted. Marimar permits even the eighth. The Gemara notes that Sura follows Marimar, Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi follows Abaye, and the halakha is like Abaye. Rav Yehuda bar Rav Shmuel bar Shilat quotes Rav that the eighth day is seventh for sukkah and eighth for blessing, while Rabbi Yochanan says the eighth is for both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how those in the Diaspora who observe two days of Yom Tov should act regarding the etrog and sukkah.
Abaye rules that the eighth day (doubtful seventh) is forbidden for etrog, but the ninth (doubtful eighth) is permitted.
Marimar permits even the eighth day (doubtful seventh) for etrog.
The Gemara reports that Sura follows Marimar, Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi follows Abaye, and the halakha is like Abaye.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda bar Rav Shmuel bar Shilat quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Rav Shmuel bar Shilat quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Rav Shmuel bar Shilat quotes Rav that the eighth day is seventh for sukkah and eighth for blessing.
Rabbi Yochanan says the eighth day is for both sukkah and blessing.
The Gemara notes that everyone agrees one sits in the sukkah on the eighth day; the dispute is only about the blessing.

items.text: Dispute about blessing and sitting on the eighth day
items.text_en: Dispute about blessing and sitting on the eighth day
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: according to the opinion that the seventh day is for the sukkah, one recites a blessing on the eighth day; according to the opinion that the eighth day is for both, one does not bless. Rav Yosef cites a precedent that Rabbi Yochanan and other greats sat in the sukkah on the eighth day of uncertainty but did not bless.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: according to the opinion that the seventh day is for the sukkah, we recite a blessing on the eighth day; according to the opinion that the eighth day is for both sukkah and festival, we do not recite a blessing.
Rav Yosef cites a precedent that Rabbi Yochanan and other greats sat in the sukkah on the eighth day of uncertainty but did not recite a blessing.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding the precedent
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding the precedent
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the precedent might align with the view that once one blesses the first festival day, one does not bless again. It resolves that they came from Afar (a place where the festival was observed for one day), so the precedent is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the precedent by suggesting that the rabbis might hold the view that once one blesses the first festival day, one does not bless again.
The Gemara resolves that the precedent is valid because those rabbis came from Afar, where the festival was observed for only one day, so they had not yet blessed the festival day.

items.text: Alternative version: dispute about sitting, not blessing
items.text_en: Alternative version: dispute about sitting, not blessing
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that all agree one does not bless; the dispute is about sitting. According to the opinion that seven days are for the sukkah, one sits; according to the opinion that the eighth day is for both, one does not sit. Rav Yosef cites a precedent that Rabbi Yehuda bar Shmuel bar Shilat sat outside the sukkah on the eighth day of uncertainty. The halakha is that one sits but does not bless.

sub.desc_en: The alternative version states that all agree one does not recite the blessing; the dispute is only about sitting.
The dispute is about sitting: according to the opinion that seven days are for the sukkah, one sits; according to the opinion that the eighth day is for both, one does not sit.
Rav Yosef cites a precedent that Rabbi Yehuda bar Shmuel bar Shilat, a master of tradition, sat outside the sukkah on the eighth day of uncertainty.
The halakha is ruled: one sits in the sukkah on the eighth day of uncertainty but does not recite the blessing.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on reciting Shehecheyanu
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on reciting Shehecheyanu
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that one recites the blessing of time (Shehecheyanu) on the eighth day of Sukkot but not on the seventh day of Passover.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the blessing of time (Shehecheyanu) is recited on the eighth day of Sukkot but not on the seventh day of Passover.

items.text: Proof for the distinction: three differences
items.text_en: Proof for the distinction: three differences
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Chama (or Rabbi Chama bar Chanina) provides a proof: the eighth day of Sukkot is distinct in three matters—sukkah, lulav, and water libation. According to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that water libation is performed all eight days, it is distinct in two matters.

sub.text: Rabbi Levi bar Chama (or Rabbi Chama bar Chanina)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Levi bar Chama (or Rabbi Chama bar Chanina)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Chama (or Rabbi Chama bar Chanina) provides a proof that the eighth day of Sukkot is distinct in three matters—sukkah, lulav, and water libation—and according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that water libation is performed all eight days, it is distinct in two matters.

items.text: Objection: the seventh day of Passover is also distinct
items.text_en: Objection: the seventh day of Passover is also distinct
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the seventh day of Passover is also distinct in the matter of eating matzah, as the Master said: the first night is obligatory, thereafter it is optional. The Gemara responds: there, the distinction is only from the night, not from the day; here, the distinction is even from the day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the seventh day of Passover is also distinct in the matter of eating matzah, as the Master said: the first night is obligatory, thereafter it is optional.
The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that there the distinction is only from the night, not from the day, whereas here the distinction is even from the day.

items.text: Multiple answers distinguishing the eighth day
items.text_en: Multiple answers distinguishing the eighth day
items.desc_en: Ravina, Rav Pappa, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, and Rav Ashi each offer a scriptural distinction: the eighth day's offerings are written with singular terms (e.g., 'par' vs. 'parim', 'bayom' vs. 'uvayom', 'kamishpat' vs. 'kemishpatam'), indicating it is a separate festival.

sub.desc_en: Ravina distinguishes the eighth day from the preceding days by noting it is separate from both the day before and the day before that.
Rav Pappa distinguishes the eighth day by noting the Torah uses singular 'פַּר' (bull) for the eighth day versus plural 'פָּרִים' (bulls) for the other days.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak distinguishes the eighth day by noting the Torah writes 'בַּיּוֹם' (on the day) for the eighth day versus 'וּבַיּוֹם' (and on the day) for the other days.

Rav Ashi distinguishes the eighth day by noting the Torah writes 'כַּמִּשְׁפָּט' (according to the ordinance) for the eighth day versus 'כְּמִשְׁפָּטָם' (according to their ordinances) for the other days.

items.text: Support from a baraita about offerings
items.text_en: Support from a baraita about offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: the bulls, rams, and lambs of the festival offerings interdict each other, but Rabbi Yehuda says bulls do not interdict because they diminish. The Sages object that all diminish on the eighth day; Rabbi Yehuda responds that the eighth day is a separate festival, requiring offerings, song, blessing, and lodging like the seven days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that the bulls, rams, and lambs of the festival offerings interdict each other, but Rabbi Yehuda says bulls do not interdict because they diminish.
The Sages object that all offerings diminish on the eighth day, so Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is inconsistent.
Rabbi Yehuda responds that the eighth day is a separate festival, requiring offerings, song, blessing, and lodging like the seven days.

items.text: Gemara's question: What is the blessing?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What is the blessing?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the blessing referred to is the time-based blessing (זמן) or the blessings of Grace after Meals and prayer. It clarifies that the blessing of זמן is not limited to the first day but can be recited any day of the festival.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the blessing in the Mishnah is the time-based blessing (זמן) or the blessings of Grace after Meals and prayer.

items.text: Support for Rav Nachman regarding the cup
items.text_en: Support for Rav Nachman regarding the cup
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the blessing of זמן requires a cup of wine, supporting Rav Nachman who says it can be recited even in the market. It suggests that if a cup is needed, one might not always have one, but the Gemara deflects by saying it applies when a cup happens to be available.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the blessing of זמן (the time-based blessing) can be recited all seven days, so if one missed it today, they can say it tomorrow.
The Gemara objects that the blessing of זמן requires a cup of wine, which seems to contradict Rav Nachman's view that it can be said in the market.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Nachman's statement applies when a cup happens to be available, so the requirement for a cup does not contradict his ruling.

items.text: Challenge: Does Rabbi Yehuda require an overnight stay on the eighth day?
items.text_en: Challenge: Does Rabbi Yehuda require an overnight stay on the eighth day?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether Rabbi Yehuda holds that the eighth day of Sukkot requires an overnight stay (לינה), citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse that only a festival with six days of eating matzah requires לינה, excluding the second Passover and presumably the eighth day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether Rabbi Yehuda requires an overnight stay (לינה) on the eighth day of Sukkot, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse that only a festival with six days of eating matzah requires לינה, excluding the second Passover and presumably the eighth day.
The Gemara asks what the baraita excludes, suggesting it also excludes the eighth day of Sukkot.

items.text: Rejection: The exclusion is only for second Passover
items.text_en: Rejection: The exclusion is only for second Passover
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the challenge, explaining that the exclusion is only for the second Passover, not the eighth day. It supports this by citing a mishnah that first fruits require an overnight stay, and Rabbi Yehuda is the one who requires waving (תנופה), so he must also require לינה for the eighth day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the challenge, explaining that the exclusion is only for the second Passover (פסח שני), not the eighth day.

The Gemara supports this by citing a mishnah that first fruits (ביכורים) require an overnight stay (לינה), and since Rabbi Yehuda is the one who requires waving (תנופה), he must also require לינה for the eighth day.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's view on first fruits
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's view on first fruits
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on Rabbi Yehuda's derivation that first fruits require waving (תנופה) from the verse, and then considers whether the source might be Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov instead. It explains Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's reasoning using a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'hand' in the context of peace offerings.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda derives that first fruits require waving (תנופה) from the verse 'והנחתו'.
The Gemara objects that the source for waving might be Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, not Rabbi Yehuda, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives waving from the verse 'ולקח הכהן הטנא מידך'.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's reasoning: he derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'יד' (hand) used in the context of peace offerings.

The Gemara resolves the analogy: just as in peace offerings the priest places his hand under the owner's hand and waves, so too with first fruits the priest places his hand under the owner's hand and waves.

items.text: Conclusion: The halakha on reciting זמן on the eighth day
items.text_en: Conclusion: The halakha on reciting זמן on the eighth day
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the debate between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet: Rav Nachman says one recites זמן on the eighth day, Rav Sheshet says one does not. The halakha follows Rav Nachman, and a baraita supports his view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the conclusion is regarding the dispute about reciting זמן (Shehecheyanu) on the eighth day of Sukkot.
Rav Nachman states that one recites זמן (Shehecheyanu) on the eighth day of the festival.
Rav Sheshet states that one does not recite זמן (Shehecheyanu) on the eighth day of the festival.
The Gemara rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rav Nachman: one recites זמן (Shehecheyanu) on the eighth day.
A baraita is cited that supports Rav Nachman's position regarding the eighth day.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: List of independent elements
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: List of independent elements
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists that the festival (regel), the lottery (payis), the time (zman), the sacrifice (korban), the song (shirah), and the blessing (berakhah) are each independent matters.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists that the festival (regel), the lottery (payis), the time (zman), the sacrifice (korban), the song (shirah), and the blessing (berakhah) are each independent matters.

items.text: Mishnah: Hallel and joy for eight days
items.text_en: Mishnah: Hallel and joy for eight days
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Hallel and joy are observed for eight days, teaching that one is obligated in Hallel, joy, and honor of the last day of the festival like all other days.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Hallel and rejoicing apply for eight days, including the last day of Sukkot, and explains that one is obligated in Hallel, rejoicing, and honoring the festival on the last day as on all other days.

items.text: Gemara: Source for joy on the last night
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for joy on the last night
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of this obligation, citing a baraita that derives from the verse "וְהָיִיתָ אַךְ שָׂמֵחַ" that the last night is included, while the first night is excluded because there is no preceding joy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the Mishnah's ruling that joy applies on the last night of the festival.
The baraita cites the verse 'וְהָיִיתָ אַךְ שָׂמֵחַ' and interprets the word 'אַךְ' to exclude the first night, implying the last night is included.
The Gemara explains the reasoning: the last night is included because it follows a day of joy, while the first night is excluded because it has no preceding joy.

items.text: Mishnah: Sukkah for seven days
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sukkah for seven days
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that the sukkah obligation is for seven days; once one finishes eating, they may not dismantle the sukkah but may remove vessels from mincha time onward out of respect for the last day.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the sukkah obligation is for seven days, and that one who finishes eating should not dismantle the sukkah but may remove vessels from the afternoon onward out of respect for the last day of the festival.

items.text: Gemara: What if one has no place to remove vessels?
items.text_en: Gemara: What if one has no place to remove vessels?
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the case: if one has no place to remove vessels, Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav says to reduce the sukkah by four handbreadths, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says to light a lamp in it. They do not disagree: one applies to us (Babylon) and one to them (Eretz Yisrael).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if one has no place to remove vessels from the sukkah, what is the law?
The Gemara objects: if he has no vessels, with what did he use the sukkah?
The Gemara clarifies: the case is one who has no place to remove his vessels, not that he lacks vessels.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav says: one reduces the sukkah by four handbreadths (to invalidate it as a sukkah).
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: one lights a lamp in it (to make it unfit for dwelling).
The Gemara resolves: they do not disagree; one applies to us (Babylon) and the other to them (Eretz Yisrael).

items.text: Gemara: Large sukkah and food vessels
items.text_en: Gemara: Large sukkah and food vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a large sukkah and answers that one brings in food vessels, citing Rava: food vessels are outside the shading, drink vessels are inside the shading.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what applies to a large sukkah, since the previous solutions are only for a small one.
Rava answers that in a large sukkah one brings in eating vessels outside the sukkah, while drinking vessels remain inside.
Rava clarifies the distinction: food vessels are placed outside the shading (the sukkah's roofed area), while drink vessels are placed inside the shading.

items.text: Mishnah: Water libation ceremony
items.text_en: Mishnah: Water libation ceremony
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the water libation: a golden flask holding three logs is filled from the Shiloach; upon reaching the Water Gate, they blow trumpets; the priest ascends the ramp and turns left to two silver bowls (or lime bowls blackened by wine, according to Rabbi Yehuda) that are perforated.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the water libation ceremony: a golden flask holding three logs is filled from the Shiloach, they blow trumpets at the Water Gate, the priest ascends the ramp and turns left to two silver bowls (or lime bowls according to Rabbi Yehuda) that are perforated.
The Mishnah describes filling the flask from the Shiloach and blowing trumpets upon reaching the Water Gate.
The Mishnah describes the priest ascending the ramp and turning left to two silver bowls.
Rabbi Yehuda says the bowls were of lime, blackened by wine, and perforated.

items.text: Description of the libation vessels
items.text_en: Description of the libation vessels
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the two libation vessels: one for water and one for wine, each with a spout shaped like a narrow tube, one thick and one thin, so that both empty simultaneously. The western spout is for water, the eastern for wine. If one poured water into the wine vessel or wine into the water vessel, he has fulfilled the obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the two libation vessels with spouts of different thicknesses, their placement, and the rule that swapping the liquids still fulfills the obligation.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion and an incident
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion and an incident
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says that the libation was performed with a log measure all eight days. The one pouring is told to raise his hand, because once someone poured on his feet and the people pelted him with their etrogim.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that the water libation was performed with a לוג (log measure) all eight days of Sukkot.
The one pouring the libation is told to raise his hand, to avoid spilling on his feet.
An incident is cited where a person once poured the libation on his feet, and the people pelted him with their etrogim (אתרוגים).

items.text: Procedure on Shabbat
items.text_en: Procedure on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The procedure on Shabbat is the same as on a weekday, except that he fills a golden jug that is not sanctified from the Shiloach on Shabbat eve and places it in the chamber. If it was spilled or uncovered, he fills from the laver, because uncovered wine and water are invalid for the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the water-drawing procedure on Shabbat is identical to the weekday procedure, except that a golden jug of water is filled from the Shiloach on Shabbat eve and stored in the chamber; if spilled or uncovered, water is drawn from the laver, because uncovered wine and water are invalid for the altar.

items.text: Source for water libation and allegorical debate
items.text_en: Source for water libation and allegorical debate
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the water libation. Rav Eina cites the verse 'And you shall draw water with joy' (Yeshayahu 12:3). Then follows an allegorical debate between two personified concepts, 'Sason' (gladness) and 'Simcha' (joy), each claiming superiority. A heretic named Sason challenges Rabbi Avahu about the future, and Rabbi Avahu responds with a pun on the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the water libation.
Rav Eina cites the verse 'וּשְׁאַבְתֶּם מַיִם בְּשָׂשׂוֹן' (Yeshayahu 12:3) as the source for the water libation.

The Gemara introduces an allegorical debate between two personified concepts, Sason (gladness) and Simcha (joy), where Sason claims superiority by citing the verse 'שָׂשׂוֹן וְשִׂמְחָה יַשִּׂיגוּ' (gladness and joy shall overtake).
Simcha counters Sason's claim by citing the verse 'שִׂמְחָה וְשָׂשׂוֹן לַיְּהוּדִים' (joy and gladness for the Jews), where joy is mentioned first.
Sason rebuts Simcha by noting that Simcha is abandoned on the day of exile, as the verse says 'כִּי בְשִׂמְחָה תֵצֵאוּ' (for you shall go out with joy), implying joy is temporary.
Simcha counters that Sason is used for drawing water, as the verse says 'וּשְׁאַבְתֶּם מַיִם בְּשָׂשׂוֹן' (and you shall draw water with gladness), implying Sason is a mere vessel.
A heretic named Sason challenges Rabbi Avahu, claiming that in the future world, the Jews will serve him water based on the verse 'וּשְׁאַבְתֶּם מַיִם בְּשָׂשׂוֹן'.

Rabbi Avahu responds with a pun: if the verse said 'לְשָׂשׂוֹן' (to Sason), it would mean serving him, but since it says 'בְּשָׂשׂוֹן' (with gladness), it means they will make a water-skin from the heretic's skin and fill it with water.

items.text: The ascent to the altar for libation
items.text_en: The ascent to the altar for libation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that he ascends the ramp and turns to his left. The Gemara cites a baraita: All who ascend the altar ascend on the right and circle to descend on the left, except for three things: water libation, wine libation, and the bird-offering when it is abundant in the east.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the priest ascends the ramp and turns to his left for the libation.

A baraita teaches that all who ascend the altar go up on the right and descend on the left, except for three things: water libation, wine libation, and the bird-offering when it is abundant in the east.

items.text: Why water also blackens the spout
items.text_en: Why water also blackens the spout
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the spouts were blackened. Wine blackens, but why does water blacken? Since the master said that if one poured water into the wine vessel or wine into the water vessel he has fulfilled the obligation, the water vessel also becomes blackened from residual wine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted that wine blackens the spout, but why does water blacken it?
The Gemara answers: since the master said that pouring water into a wine vessel or wine into a water vessel fulfills the obligation, the water vessel also becomes blackened from residual wine.

items.text: Identifying the Mishnah with Rabbi Yehuda or the Sages
items.text_en: Identifying the Mishnah with Rabbi Yehuda or the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's description of the spouts (one thick, one thin) aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who says the libation is with a log all eight days, implying equal amounts. The Sages would require equal spouts. However, the Gemara answers that even according to the Sages, wine is thick and water is thin, so the spouts differ. It then proves that the Mishnah is not Rabbi Yehuda, because he holds that the wine vessel has a wide mouth and the water vessel a narrow mouth, not the spouts described.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's description of one thick and one thin spout aligns only with Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that the libation is with a log all eight days (implying equal amounts), whereas the Sages would require equal spouts.
The Gemara answers that even according to the Sages, wine is thick (סמיך) and water is thin (קליש), so the spouts would naturally differ in size.

The Gemara proves that the Mishnah is not Rabbi Yehuda's view, because Rabbi Yehuda holds that the wine vessel has a wide mouth and the water vessel a narrow mouth, not the spouts described in the Mishnah.

items.text: Incident with a Sadducee and repair of the altar
items.text_en: Incident with a Sadducee and repair of the altar
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts that a Sadducee once poured the libation on his feet, and the people pelted him with their etrogim. That day the horn of the altar was damaged, and they brought a block of salt and plugged it, not because it was fit for service, but so that the altar would not appear damaged.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts an incident where a Sadducee poured the libation on his feet, the people pelted him with etrogim, and the damaged altar was temporarily plugged with salt to avoid appearing defective.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any altar lacking a ramp, horn, base, or square is invalid for service. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds that it also requires a surrounding ledge.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any altar lacking a ramp, horn, base, or square is invalid for service.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds that the altar also requires a surrounding ledge (סוֹבֵב).

items.text: Gemara's exposition on the shittin
items.text_en: Gemara's exposition on the shittin
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan teaches that the shittin were created during the six days of Creation, citing the verse 'The turnings of your thighs are like jewels, the work of the hands of a craftsman.' The school of Rabbi Yishmael interprets 'Bereishit' as 'bara sheet' (He created six).

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan teaches that the shittin were created during the six days of Creation, citing the verse 'The turnings of your thighs are like jewels, the work of the hands of a craftsman' and interpreting each phrase.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael interprets the word 'Bereishit' as 'bara sheet' (He created six), providing a homiletic support for the creation of the shittin.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei on the shittin
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei on the shittin
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Rabbi Yosei says the shittin are hollow and descend to the abyss, citing the verse from Isaiah about a vineyard, interpreting 'he hewed a vat' as referring to the shittin.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Rabbi Yosei says the shittin are hollow and descend to the abyss, citing the verse from Isaiah about a vineyard, interpreting 'he hewed a vat' as referring to the shittin.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok on the cavity
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok on the cavity
items.desc_en: A baraita relates that Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok said there was a small cavity between the ramp and the altar on the west side of the ramp. Once every seventy years, young priests would descend there and collect congealed wine resembling fig cakes, then burn it in sanctity, as per the verse 'In the sanctuary pour out a libation of strong drink to the Lord.'

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
sub.desc_en: A baraita reports that Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok described a small cavity between the ramp and the altar, where young priests would collect congealed wine every seventy years and burn it in sanctity, citing the verse about pouring a libation in the sanctuary.

items.text: Derivation of the sanctity of burning libations
items.text_en: Derivation of the sanctity of burning libations
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the burning of leftover libations must be done in a sacred manner, just as their libation is. Ravina derives it via a verbal analogy (גזירה שוה) between the word 'קֹדֶשׁ' used in the verse about libation and in the verse about burning leftover sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the burning of leftover libations must be performed in a sacred manner, just as their libation is.
Ravina derives the sacred manner of burning via a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) between the word 'קֹדֶשׁ' in the libation verse and in the verse about burning leftover sacrifices.

items.text: The status of libations after they descend into the shittin
items.text_en: The status of libations after they descend into the shittin
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines a baraita stating that libations initially have sanctity (מעילה), but once they descend into the shittin (the underground channels), they no longer have sanctity. It considers whether this follows Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok or the Rabbis, and discusses the possibility that the wine is absorbed before reaching the depths. Resh Lakish adds that when libating wine on the altar, one must plug the shittin to fulfill the verse 'בַּקֹּדֶשׁ הַסֵּךְ נֶסֶךְ'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion the baraita follows, noting that if it follows the Rabbis, the wine has already descended to the depths and should have no sanctity.
The Gemara answers that even according to the Rabbis, the baraita refers to a case where the wine was absorbed before reaching the depths.
An alternative version suggests the baraita follows the Rabbis, not Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok, because according to Rabbi Elazar the libations would still retain their sanctity.
The Gemara answers that even according to Rabbi Elazar, once a mitzvah has been performed with an item, it no longer has sanctity.
Resh Lakish adds that when libating wine on the altar, one must plug the shittin to fulfill the verse 'בַּקֹּדֶשׁ הַסֵּךְ נֶסֶךְ' (in holiness you shall pour a libation).

items.text: The meaning of 'שכר' and a practical lesson
items.text_en: The meaning of 'שכר' and a practical lesson
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'שֵׁכָר' teaches in the verse. Rav Papa explains that it implies drinking, satiety, and intoxication. He then derives that when a person is satiated with wine, it is from the throat. Rava advises a scholar who lacks wine to sip it, and Rava himself did so at the blessing cup.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the word 'שֵׁכָר' in the verse implies plugging the shittin.
Rav Papa explains that 'שֵׁכָר' connotes drinking, satiety, and intoxication, implying the wine should be retained and not immediately drained.
Rav Papa deduces from this that when a person is satiated with wine, the satiety is felt in the throat.
Rava advises that a Torah scholar who lacks wine should drink it in gulps, and Rava himself did so at the blessing cup.
Rava himself sipped the blessing cup.

items.text: The beauty of Israel's pilgrimage and Abraham's title
items.text_en: The beauty of Israel's pilgrimage and Abraham's title
items.desc_en: Rava expounds a verse from Song of Songs, explaining that 'מַה יָּפוּ פְעָמַיִךְ בַּנְּעָלִים' refers to the beauty of Israel's footsteps when ascending for the pilgrimage. 'בַּת נָדִיב' refers to the daughter of Abraham, who is called 'נָדִיב' because he was the first to convert people.

sub.desc_en: Rava expounds the verse 'מה יפו פעמיך בנעלים בת נדיב', interpreting 'בת נדיב' as the daughter of Abraham, who was the first to welcome converts.

items.text: Torah compared to a thigh and the three things God requires
items.text_en: Torah compared to a thigh and the three things God requires
items.desc_en: The school of Rav Anan explains why Torah is compared to a thigh: just as a thigh is hidden, so too Torah should be studied in private. Rabbi Elazar then expounds the verse 'הִגִּיד לְךָ אָדָם מַה טּוֹב', identifying 'עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט' as judgment, 'אַהֲבַת חֶסֶד' as acts of kindness, and 'הַצְנֵעַ לֶכֶת' as attending to the dead and escorting a bride. He argues that if even public matters require modesty, private matters certainly do.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rav Anan explains why Torah is compared to a thigh: just as a thigh is hidden, so too Torah should be studied in private.

Rabbi Elazar expounds the verse 'הִגִּיד לְךָ אָדָם מַה טּוֹב', identifying 'עֲשׂוֹת מִשְׁפָּט' as judgment, 'אַהֲבַת חֶסֶד' as acts of kindness, and 'הַצְנֵעַ לֶכֶת' as attending to the dead and escorting a bride, concluding with a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument that if public matters require modesty, private matters certainly do.

items.text: The superiority of charity and kindness over sacrifices
items.text_en: The superiority of charity and kindness over sacrifices
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that charity is greater than all sacrifices, and that gemilut chasadim (acts of kindness) is even greater than charity, as derived from verses. The Rabbis elaborate on three ways gemilut chasadim surpasses charity: it can be done with one's body or money, for rich or poor, and for the living or dead. Rabbi Elazar further teaches that one who performs charity and justice fills the world with kindness, but only the God-fearing truly possess this kindness.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar opens by stating that performing charity (צדקה) is greater than all sacrifices, citing the verse 'עֲשֹׂה צְדָקָה וּמִשְׁפָּט נִבְחָר לַה׳ מִזָּבַח'.

Rabbi Elazar further states that gemilut chasadim (acts of kindness) is greater than charity, deriving from the verse 'זִרְעוּ לָכֶם לִצְדָקָה וְקִצְרוּ לְפִי חֶסֶד' with a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: one who sows may or may not eat, but one who reaps certainly eats.
Rabbi Elazar adds that charity is rewarded only according to the kindness (חסד) within it, citing the same verse.
The Rabbis elaborate on three ways gemilut chasadim surpasses charity: it can be done with one's body or money, for rich or poor, and for the living or dead.
Rabbi Elazar concludes that one who performs charity and justice fills the world with kindness, but only the God-fearing truly possess this kindness, as derived from verses.

items.text: The connection between grace, fear of Heaven, and Torah study
items.text_en: The connection between grace, fear of Heaven, and Torah study
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Pappa teaches that a person who has grace (חן) is known to be God-fearing. Rabbi Elazar then explains the phrase 'תּוֹרַת חֶסֶד' in Proverbs: Torah studied for its own sake is a Torah of kindness, while Torah studied not for its own sake is not. An alternative interpretation says Torah taught to others is a Torah of kindness.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Pappa states that anyone who has grace (חן) is known to be God-fearing.
Rabbi Elazar expounds the verse 'פיה פתחה בחכמה ותורת חסד על לשונה', explaining that Torah studied for its own sake is a Torah of kindness, while Torah studied for ulterior motives is not.
Rabbi Elazar explains that Torah studied for its own sake (לשמה) is a Torah of kindness, while Torah studied not for its own sake is not.
An alternative interpretation says Torah taught to others (ללמדה) is a Torah of kindness, while Torah not taught is not.

items.text: Return to the Mishnah: why not use sanctified water?
items.text_en: Return to the Mishnah: why not use sanctified water?
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the Mishnah's statement that the water libation is performed as on a weekday. It asks why sanctified water is not used. Ze'iri answers that the Sage holds that there is no fixed measure for water, and that sacred vessels sanctify only with intent, not unknowingly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah uses ordinary water for the water libation on Sukkot, rather than sanctified water.
Ze'iri answers that there is no fixed measure for water, and the sacred vessels sanctify even without intention.

items.text: Chizkiyah's explanation for not bringing sanctified water
items.text_en: Chizkiyah's explanation for not bringing sanctified water
items.desc_en: Chizkiyah explains that if one brings already sanctified water, it would become invalid due to overnight stay (linah). He states that service vessels only sanctify with intent, and there is a decree lest people say they were sanctified with intent.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises the problem that if one brings already sanctified water, it would become invalid due to overnight stay (לינה).
Chizkiyah explains that service vessels only sanctify with intent, and there is a decree lest people say they were sanctified with intent.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai citing Rabbi Zeira offers a different reason: even if there is a measure for water, and service vessels only sanctify with intent, the decree is lest people say they filled them for sanctification of hands and feet.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai in the name of Rabbi Zeira offers an alternative explanation: even if water has a measure and service vessels only sanctify with intent, the decree is lest people say they filled them for sanctification of hands and feet.

items.text: Question about using a strainer for uncovered water
items.text_en: Question about using a strainer for uncovered water
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah rules that water that was spilled or uncovered is invalid; why not pass it through a strainer? It suggests the mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Nechemiah, who holds that a strainer is not subject to the law of uncovered liquids because the venom floats like a sponge.
