sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the mishnah invalidates uncovered water, suggesting it could be passed through a strainer to remove the venom.
The Gemara suggests that the mishnah follows the view of Rabbi Nechemiah, who holds that a strainer is subject to the law of uncovered liquids.

The baraita cites Rabbi Nechemiah's position that a strainer is subject to the law of uncovered liquids only when the lower vessel is uncovered, because the venom floats like a sponge and stays in place.

items.text: Rejection: Even Rabbi Nechemiah would not permit for the Temple
items.text_en: Rejection: Even Rabbi Nechemiah would not permit for the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the suggestion, arguing that even if Rabbi Nechemiah permits a strainer for ordinary people, he would not permit it for the Temple, citing the verse 'Present it now to your governor—will he accept you?'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the suggestion that Rabbi Nechemiah would permit a strainer for the Temple, arguing that even if he permits it for ordinary people, he would not permit it for the Temple, citing the verse 'Present it now to your governor—will he accept you?'

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The standard closing formula 'Hadran alach Lulav va'Aravah' marks the end of the chapter.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'Hadran alach Lulav va'Aravah' (we return to you, Lulav and Willow).

items.text: Opening mishnah of the next chapter: The flute
items.text_en: Opening mishnah of the next chapter: The flute
items.desc_en: The mishnah begins the new chapter, stating that the flute (for the water-drawing celebration) is played for five or six days, and this is the flute of the Beit HaSho'eivah, which does not override Shabbat or Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens the new chapter, stating that the flute (for the water-drawing celebration) is played for five or six days, and this is the flute of the Beit HaSho'eivah, which does not override Shabbat or Yom Tov.

items.text: Dispute over the name: Sho'evah vs. Chashuvah
items.text_en: Dispute over the name: Sho'evah vs. Chashuvah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah and Rav Eina disagree on the correct name for the celebration: one teaches 'Sho'evah' (drawing) and the other 'Chashuvah' (important). Mar Zutra defends both readings: 'Sho'evah' is supported by the verse 'And you shall draw water with joy', and 'Chashuvah' by Rav Nachman's statement that it is a precious mitzvah from the six days of creation.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports a dispute: Rav Yehudah and Rav Eina disagree on the name of the celebration — one teaches 'Sho'evah' (drawing) and the other 'Chashuvah' (important).

Mar Zutra defends both readings: 'Sho'evah' is supported by the verse 'וּשְׁאַבְתֶּם מַיִם בְּשָׂשׂוֹן' (And you shall draw water with joy), and 'Chashuvah' by Rav Nachman's statement that it is a precious mitzvah from the six days of creation.

Mar Zutra supports the version 'שׁוֹאֵבָה' with the verse 'וּשְׁאַבְתֶּם מַיִם בְּשָׂשׂוֹן' and the version 'חֲשׁוּבָה' with Rav Nachman's statement that it is a 'חֲשׁוּבָה' (important) mitzvah originating from the six days of creation.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute: flute overrides Shabbat?
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: flute overrides Shabbat?
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah says the flute overrides Shabbat, while the Sages say it does not even override Yom Tov. Rav Yosef explains that the dispute concerns the song of the daily offering: Rabbi Yosei holds that primary song is with an instrument, which is a Temple service and overrides Shabbat; the Sages hold that primary song is vocal, not a service, and does not override Shabbat. However, for the song of Sho'evah, all agree it is mere joy and does not override Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: the flute overrides Shabbat — the statement of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah.
The Sages say: even Yom Tov does not override the flute.

Rav Yosef explains: the dispute is about the song of the sacrifice — Rabbi Yosei holds that primary song is with an instrument, which is Temple service and overrides Shabbat, while the Sages hold that primary song is vocal and does not override Shabbat; but regarding the song of the Water-Drawing, all agree it is joy and does not override Shabbat.

items.text: Rav Yosef's proof from wooden Temple vessels
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's proof from wooden Temple vessels
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef claims that the dispute about song is the same as a tannaitic dispute about wooden Temple vessels: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah validates them, while Rabbi (Yehudah HaNasi) invalidates them. He suggests that the one who validates holds that primary song is instrumental, learning from Moses' copper pipes, while the one who invalidates holds that primary song is vocal and does not learn from that precedent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks: from where do I say that they dispute about this? A baraita is cited: service vessels made of wood — Rabbi (Yehudah HaNasi) invalidates and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah validates.

Rav Yosef infers: is it not that they dispute about this — the one who validates holds that primary song is with an instrument and we learn from Moses' pipe, and the one who invalidates holds that primary song is vocal and we do not learn from Moses' pipe.

Rav Yosef infers that the one who validates holds that primary song is instrumental, learning from Moses' copper pipes, while the one who invalidates holds that primary song is vocal and does not learn from that precedent.

items.text: First rejection: dispute is about deriving possible from impossible
items.text_en: First rejection: dispute is about deriving possible from impossible
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rav Yosef's proof: perhaps all agree that primary song is instrumental, but the dispute is about whether we can derive a possible case (wooden vessels) from an impossible case (Moses' copper pipes, which cannot be made of wood). Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah says we can derive possible from impossible, while Rabbi says we cannot.

sub.desc_en: The gemara rejects: no, all agree that primary song is with an instrument, and here they dispute about whether we derive a possible case from an impossible case.

items.text: Second alternative: dispute is about hermeneutical methods
items.text_en: Second alternative: dispute is about hermeneutical methods
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another alternative: perhaps all agree that primary song is vocal and that we do not derive possible from impossible. Instead, the dispute about wooden vessels is about whether to interpret the Torah using the principles of כלל ופרט (general and particular) or ריבוי ומיעוט (amplification and limitation). Rabbi uses כלל ופרט, limiting the menorah to metal; Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah uses ריבוי ומיעוט, including all materials except earthenware.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a second alternative: all agree that primary song is vocal and that we do not derive possible from impossible, and the dispute about wooden vessels is about whether to interpret the Torah using the principles of כלל ופרט (general and particular) or ריבוי ומיעוט (amplification and limitation).
Rabbi interprets the verses about the menorah using the method of כלל ופרט (general and particular), which limits the material to metal only.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah interprets the verses using the method of ריבוי ומיעוט (amplification and limitation), which includes all materials except earthenware.

items.text: Rav Pappa begins a new statement
items.text_en: Rav Pappa begins a new statement
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa begins to speak, but the daf ends here, leaving his statement incomplete.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa begins a statement (the content is cut off in the source).

items.text: Opening Tannaitic dispute about the Temple musicians
items.text_en: Opening Tannaitic dispute about the Temple musicians
items.desc_en: The baraita presents three opinions: Rabbi Meir says they were slaves of priests, Rabbi Yosei says they were from specific families of Israelites, and Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus says they were Levites.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents three opinions: Rabbi Meir says the Temple musicians were slaves of priests, Rabbi Yosei says they were from specific Israelite families, and Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus says they were Levites.
The Gemara asks whether the dispute is about whether the essence of song is vocal (בפה) or instrumental (בכלי).
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei's position (Israelites) does not fit either view, since if song is vocal even slaves suffice, and if instrumental only Levites are valid.
The Gemara resolves that all agree the essence of song is vocal, and the dispute is merely about what actually happened historically.
The Gemara asks what practical difference the dispute makes, and answers that it concerns whether one can elevate from the platform (דוכן) to lineage and tithe status.
The Gemara explains each opinion's practical implication: slaves cannot elevate at all, Israelites elevate for lineage but not tithe, and Levites elevate for both.

items.text: Gemara's initial assumption about the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's initial assumption about the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute is about whether the main aspect of song is vocal (so slaves suffice) or instrumental (so Levites are required).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute among the Tannaim is whether the primary aspect of song is vocal (so slaves suffice) or instrumental (so Levites are required).

items.text: Rejection of the initial assumption
items.text_en: Rejection of the initial assumption
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects this, pointing out that Rabbi Yosei's position is inconsistent with either view. Instead, all agree that the main aspect of song is vocal, and the dispute is merely about what actually happened historically.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosei's position is inconsistent with either view of the dispute's underlying principle.
The Gemara resolves that all agree the main aspect of song is vocal, and the dispute is merely about what actually happened historically.

items.text: Practical difference between the opinions
items.text_en: Practical difference between the opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the practical difference: whether one can elevate from the platform (duchan) for lineage and tithe purposes. Slaves cannot be elevated at all, Israelites can be elevated for lineage but not tithe, and Levites can be elevated for both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference emerges from the dispute about the identity of the singers.

The Gemara explains the practical difference: one who says they were slaves holds that one cannot elevate from the platform (duchan) for lineage or tithe; one who says Israelites holds one can elevate for lineage but not tithe; one who says Levites holds one can elevate for both.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says the dispute is about the song of the water-drawing celebration (shir shel sho'eivah), whether it overrides Shabbat. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says it does, the Rabbis say it does not. But for the song of the daily offering, all agree it is service and overrides Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba shifts the discussion: the dispute about whether song overrides Shabbat applies only to the water-drawing song (שיר של שואבה), but all agree that the song of the daily sacrifice (שיר של קרבן) overrides Shabbat.

items.text: Refutation of Rav Yosef's position
items.text_en: Refutation of Rav Yosef's position
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that explicitly states that the song of the water-drawing celebration overrides Shabbat according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, but the Rabbis say it does not even override a Festival. This is a refutation of Rav Yosef's position.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is brought as an objection: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says the water-drawing song overrides Shabbat, but the Sages say it does not even override a festival, refuting Rav Yosef's position.

items.text: Attempt to limit the refutation
items.text_en: Attempt to limit the refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that perhaps the dispute is only about the water-drawing song, but for the song of the daily offering all agree it overrides Shabbat. Rav Yosef responds that the dispute applies to both, and the specific mention of the water-drawing song is to show the extent of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that perhaps the dispute is only about the water-drawing song, but for the song of the daily offering all agree it overrides Shabbat, which would make Rav Yosef's refutation double.
Rav Yosef responds that the dispute applies to both songs, and the specific mention of the water-drawing song is only to show the extent of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's leniency.

items.text: Final refutation of Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Final refutation of Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: A mishnah states that the flute of the water-drawing celebration does not override Shabbat or Yom Tov. The Gemara analyzes that this must be according to the Rabbis, and thus it is a double refutation of Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita stating that the flute of the water-drawing does not override Shabbat or festivals, implying the sacrifice song does, which refutes Rav Yosef doubly.
The Gemara asks: this mishnah implies that only the flute of the water-drawing does not override, but the flute of the sacrifice does override — whose opinion does that follow?
The Gemara rejects the possibility that it follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, since he holds that even the water-drawing song overrides Shabbat.
The Gemara concludes that the mishnah must follow the Rabbis, and thus it is a double refutation of Rav Yosef.

items.text: מקורות למחלוקת על עיקר השירה
items.text_en: Scriptural support for the two views on song
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings verses to support the two views: for instrumental song, a verse about Hezekiah; for vocal song, a verse about the singers and trumpeters. Each side interprets the other's verse to align with its own view.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה פסוקים התומכים בשתי הדעות: האחת גורסת שעיקר השירה בכלי (דברי הימים ב' כט, כז), והשנייה גורסת שעיקר השירה בפה (דברי הימים ב' ה, יג). כל צד מיישב את הפסוק השני לפי שיטתו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of the view that instrumental song (עיקר שירה בכלי) is primary, and cites the verse about Hezekiah where song is accompanied by trumpets and Davidic instruments.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו מקור הדעה שעיקר השירה בכלי, ומביאה פסוק מספר דברי הימים ב' כפי שפירש אותו חזקיהו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of the view that vocal song (עיקר שירה בפה) is primary, and cites the verse about singers and trumpeters making one sound.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה פסוק מספר דברי הימים ב' המוכיח שעיקר השירה בפה, שהרי נאמר 'כאחד למחצצרים ולמשוררים'.

sub.desc_en: The pro-vocal-song side reinterprets the Hezekiah verse: 'החל שיר ה׳' refers to vocal song, and the instruments only sweeten the sound (לבסומי קלא).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על הדעה שעיקר השירה בפה מהפסוק בחזקיהו, ומתרצת שהפסוק מדבר על שירה בפה עם כלים לסיוע הקול.

sub.desc_en: The pro-instrumental-song side reinterprets the verse about singers and trumpeters: just as trumpeters use instruments, so too singers must use instruments.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שגם הפסוק 'כאחד למחצצרים ולמשוררים' מלמד שהמשוררים דומים למחצצרים — מה מחצצרים בכלי, אף משוררים בכלי.

items.text: משנת שמחת בית השואבה
items.text_en: Mishnah: Description of the water-drawing celebration
items.desc_en: The mishnah describes the great joy of the water-drawing celebration, including the lighting of golden menorahs in the Women's Courtyard, the use of worn priestly garments for wicks, and the dancing of the pious and men of deeds.
items.desc: המשנה מתארת את שמחת בית השואבה: ירידת הכהנים והלויים לעזרת נשים, הדלקת מנורות זהב גבוהות, והריקודים של חסידים ואנשי מעשה.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by declaring that one who never saw the water-drawing celebration has never seen true joy, then describes the elaborate setup in the Women's Courtyard with golden menorahs, wicks from worn priestly garments, and the resulting illumination throughout Jerusalem.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בתיאור שמחת בית השואבה: מי שלא ראה אותה לא ראה שמחה מימיו; הכהנים יורדים לעזרת נשים, מדליקים מנורות זהב גבוהות, וחסידים ואנשי מעשה מרקדים לפניהם.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah concludes its description by noting that the pious and men of deeds would dance before the celebrants.

items.text: Mishnah: The Water-Drawing Celebration and Trumpet Blasts
items.text_en: Mishnah: The Water-Drawing Celebration and Trumpet Blasts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the Levites playing instruments on the fifteen steps, the priests with trumpets at the upper gate, and the sequence of trumpet blasts as they proceed to the Eastern Gate, where they turn and declare their devotion to God.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the Levites playing instruments on the fifteen steps corresponding to the fifteen Psalms of Ascents.
The Mishnah details the priests with trumpets at the upper gate and the sequence of blasts as they descend.
The Mishnah concludes with the procession to the Eastern Gate, the turning westward, and the declaration of devotion, with Rabbi Yehuda's alternative formulation.

items.text: Gemara: The Beauty of the Temple and Herod's Construction
items.text_en: Gemara: The Beauty of the Temple and Herod's Construction
items.desc_en: The Gemara praises the Temple's beauty, attributing it to Herod's building with marble and stone, and discusses the rabbis' advice against gilding it.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with hyperbolic praise: one who never saw the Simchat Beit HaSho'eva never saw joy, one who never saw Jerusalem in its glory never saw a beautiful city, and one who never saw the Temple in its construction never saw a magnificent building.
The Gemara asks: what is this magnificent building referred to in the baraita?
Abaye (or alternatively Rav Chisda) answers: it is Herod's building of the Temple.
The Gemara asks: with what material did Herod build it?
Rava answers that Herod built it with marble and stone; some say with marble, alabaster, and marble.
The Gemara digresses to describe the construction technique: Herod set back and advanced the stone courses to receive plaster.
Herod intended to gild it with gold, but the rabbis advised him to leave it as is, because the marble's appearance like the waves of the sea is more beautiful.

items.text: Gemara: The Alexandrian Synagogue's Grandeur
items.text_en: Gemara: The Alexandrian Synagogue's Grandeur
items.desc_en: A baraita describes the magnificent synagogue of Alexandria, with its vast size, golden cathedrae, and orderly seating by trade, ensuring the poor could find support.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda opens with a baraita praising the Alexandrian synagogue's grandeur, describing its vast size and seventy-one golden cathedrae.
The baraita describes the wooden platform in the center and the sexton's use of a cloth to signal the congregation's 'Amen' response.
The baraita explains that the congregation sat in separate guilds, enabling a poor artisan to identify his trade colleagues and receive support.

items.text: Gemara: Alexander the Great's Destruction of Alexandria
items.text_en: Gemara: Alexander the Great's Destruction of Alexandria
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that Alexander of Macedon killed the Jews of Alexandria because they violated the prohibition against returning to Egypt, and he found them reading a verse about a distant nation, which he interpreted as referring to himself.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that Alexander of Macedon killed all the Jews of Alexandria because they violated the prohibition against returning to Egypt.
The gemara recounts that when Alexander arrived, he found them reading a verse about a distant nation, interpreted it as referring to himself, and killed them.

items.text: Gemara: The Great Improvement of Separating Men and Women
items.text_en: Gemara: The Great Improvement of Separating Men and Women
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the 'great improvement' of separating men and women in the Temple courtyard, citing the original practice, the problems it caused, and the eventual solution of women above and men below, supported by a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the 'great improvement' mentioned in the Mishnah refers to.
Rabbi Elazar answers that the improvement refers to the change described in the baraita: originally the women's section was flat, then they added a balcony and seated women above and men below.
A baraita is cited detailing the three stages of seating arrangements in the Temple courtyard, culminating in women above and men below to prevent frivolity.
The Gemara objects: how could the Sages institute such a change, given the verse that all Temple construction was given by divine inspiration and cannot be altered?
Rav resolves the objection: the Sages found a verse and derived the change from it, meaning the innovation was based on scriptural authority.

items.text: Opening kal vachomer about separation of men and women during mourning
items.text_en: Opening kal vachomer about separation of men and women during mourning
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse about future mourning that even then men and women mourn separately, and argues that all the more so now when the evil inclination is active, they should be separate during rejoicing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if in the future, when people mourn and the evil inclination does not rule, the Torah requires men and women to be separate, then all the more so now, when they rejoice and the evil inclination rules, they should be separate.

items.text: Dispute about the subject of the mourning
items.text_en: Dispute about the subject of the mourning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Dosa and the Rabbis dispute whether the mourning is for the slain Messiah son of Joseph or for the slain evil inclination.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the subject of this mourning?
Rabbi Dosa and the Rabbis dispute: one says the mourning is for the slain Messiah son of Joseph, and the other says it is for the slain evil inclination.

items.text: Question on the view that mourning is for the evil inclination
items.text_en: Question on the view that mourning is for the evil inclination
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why there would be mourning for the evil inclination's death, since its destruction should be a cause for rejoicing, not mourning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why there would be mourning for the evil inclination's death, since its destruction should be a cause for rejoicing, not mourning.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's explanation of the mourning for the evil inclination
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's explanation of the mourning for the evil inclination
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda explains that in the future, the evil inclination will be slaughtered before the righteous and wicked, appearing differently to each, causing both groups to weep.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda explains that in the future, God will slaughter the evil inclination before the righteous and wicked, appearing as a high mountain to the righteous and as a thin hair to the wicked, causing both groups to weep, and God Himself is astonished.

items.text: Rabbi Assi's analogy of the evil inclination's growth
items.text_en: Rabbi Assi's analogy of the evil inclination's growth
items.desc_en: Rabbi Assi compares the evil inclination initially to a spider's thread and ultimately to cart ropes, citing a verse from Isaiah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Assi states that the evil inclination (יצר הרע) initially resembles a spider's thread but ultimately becomes like cart ropes, citing the verse from Isaiah.

items.text: Messiah son of David's request for life after seeing Messiah son of Joseph slain
items.text_en: Messiah son of David's request for life after seeing Messiah son of Joseph slain
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that when the Messiah son of David sees the slain Messiah son of Joseph, he asks only for life, and God responds that David already prophesied this request.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces that God will offer the Messiah son of David anything he requests, citing the verse 'שאל ממני ואתנה גוים נחלתך' (Ask of Me and I will give nations as your inheritance).
When the Messiah son of David sees the slain Messiah son of Joseph, he asks God only for life.
God responds that David already prophesied this request in the verse 'חיים שאל ממך נתתה לו' (He asked life of You, and You gave it to him).

items.text: Seven names of the evil inclination
items.text_en: Seven names of the evil inclination
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avira or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi enumerates seven names for the evil inclination from Scripture: God calls it 'evil', Moses 'uncircumcised', David 'unclean', Solomon 'enemy', Isaiah 'stumbling block', Ezekiel 'stone', and Joel 'northern one'.

sub.text: Rabbi Avira / Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avira / Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avira or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi opens by stating that the evil inclination has seven names, beginning with God calling it 'רע' (evil) and Moses calling it 'ערל' (uncircumcised), and David calling it 'טמא' (unclean).

sub.text: Rabbi Avira / Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (continued)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avira / Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (continued)
sub.desc_en: Solomon calls the evil inclination 'שונא' (enemy), with a homiletic reading of the verse to show that feeding the enemy subdues the inclination.

sub.text: Rabbi Avira / Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (continued) and a baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avira / Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi (continued) and a baraita
sub.desc_en: Isaiah calls it 'מכשול' (stumbling block), Ezekiel calls it 'אבן' (stone), and Joel calls it 'צפוני' (northern one), with a baraita explaining that 'צפוני' refers to the evil inclination hidden in the heart.

items.text: Interpretation of Joel's prophecy about the northern one
items.text_en: Interpretation of Joel's prophecy about the northern one
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verses about the 'northern one' as referring to the evil inclination's destruction of the First and Second Temples and its targeting of Torah scholars.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'וְהִדַּחְתִּיו אֶל אֶרֶץ צִיָּה וּשְׁמָמָה' as referring to the evil inclination being driven to a desolate place where there are no people to provoke.
The Gemara interprets 'אֶת פָּנָיו אֶל הַיָּם הַקַּדְמוֹנִי' as the evil inclination focusing on the First Temple, destroying it and killing the Torah scholars within.
The Gemara interprets 'וְסוֹפוֹ אֶל הַיָּם הָאַחֲרוֹן' as the evil inclination focusing on the Second Temple, destroying it and killing the Torah scholars within.
The Gemara interprets 'וְעָלָה בׇאְשׁוֹ וְתַעַל צַחֲנָתוֹ' as the evil inclination abandoning the nations and targeting the enemies of Israel.
Abaye concludes from the verse 'כִּי הִגְדִּיל לַעֲשׂוֹת' that the evil inclination targets Torah scholars more than anyone else.

items.text: Abaye's encounter with the evil inclination and the elder's teaching
items.text_en: Abaye's encounter with the evil inclination and the elder's teaching
items.desc_en: Abaye follows a man and woman to prevent sin, overhears their conversation, and later an elder teaches him that the greater a person is, the greater their evil inclination.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Abaye's story: he overhears a man and woman planning to travel together and follows them to prevent sin, but they part chastely.

sub.text: Abaye's reflection and the elder's teaching
sub.text_en: Abaye's reflection and the elder's teaching
sub.desc_en: Abaye despairs at his own weakness, and an elder teaches him that the greater a person is, the greater their evil inclination.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's statement about the daily struggle with the evil inclination
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's statement about the daily struggle with the evil inclination
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that a person's evil inclination overcomes them daily, citing a verse from Psalms.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that a person's evil inclination (יצר הרע) overcomes them daily, citing the verse beginning with 'רק' (only).

items.text: Resh Lakish on the daily struggle with the evil inclination
items.text_en: Resh Lakish on the daily struggle with the evil inclination
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish teaches that a person's evil inclination grows stronger each day and seeks to kill him, but God helps him overcome it, as derived from Psalms.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish teaches that a person's evil inclination (יצר הרע) grows stronger daily and seeks to kill him, but God helps him overcome it, citing Psalms.

items.text: The school of Rabbi Yishmael's advice: drag the evil inclination to the study hall
items.text_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael's advice: drag the evil inclination to the study hall
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that if the evil inclination (called 'menuvval') attacks, one should drag it to the study hall, where Torah study will crush it like water on stone or shatter it like a hammer on rock.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael advises that if one encounters the evil inclination (מנוול), one should drag it to the study hall, where Torah, compared to water and fire, will dissolve or shatter it.

items.text: Rabbi Yonatan: The evil inclination entices in this world and testifies in the next
items.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan: The evil inclination entices in this world and testifies in the next
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan says the evil inclination entices a person in this world and then testifies against him in the World to Come, based on a verse and the Atbash code of Rabbi Chiya.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan teaches that the evil inclination seduces a person in this world and testifies against him in the World to Come, as derived from a verse and the atbash cipher of Rabbi Chiyya.

items.text: Rav Huna and Rava: The progression of the evil inclination
items.text_en: Rav Huna and Rava: The progression of the evil inclination
items.desc_en: Rav Huna resolves a contradiction between two verses about the evil inclination: initially it leads astray, but ultimately it dwells within. Rava adds that the evil inclination progresses from a 'guest' to a 'lodger' to a 'man' who takes over, as shown by the story of the poor man's lamb.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna raises a contradiction between two verses: one says the evil inclination leads astray, the other says it is within them.
Rav Huna resolves: initially the evil inclination leads them astray, but ultimately it dwells within them.
Rava adds that the evil inclination progresses from a 'guest' to a 'lodger' to a 'man' who takes over, citing the story of the poor man's lamb.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan: The paradox of the small organ
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan: The paradox of the small organ
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says a person has a small organ (the evil inclination) that is satisfied when starved and hungry when fed, as derived from the verse about Israel's satisfaction leading to straying.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches that a person has a small organ (the evil inclination) that is satisfied when starved and hungry when fed, citing a verse.

items.text: Four things God regrets creating, and the three verses that sustain Israel
items.text_en: Four things God regrets creating, and the three verses that sustain Israel
items.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Acha (or Bei Rav) lists four things God regrets creating: exile, Chaldeans, Ishmaelites, and the evil inclination, each supported by verses. Rabbi Yochanan then says that without three specific verses (including 'I have done evil'), Israel's feet would falter, and Rav Papa adds a fourth.

sub.text: Rav Chana bar Acha / Bei Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chana bar Acha / Bei Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Acha (or Bei Rav) lists four things God regrets creating: exile, Chaldeans, Ishmaelites, and the evil inclination, each supported by verses.

sub.text: Rav Chana bar Acha / Bei Rav (continued)
sub.text_en: Rav Chana bar Acha / Bei Rav (continued)
sub.desc_en: The evil inclination is supported by the verse 'וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי' (and that I have done evil).
Rabbi Yochanan says that without three specific verses (including 'וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי'), Israel's feet would falter.
Rav Papa adds a fourth verse, 'וְאֶת רוּחִי אֶתֵּן בְּקִרְבְּכֶם' (and I will put My spirit within you), as sustaining Israel.

items.text: The identity of the four craftsmen and Rav Sheshet's objection
items.text_en: The identity of the four craftsmen and Rav Sheshet's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida identifies the four craftsmen from Zechariah as Messiah ben David, Messiah ben Yosef, Elijah, and the Righteous Priest. Rav Sheshet objects that the horns scattered Judah, but the response explains that the craftsmen come to terrify the nations who scattered Judah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who are the four craftsmen mentioned in the verse from Zechariah.

sub.text: Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.text_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida identifies the four craftsmen as Messiah ben David, Messiah ben Yosef, Elijah, and the Righteous Priest.
Rav Sheshet objects that if these are the craftsmen, they come to restore Judah, but the verse says the horns scattered Judah, implying the craftsmen should be destroyers.
The response directs Rav Sheshet to the end of the verse, which says the craftsmen come to terrify and cast down the horns of the nations who scattered Judah.
Rav Sheshet dismisses the aggadic discussion, saying he has no need for such aggadic interpretations.

items.text: The seven shepherds and eight princes of man
items.text_en: The seven shepherds and eight princes of man
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse about seven shepherds and eight princes of man: David in the center, Adam, Seth, and Methuselah on his right, Abraham, Jacob, and Moses on his left; the eight princes are Jesse, Saul, Samuel, Amos, Zephaniah, Zedekiah, Messiah, and Elijah.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: who are the seven shepherds mentioned in the verse?

The gemara answers: David in the center, Adam, Seth, and Methuselah on his right, Abraham, Jacob, and Moses on his left; the eight princes are Jesse, Saul, Samuel, Amos, Zephaniah, Zedekiah, Messiah, and Elijah.

items.text: The four ladders and the strength of the young priests
items.text_en: The four ladders and the strength of the young priests
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the four ladders of the menorah, its height of fifty cubits, and the four young priests carrying oil jugs. A question arises about the total oil (120 log total or each), resolved by a baraita. The priests are praised for their strength, compared to Martha bat Baitos's son, and the advantage of ladders over a ramp is explained.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states that the menorah was fifty cubits high, with four young priests each holding oil jugs of one hundred twenty log.
The Gemara raises a question: whether the one hundred twenty log was the total for all jugs or each jug individually.
The Gemara resolves the question by citing a baraita that each jug held thirty log, totaling one hundred twenty log.
The Tanna praises the young priests as more praiseworthy than Martha bat Baitos's son, who could carry two large thighs but was restrained by his fellow priests for the sake of royal honor.
The Gemara asks what the praise consists of, questioning whether it is due to weight, since Martha's son carried heavier loads.
The Gemara explains that Martha's son used a ramp (כֶּבֶשׁ) which is square and not steep, while the priests used ladders (סוּלָּמוֹת) which are very steep, making their feat more impressive.
The Tanna introduces a new topic: there was no courtyard in Jerusalem that was not used for the water-drawing celebration.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the water-drawing celebration, noting that a woman could sort wheat by the light of the celebration.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing the water-drawing celebration (שמחת בית השואבה), noting that a woman could sort wheat by its light.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on the pious and penitents
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on the pious and penitents
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about different groups: the pious who say 'fortunate is our youth that did not shame our old age', and penitents who say 'fortunate is our old age that atoned for our youth'. Both agree that one who has not sinned is fortunate, and one who has sinned should repent.

sub.desc_en: A baraita (תנו רבנן) records three sayings: some say 'fortunate is our youth that did not shame our old age' (the pious), others say 'fortunate is our old age that atoned for our youth' (penitents), and both say 'fortunate is one who never sinned, and if one sinned — let him repent and be forgiven.'
The baraita cites penitents who say 'fortunate is our old age that atoned for our youth'.
The baraita concludes that both groups agree: fortunate is one who never sinned, and one who sinned should repent and be forgiven.

items.text: Hillel's sayings and the floating skull
items.text_en: Hillel's sayings and the floating skull
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts Hillel's sayings during the water-drawing celebration: 'If I am here, all is here; if I am not here, who is here?' and 'Where I love, there my feet lead me.' He also saw a floating skull and said: 'Because you drowned others, they drowned you, and those who drowned you will be drowned.' Rabbi Yochanan comments that a person's feet are responsible for him, leading him to where he is needed.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces Hillel's sayings during the water-drawing celebration, beginning with 'If I am here, all is here.'
Hillel states that his feet lead him where he loves, and cites the verse 'In every place where I mention My name, I will come to you and bless you.'
Hillel sees a floating skull and declares that those who drowned others will be drowned, and their drowners will also be drowned.
Rabbi Yochanan comments that a person's feet are responsible for him, leading him to the place where he is needed.

items.text: Story of Solomon and the two scribes
items.text_en: Story of Solomon and the two scribes
items.desc_en: The Gemara tells a story about two scribes of Solomon, Elihoreph and Ahiah, who were sought by the Angel of Death. The Angel sent them to the city of Luz, where they died. The next day, the Angel rejoiced, and Solomon declared: 'A person's feet are responsible for him, leading him to where he is needed.'

sub.text: Story about Solomon and the scribes
sub.text_en: Story about Solomon and the scribes
sub.desc_en: A story about two scribes of Solomon, Elihoreph and Ahiah, whom the Angel of Death sought; Solomon sent them to Luz, where they died, and Solomon exclaimed: 'A person's feet are his guarantors; to the place where he is needed, they lead him.'
The Angel of Death is seen sad, and explains that he is being asked for these two scribes.
Solomon hands the scribes over to demons, who send them to the city of Luz, where they die.
The next day, the Angel of Death is seen rejoicing, explaining that he sent the scribes to the place where they were sought.
Solomon declares that a person's feet are responsible for him, leading him to the place where he is needed.

items.text: Shimon ben Gamliel's juggling and prostration
items.text_en: Shimon ben Gamliel's juggling and prostration
items.desc_en: A baraita describes Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's feats during the water-drawing celebration: he would juggle eight flaming torches, and when prostrating, he would bow and kiss the floor without using his hands, which is called 'kiddah'.

sub.text: Supporting baraita about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
sub.desc_en: A baraita describes Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel juggling eight flaming torches and performing a deep bow (קידה) during the water-drawing celebration.

items.text: Levi's injury and other feats
items.text_en: Levi's injury and other feats
items.desc_en: Levi performed a 'kiddah' before Rabbi and became lame. The Gemara questions whether this was caused by the act or by his earlier irreverent speech, citing Rabbi Elazar's warning. It then lists other feats: Levi juggled eight knives before Rabbi, Samuel juggled eight cups of wine before King Shapur, and Abaye juggled eight eggs (or four) before Rava.

sub.desc_en: The narrative reports that Levi performed a קידה (kiddah prostration) before Rabbi and became lame.
The Gemara questions whether the act of prostration alone caused the injury.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Elazar's warning that one should never speak irreverently toward Heaven, as a great man (Levi) did so and became lame.
The Gemara resolves that both the irreverent speech and the prostration caused Levi's lameness.
The Gemara lists other feats: Levi juggled eight knives before Rabbi, Samuel juggled eight cups of wine before King Shapur, and Abaye juggled eight eggs (or four) before Rava.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananiah's schedule and the nature of sleep
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananiah's schedule and the nature of sleep
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananiah describes the schedule during the water-drawing celebration, saying they never slept. The Gemara questions this, citing Rabbi Yochanan that one who vows not to sleep for three days is flogged and must sleep immediately. The Gemara resolves that they did not taste sleep but dozed on each other's shoulders.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananiah describes the schedule during the water-drawing celebration, stating they never saw sleep in their eyes.
The Gemara questions how they could never sleep, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one who vows not to sleep for three days is flogged and must sleep immediately.
The Gemara resolves that they did not taste actual sleep but dozed on each other's shoulders.

items.text: The fifteen Ma'alot and David's digging of the foundation
items.text_en: The fifteen Ma'alot and David's digging of the foundation
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks a rabbi about the fifteen 'Ma'alot' (ascents) in Psalms. The rabbi reports Rabbi Yochanan's teaching: when David dug the foundation, the deep threatened to flood the world, so David recited fifteen 'Ma'alot' and lowered them. The Gemara objects that they should be called 'Yordot' (descents). The rabbi then clarifies that David asked if it was permitted to write the Name, and the deep subsided.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks a rabbi who arranges aggadot before him: 'Have you heard, these fifteen Ma'alot (ascents) — corresponding to whom did David say them?'
The rabbi reports Rabbi Yochanan's teaching: when David dug the foundation (שיתין), the deep threatened to flood the world, so David recited fifteen 'Ma'alot' and lowered them.
The Gemara objects: if David lowered the deep, the psalms should be called 'Yordot' (descents), not 'Ma'alot' (ascents).

The rabbi clarifies: since you reminded me, the full story is that David asked whether it was permitted to write the Name (שם), and the deep subsided — hence the psalms are called 'Ma'alot' because they arose from David's question.

items.text: David casts God's name into the deep
items.text_en: David casts God's name into the deep
items.desc_en: David asks for permission to cast a shard with God's name into the deep to subdue the waters. Achitophel infers from the law of the sotah that making peace between a man and his wife justifies erasing God's name, so all the more so for making peace for the entire world. David writes the name and casts it into the deep, which sinks 16,000 cubits, but then he raises it to 1,000 cubits to prevent the world from being flooded. Ulla deduces that the earth's depth is 1,000 cubits, and Rav Mesharshiya explains that water drawn from a well comes from the Euphrates.

sub.desc_en: David requests to cast a shard with God's name into the deep and threatens to choke anyone who knows how to respond but remains silent.
Achitophel infers from the law of the sotah (סוטה) that if God's name may be erased for peace between a man and his wife, it is certainly permitted for peace for the entire world.
David acknowledges Achitophel's permission and proceeds to write the name and cast it into the deep.
David writes the name, casts it into the deep, which sinks 16,000 cubits, then raises it to 1,000 cubits to prevent the world from being flooded.
Ulla deduces that the earth's depth is 1,000 cubits.
The Gemara objects that we see water drawn from shallow wells contradicts the depth of 1,000 cubits.
Rav Mesharshiya explains that the water drawn from shallow wells comes from the Euphrates, not from the deep.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about the upper gate
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about the upper gate
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether the priests standing at the upper gate descended five steps and stood at ten, or descended ten and stood at five. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya questions whether the priests stood above the tenth step that descended five steps and stood on ten, or descended ten and stood on five.
The question is concluded as unresolved (תֵּיקוּ - teiku, stands unresolved).

items.text: The priests' posture in the Temple
items.text_en: The priests' posture in the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'their backs were toward the Temple of the Lord' — it teaches that the priests would expose themselves and defecate downward.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the verse and deduces that the priests' faces were eastward.
The baraita explains that the extra phrase teaches that they were exposing themselves and defecating downward.

items.text: The correct formulation of the prayer
items.text_en: The correct formulation of the prayer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the phrase 'we to Yah and our eyes to Yah' — Rabbi Zeira says that saying 'Shema' twice is like saying 'Modim' twice (a prohibited repetition). The Gemara explains that the correct formulation is: 'They bow eastward, but we thank Yah, and our eyes hope to Yah.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that saying 'שמע' twice seems like repeating 'מודים' twice, which is improper.
The Gemara resolves that they actually said 'המה משתחוים קדמה, ואנו ליה (אנחנו מודים), ועינינו ליה מיחלות', meaning 'They bow eastward, but we give thanks to God and our eyes hope to God.'
The Gemara resolves that the correct formulation is: 'They bow eastward, but we thank Yah, and our eyes hope to Yah.'

items.text: Mishnah: The number of shofar blasts
items.text_en: Mishnah: The number of shofar blasts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in the Temple they do not reduce from 21 blasts nor add to 48. On a regular day there are 21: three for opening the gates, nine for the morning tamid, and nine for the afternoon tamid. On Shabbat eve they add six: three to stop work and three to separate between holy and profane. On Shabbat eve during Sukkot there are 48 blasts, listing all the components.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule: in the Temple, no fewer than 21 blasts and no more than 48; on an ordinary day there are 21 blasts — three for opening the gates, nine for the morning tamid, nine for the afternoon tamid — and on days with additional offerings add another nine.
The Mishnah notes that on Shabbat eve six additional blasts are added: three to stop work and three to separate between holy and profane.
The Mishnah concludes by specifying the exceptional case: when Shabbat eve falls during Sukkot, there are 48 blasts, listing all the components that add up to this number.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis on blasts
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis on blasts
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda, who says the minimum is seven and the maximum sixteen. The dispute is whether tekiah and teruah are one unit (Rabbi Yehuda) or separate (Rabbis). Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse 'and you shall sound a teruah' that tekiah and teruah are one. The Rabbis derive from 'when you assemble the congregation, you shall blow but not sound a teruah' that they are separate. Rav Kahana says there is no difference between tekiah and teruah, aligning with Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the Mishnah's position disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's position that the minimum is seven blasts and the maximum sixteen.
The Gemara asks what the dispute is between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, and explains that Rabbi Yehuda considers tekiah and teruah as one unit, while the Rabbis consider them separate.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: the verse 'וּתְקַעְתֶּם תְּרוּעָה' (and you shall sound a teruah) shows that tekiah and teruah are one unit.
The Rabbis object that the verse is needed for the simple rule of a blast before and after the teruah, and Rabbi Yehuda derives that from the word 'שֵּׁנִית' (second).

The Gemara explains the Rabbis' reasoning: the verse 'וּבְהַקְהִיל אֶת הַקָּהָל תִּתְקְעוּ וְלֹא תָרִיעוּ' (when you assemble the congregation, you shall blow but not sound a teruah) shows that tekiah and teruah are separate, otherwise the Torah would command half a mitzvah.
Rabbi Yehuda rejects this, saying that verse is merely a sign (for when to blow) and not a halachic distinction.
The Rabbis object that even if it is a sign, the Torah has made it a mitzvah.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Kahana's statement that there is no difference between tekiah and teruah aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, and notes that this is obvious.

items.text: Gemara's conclusion that the mishnah follows the Rabbis
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion that the mishnah follows the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the mishnah's ruling that one who hears nine blasts in nine hours has fulfilled his obligation is meant to exclude Rabbi Yochanan's lenient view, not to include it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the mishnah's ruling that one who hears nine blasts in nine hours has fulfilled his obligation is meant to exclude Rabbi Yochanan's lenient view, not to include it.

items.text: Gemara's objection and answer
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mishnah could be interpreted as Rabbi Yochanan's view, but then notes that the phrase 'and not at all' in the mishnah disproves this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the mishnah could be interpreted as Rabbi Yochanan's view, asking why it cannot be understood that way.
The Gemara answers that the phrase 'and not at all' in the mishnah disproves this interpretation, as it would be superfluous under Rabbi Yochanan's view.

items.text: Identifying the mishnah's author and the dispute about the tenth blast
items.text_en: Identifying the mishnah's author and the dispute about the tenth blast
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the mishnah as following Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who holds that three blasts are for the altar, not for the tenth gate. It explains the reasoning of both Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Rabbis regarding whether to blow for the tenth gate or the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah lists blasts for the altar but not for the tenth gate, and asks which Tanna authored this mishnah.
The Gemara identifies the mishnah as following Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who holds that three blasts are for the altar, not for the tenth gate.
The baraita clarifies that the two positions are mutually exclusive: one who holds blasts for the tenth gate does not hold for the altar, and vice versa.

The Gemara explains the reasoning of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov (since blasts already opened gates, the tenth gate is not a gate, so the altar is preferable) and the Rabbis (since blasts already accompanied the water libation, the altar is unnecessary, so the tenth gate is preferable).

items.text: Baraita about blowing for each additional offering
items.text_en: Baraita about blowing for each additional offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina brings a baraita from the verse 'And the sons of Aaron shall blow the trumpets' to teach that blasts are added for each additional offering (musaf).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina brings a baraita from the verse 'וּבְנֵי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֲנִים יִתְקְעוּ בַּחֲצוֹצְרוֹת' to prove that blasts are added for each additional offering (מוסף).

items.text: Question about Shabbat within the festival
items.text_en: Question about Shabbat within the festival
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah lists 48 blasts for the eve of Shabbat, but if Shabbat itself fell during the festival, there would be 51 blasts. Rabbi Zeira answers that they do not blow for the opening of the gates on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah lists 48 blasts for the eve of Shabbat during the festival, when Shabbat itself would require 51 blasts.
Rabbi Zeira answers that the blasts for the opening of the gates are not performed on Shabbat, reducing the total.

items.text: Rava's objection to Rabbi Zeira
items.text_en: Rava's objection to Rabbi Zeira
items.desc_en: Rava objects that Rabbi Zeira's answer is inconsistent because the mishnah already states 'on every day', and even if the numbers were equal, the mishnah could have taught both cases to imply two teachings.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that Rabbi Zeira's answer is inconsistent because the mishnah already states 'on every day', and even if the numbers were equal, the mishnah could have taught both cases to imply two teachings.

items.text: Rava's alternative answer and further discussion
items.text_en: Rava's alternative answer and further discussion
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the mishnah does not list Shabbat because they do not blow for the Water Libation on Shabbat, reducing the count. The Gemara then asks why the mishnah does not also list Rosh Hashanah on Shabbat, and answers that the mishnah teaches the case of the eve of Shabbat to convey Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view, and that the tanna omitted other cases, such as the eve of Passover.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the mishnah does not list Shabbat because they do not blow for the Water Libation (מילוי מים) on Shabbat, reducing the count.
The Gemara asks why the mishnah does not also list Rosh Hashanah that falls on Shabbat, which would have three additional blasts.
The Gemara answers that the mishnah teaches the case of the eve of Shabbat to convey Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view, and that the tanna omitted other cases, such as the eve of Passover.

items.text: Questioning the exclusion of Passover eve
items.text_en: Questioning the exclusion of Passover eve
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Passover eve is not considered a leftover (שיורא) from the list of Hallel recitations, suggesting it aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's view that the third group never reached the Hallel. It then considers that the Tanna might agree with Rabbi Yehuda on one point but disagree on another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Passover eve is not considered a leftover (שיורא) from the list of Hallel recitations, suggesting it aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's view that the third group never reached the Hallel.
The Gemara answers that the Tanna might agree with Rabbi Yehuda on one point but disagree on another, allowing the exclusion of Passover eve.

items.text: Identifying the true leftover
items.text_en: Identifying the true leftover
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the actual leftover: Passover eve that occurs on Friday, where six Hallel recitations are removed and six are added, maintaining the total.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what leftover is actually being referred to in the Mishnah's statement about the total number of Hallel recitations.
The Gemara answers that the leftover refers to Passover eve that falls on Friday, where six Hallel recitations are removed and six are added, keeping the total unchanged.

items.text: Objection regarding Passover on Shabbat
items.text_en: Objection regarding Passover on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the total should be more than forty-eight, as Passover eve on Shabbat would add extra Hallel recitations according to both Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis. The answer is that the Mishnah only includes cases that occur every year, excluding Passover on Shabbat which is not annual.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's total of forty-eight is too low, because when Passover eve falls on Shabbat, the Hallel recitations would be more: fifty-one according to Rabbi Yehuda or fifty-seven according to the Rabbis.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah only counts cases that occur every year, excluding Passover eve on Shabbat which does not occur annually.

items.text: Challenge about the intermediate Shabbat of Sukkot
items.text_en: Challenge about the intermediate Shabbat of Sukkot
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the intermediate Shabbat of Sukkot is also not annual, as it depends on the calendar. It explains that when the first day of Sukkot falls on Friday, that Shabbat is postponed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the intermediate Shabbat of Sukkot is not annual, as it depends on the calendar.
The Gemara explains that when the first day of Sukkot falls on Friday, that Shabbat is postponed.

items.text: Support and dispute about postponing Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Support and dispute about postponing Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Yom Kippur can be postponed, citing a Mishnah that fats of Shabbat are offered on Yom Kippur. Rabbi Zeira reports that in Babylonia they said the ruling about Yom Kippur on Friday is unanimous, but upon ascending to Israel, he found Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi stating it is Rabbi Akiva's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Yom Kippur can be postponed, citing a Mishnah that fats of Shabbat are offered on Yom Kippur.

Rabbi Zeira reports that in Babylonia they said the ruling about Yom Kippur on Friday is unanimous, but upon ascending to Israel, he found Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi stating it is Rabbi Akiva's view.

items.text: Resolution: two different opinions
items.text_en: Resolution: two different opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the two views to different Tannaim: one to the Rabbis and one to Acheirim, who limit the interval between festivals to four days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the two views to different Tannaim: one to the Rabbis and one to Acheirim.
A baraita is cited in which Acheirim state that the interval between festivals is only four days, or five in a leap year, confirming their position.

items.text: Discussion on Rosh Chodesh and Shabbat
items.text_en: Discussion on Rosh Chodesh and Shabbat
items.desc_en: A challenge is raised from a baraita that the song of Rosh Chodesh overrides that of Shabbat, implying a conflict. Rav Safra explains it means the Rosh Chodesh song is recited first. Rabbi Yochanan says this is to publicize that Rosh Chodesh was established on time, and another recognition is cited from a baraita about the placement of sacrificial fats.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge from a baraita stating that the song of Rosh Chodesh overrides that of Shabbat, implying a conflict between the two.
Rav Safra explains that 'overrides' means the Rosh Chodesh song is recited first, but the Gemara objects that the regular Shabbat song should take precedence.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Rosh Chodesh song is recited first to publicize that the new month was established on time, and a supporting baraita is cited about the placement of sacrificial fats as another recognition.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the shofar is blown on Rosh Hashanah to publicize that the new month was established on time, and two recognitions are made.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the shofar is blown on Rosh Hashanah to publicize that the new month was established on time, and two recognitions are made.

items.text: Refutation of Rabbi Acha and resolution
items.text_en: Refutation of Rabbi Acha and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita taught by Rava bar Shmuel is brought as a refutation of Rabbi Acha, showing that shofar is not blown on every additional Musaf. Abaye and Rav Ashi offer different scriptural derivations to explain the verse.

sub.desc_en: A baraita taught by Rava bar Shmuel is brought as a refutation of Rabbi Acha, showing that shofar is not blown on every additional Musaf.
The Gemara asks what scriptural derivation supports the baraita's conclusion.
Abaye derives from the verse 'וּבְרָאשֵׁי חׇדְשֵׁיכֶם' that all months are compared to each other, limiting the shofar blowing to Rosh Hashanah alone.
Rav Ashi derives from the dual form 'וּבְרָאשֵׁי' and the singular 'חׇדְשְׁכֶם' that only the month with two heads (Rosh Hashanah) is included, and it is one.

items.text: Order of Psalms on Sukkot's intermediate days
items.text_en: Order of Psalms on Sukkot's intermediate days
items.desc_en: A baraita lists the Psalm recited each day of Sukkot's intermediate days, with a rule that if Shabbat falls on one of them, the Psalm 'Yimotu' is displaced. Rav Safra and Rav Pappa provide mnemonic signs for the order.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists the Psalm recited on the first three intermediate days of Sukkot.
The baraita continues listing the Psalms for the remaining intermediate days and rules that if Shabbat falls on one of them, the Psalm 'Yimotu' is displaced.
Rav Safra and Rav Pappa provide mnemonic signs for the order of the Psalms, with a mnemonic for distinguishing their versions.

items.text: Refutation of Rabbi Acha bar Chanina and alternative explanations
items.text_en: Refutation of Rabbi Acha bar Chanina and alternative explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Acha bar Chanina's statement is actually based on a verse and baraita, and Ravina and the Rabbis of Caesarea offer alternative interpretations about prolonging blasts or increasing trumpeters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Acha bar Chanina's statement is actually based on a verse and a baraita, not a mere opinion.
Ravina explains that Rabbi Acha bar Chanina's statement means that the blasts are prolonged, not that additional blasts are added.
The Rabbis of Caesarea say in the name of Rabbi Acha that the statement means one increases the number of trumpeters.

items.text: Dispute about which day's psalm is displaced when Shabbat falls
items.text_en: Dispute about which day's psalm is displaced when Shabbat falls
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava dispute whether the second day's psalm or the seventh day's psalm is displaced when Shabbat falls on Sukkot. A baraita supports Rava, and Amemar instituted a practice in Nehardea of skipping.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Since we in the Diaspora observe two days of Yom Tov, how do we arrange the psalm recitation when Shabbat falls on Sukkot?
Abaye rules that the second day's psalm (Psalm 94) is displaced when Shabbat falls.
Rava rules that the seventh day's psalm (Psalm 82) is displaced instead.
A baraita is cited that supports Rava: when Shabbat falls on any of the intermediate days, the psalm 'יִמּוֹטוּ' (Psalm 82) is displaced.
Amemar instituted a practice in Nehardea of skipping (דילוגי) the displaced psalm rather than repeating it.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Distribution of Sukkot offerings
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Distribution of Sukkot offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes how the thirteen bulls, two rams, and one goat of the first festival day are offered, and how the remaining fourteen lambs are distributed among eight watches. It details the daily progression of how many watches offer two animals and how many offer one, culminating in the seventh day where all are equal, and the eighth day where they return to the lottery system.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the distribution of Sukkot offerings among the priestly watches, starting with thirteen bulls on the first day and ending with the eighth day's return to the lottery system.

items.text: Gemara: Does the Mishnah follow Rabbi or the Rabbis?
items.text_en: Gemara: Does the Mishnah follow Rabbi or the Rabbis?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's rule about the eighth day lottery aligns with Rabbi's view that a new lottery is held for the eighth-day bull, or with the Rabbis who say one of the two watches that did not serve with bulls performs it. It defends the possibility that the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, explaining that even they require a lottery for the two watches. It then addresses a related baraita about watches that repeat but do not triple, interpreting 'did not triple' as referring to the bulls of the festival.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's rule about the eighth day lottery follows Rabbi's view that a new lottery is held for the eighth-day bull, citing the baraita where Rabbi requires a lottery and the Rabbis say one of the two watches that did not serve with bulls performs it.
The Gemara defends the possibility that the Mishnah follows the Rabbis, arguing that even they require a lottery for the two watches.
The Gemara raises a new question about a baraita that states all watches repeat and triple except two that repeat but do not triple, asking whether this aligns with Rabbi or the Rabbis.
The Gemara answers that even according to the Rabbis, 'did not triple' refers to the bulls of the festival, not to the eighth-day bull.
The Gemara explains that the baraita teaches the principle that one who offered bulls today does not offer them tomorrow, but rather they rotate in a cycle.

items.text: Symbolism of the seventy bulls and the single bull
items.text_en: Symbolism of the seventy bulls and the single bull
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that the seventy bulls of Sukkot correspond to the seventy nations, and the single bull (of the eighth day) corresponds to the unique nation of Israel. He offers a parable of a king who prepares a great feast for his servants and a small feast for his friend. Rabbi Yochanan laments the nations who lost the Temple's atonement without realizing it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that the seventy bulls of Sukkot correspond to the seventy nations, and the single bull of the eighth day corresponds to the unique nation of Israel.
Rabbi Elazar offers a parable of a king who prepares a great feast for his servants and a small feast for his friend, illustrating the relationship between the seventy bulls and the single bull.
Rabbi Yochanan laments that the nations lost the Temple's atonement without realizing it, and asks who atones for them now that the Temple is destroyed.

items.text: Mishnah: Equal sharing of festival offerings and showbread
items.text_en: Mishnah: Equal sharing of festival offerings and showbread
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that during the three pilgrimage festivals, all priestly watches are equal in the distribution of the sacrificial portions of the festival offerings and the showbread. On Shavuot, the watch whose time is fixed offers the daily offerings, vows, and other communal sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in three periods of the year all priestly watches are equal regarding the sacrificial portions of the festivals and the distribution of the showbread, and that the watch whose time is fixed offers all regular and voluntary offerings.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of equal sharing for festival portions and showbread
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of equal sharing for festival portions and showbread
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that 'אימרי הרגלים' refers to what is said about the festivals, not the offerings themselves. A baraita derives from Deuteronomy 18:6-8 that all watches are equal in the festival portions, but only when all Israel enters through one gate (i.e., during the pilgrimage). Another baraita derives the same for the showbread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'אימרי הרגלים' (the portions of the festivals), noting that these portions belong to the Most High (i.e., they are offered on the altar), not to the priests for distribution.
Rav Chisda answers that the Mishnah means 'what is said about the festivals' (i.e., the verses that discuss the festival offerings), not the offerings themselves.
A baraita derives from Deuteronomy 18:6-8 that all priestly watches are equal in the festival portions, but only when all Israel enters through one gate (i.e., during the pilgrimage festivals).
Another baraita derives that all priestly watches are equal in the distribution of the showbread.

items.text: Derivation of showbread division rule
items.text_en: Derivation of showbread division rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a verse that the division of the showbread follows the division of the service, and clarifies that this refers to the showbread, not other offerings. It then limits this rule to regular festival offerings, excluding voluntary offerings brought on the festival.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'חֵלֶק כְּחֵלֶק יֹאכֵלוּ' that the division of the showbread follows the division of the service, and clarifies that this refers to the showbread, not other offerings.

The Gemara limits the rule to regular festival offerings, excluding voluntary offerings brought on the festival, by citing the verse 'לְבַד מִמְכָּרָיו עַל הָאָבוֹת' and the analogy of the fathers' agreement about their respective Sabbaths.

items.text: Dispute on order of blessings for Sukkot
items.text_en: Dispute on order of blessings for Sukkot
items.desc_en: A dispute is recorded between Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chanah regarding the order of blessings on Sukkot: Rav says to recite the blessing on the sukkah first, then the blessing on the time (shehecheyanu), while Rabbah bar bar Chanah says the opposite. Each provides a reason: Rav prioritizes the day's obligation, Rabbah bar bar Chanah prioritizes the more frequent blessing.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the Mishnah's rule about the order of items on Shavuot and then records the dispute between Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chanah regarding the order of blessings on Sukkot.
Rav explains his position: the blessing on the sukkah comes first because the day's obligation (חיובא דיומא) takes precedence.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah explains his position: the blessing of the time (shehecheyanu) comes first because it is more frequent (תדיר) and the frequent precedes the infrequent.

items.text: Comparison to Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute
items.text_en: Comparison to Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chanah's dispute parallels a Tannaitic dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about the order of blessings on wine and the day. Beit Shammai says bless the day first because the day causes the wine to come, while Beit Hillel says bless the wine first because it is more frequent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chanah parallels a Tannaitic dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
The baraita introduces the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the order of blessings on the day and wine.
Beit Shammai argues that the day is blessed first because the day causes the wine to come, and the day is already sanctified while wine has not yet arrived.
Beit Hillel argues that wine is blessed first because wine causes the kiddush to be recited, and alternatively because the blessing over wine is more frequent (תָּדִיר) and takes precedence.

items.text: Rejection of the parallel
items.text_en: Rejection of the parallel
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the parallel: Rav can hold like Beit Hillel because there the reason is that wine causes the sanctification, but here without the time blessing one would still say the sukkah blessing. Similarly, Rabbah bar bar Chanah can hold like Beit Shammai because there the day causes the wine, but here without the sukkah one would still say the time blessing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rav's and Rabbah bar bar Chanah's dispute parallels the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the order of blessings over the day and wine.

Rav rejects the parallel, arguing that even Beit Hillel would agree with him here because in their case wine causes the sanctification, but here without the time blessing one would still say the sukkah blessing.

Rabbah bar bar Chanah rejects the parallel, arguing that even Beit Shammai would agree with him here because in their case the day causes the wine, but here without the sukkah one would still say the time blessing.

items.text: Challenge to Rav from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav from the Mishnah which says on Shavuot one says 'take matzah, take chametz,' implying matzah is mentioned first even though chametz is primary. Rav responds that this is a Tannaic dispute, as Abba Shaul says the opposite order.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav from the Mishnah which says on Shavuot one says 'take matzah, take chametz,' implying matzah is mentioned first even though chametz is primary, which contradicts Rav's ruling.
Rav responds that this is a Tannaic dispute, citing a baraita where the first Tanna says 'take matzah, take chametz' while Abba Shaul says the opposite order.

items.text: Final ruling on the order
items.text_en: Final ruling on the order
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda rules like Rabbah bar bar Chanah (time first, then sukkah), but Rav Sheishet the son of Rav Idi rules like Rav (sukkah first, then time). The halakha is decided in favor of Rav: sukkah first, then time.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda rules against Rav, stating that the blessing of time (שהחיינו) precedes the blessing of sukkah.

sub.text: Rav Sheishet bar Rav Idi's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Sheishet bar Rav Idi's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet bar Rav Idi rules like Rav, that the blessing of sukkah precedes the blessing of time.
The final halakha is decided in favor of Rav: the blessing of sukkah is recited before the blessing of time (שהחיינו).

items.text: Clarification of Mishnah terms
items.text_en: Clarification of Mishnah terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's phrase 'the watch whose time is fixed' and 'the rest of the communal offerings' – the latter includes the bull for an unwitting communal sin and the goats for idolatry. 'He offers all' includes the additional free-will offerings (keitz hamizbe'ach).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'the watch whose time is fixed' and 'the rest of the communal offerings' comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it includes the bull for an unwitting communal sin and the goats for idolatry.
The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'he offers all' comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it includes the additional free-will offerings (קֵייץ הַמִּזְבֵּחַ).

items.text: Mishnah: Division of showbread when festival adjacent to Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Division of showbread when festival adjacent to Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when a festival falls adjacent to Shabbat (either before or after), all watches share equally in the showbread. If there is one day in between, the watch whose time is fixed takes ten loaves and the delayed watch takes two. The Gemara clarifies that 'before' and 'after' refer to the last and first days of the festival, and explains the reason: so that the watches can eat together.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for dividing showbread when a festival is adjacent to Shabbat, and when there is a day in between, and the general rule for other times, with Rabbi Yehuda's dissenting opinion.
The Mishnah describes the division location for entering and exiting watches, and the special status of the Bilgah watch.
The Gemara asks what 'before' and 'after' mean, and rejects the interpretation that they refer to the first and last festival days, as that would be Shabbat within the festival.
The Gemara explains that 'before' means the last festival day and 'after' means the first festival day, and the reason is so that the watches can eat together.

items.text: Continuation of Mishnah: one day between
items.text_en: Continuation of Mishnah: one day between
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues with the case where there is one day between the festival and Shabbat, leading to the division of ten and two loaves.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case where there is one day between the festival and Shabbat, leading to the division of ten and two loaves.

items.text: Gemara's question about the two watches and Rabbi Yitzchak's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the two watches and Rabbi Yitzchak's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the two watches (the outgoing and incoming) do together. Rabbi Yitzchak answers that they receive reward for closing the doors. The Gemara suggests they could simply say 'close the door' (without reward), but Abaye explains that a lamp (the incoming watch) is better than a mere reading (the outgoing watch's role).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the two watches (the outgoing and incoming) do together.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers that they receive reward for closing the doors.
The Gemara suggests they could simply say 'close the door' (without reward).
Abaye explains that a lamp (the incoming watch) is better than a mere reading (the outgoing watch's role).

items.text: Rav Yehuda's statement and its refutation
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that the watches divide the additional offerings (musafin). The Gemara brings a baraita that lists what the outgoing and incoming watches do but does not mention dividing musafin, implying a contradiction. Rava then cites the baraita of the school of Shmuel, which also omits dividing musafin, leading to a conclusive refutation of Rav Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that the priestly watches divide the additional offerings (מוספין).

The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists the duties of the outgoing and incoming watches but does not mention dividing the additional offerings, implying that Rav Yehuda's statement is contradicted.

sub.text: Rava's refutation with the baraita of the school of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rava's refutation with the baraita of the school of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rava cites the baraita of the school of Shmuel, which explicitly deals with division of duties yet also omits dividing the additional offerings, thereby conclusively refuting Rav Yehuda's statement.

items.text: The rule of the entering and exiting watches dividing in the north and south
items.text_en: The rule of the entering and exiting watches dividing in the north and south
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: the entering watch divides in the north to show they are entering, and the exiting watch divides in the south to show they are exiting.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that the entering watch divides in the north and the exiting watch divides in the south, to make their movements visible.

items.text: The case of Bilgah: always divides in the south
items.text_en: The case of Bilgah: always divides in the south
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the watch of Bilgah always divides in the south as a penalty. It recounts the story of Miriam bat Bilgah, who apostatized, married a Greek officer, and kicked the altar, cursing it. The Sages responded by fixing her ring and sealing her window.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the ruling that the watch of Bilgah always divides in the south as a penalty.
A baraita recounts the story of Miriam bat Bilgah, who apostatized, married a Greek officer, kicked the altar, and cursed it, leading the Sages to fix her ring and seal her window as a penalty.

items.text: Alternative explanation: Yeshevav served in Bilgah's place
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Yeshevav served in Bilgah's place
items.desc_en: Some say that Bilgah's watch was delayed in arriving, so his brother Yeshevav entered and served in his place. Although neighbors of the wicked do not usually benefit, Bilgah's neighbors (Yeshevav's watch) did benefit: Bilgah always divides in the south, while Yeshevav divides in the north.

sub.desc_en: Yesh Omrim explains that Bilgah's watch was delayed, so his brother Yeshevav served in his place, and as a result Bilgah always divides in the south while Yeshevav divides in the north.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the penalty and Abaye's explanations
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the penalty and Abaye's explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the two explanations: according to the one who says the watch was delayed, the entire watch is penalized; but according to the one who says it was due to Miriam's apostasy, why penalize the father for the daughter's sin? Abaye answers with a folk saying that a child's folly is attributed to parents. The Gemara then asks why the entire watch is penalized for the father and mother, and Abaye cites the principle that woe to the wicked and woe to his neighbor, while good to the righteous and good to his neighbor.
